Name: 1000 Schools
Description: The deal will see Power China and Sino Tech helping the Iraqi government’s plans to rebuild the education system after years of war.

Name: Abuja Light Rail
Description: The projected cost of the entire proposed 290 km (180 mi) network, to be developed in six phases, was US$824 million, constructed by China Civil Engineering Construction Corporation (CCECC), with 60% of the cost funded by loans from the Exim Bank of China. In fact, $840 million was spent on Lot 1 and 3, while $500 million was financed by a 2.5% p.a. loan from an Exim Bank of China. Repayment of the loan commenced in March 2020.

Name: Addis Ababa Light Rail Transit
Description: The Addis Ababa Light Rail Transit (AALRT) is the first urban light rail system in sub-Saharan Africa, consisting of two lines totalling 34.25 km: the North–South Line (16.9 km) and the East–West Line (17.35 km). Designed and built by China Railway Engineering Corporation (CREC) and financed with a $475 million loan from China Eximbank (covering 85% of the cost), the system was inaugurated on September 20, 2015. Each line operates at grade level through the city centre with a maximum design speed of 70 km/h and a capacity of up to 60,000 passengers per hour per direction. The rolling stock — 41 Alstom Citadis trams — were supplied by French manufacturer Alstom. As of 2024, the system continues to operate but has faced persistent challenges including overcrowding, maintenance difficulties, power outages, and inadequate integration with the city's broader public transport network. Chinese technicians remained involved in operations and training for years after handover. Ethiopia owes approximately $14 billion to China across all BRI-linked projects.

Name: Addis Ababa–Djibouti Railway
Description: The Addis Ababa–Djibouti Railway is a 759 km standard-gauge electrified railway linking Ethiopia's capital Addis Ababa to the Port of Doraleh in Djibouti — the first fully electrified transnational railway in Africa. Built by a joint consortium of China Railway Engineering Corporation (CREC) and China Civil Engineering Construction Corporation (CCECC), the line cost approximately $4.5 billion total, with $2.5 billion financed by China Eximbank (85% of Ethiopia's portion, 70% of Djibouti's portion). Construction commenced in 2012 and the railway was inaugurated in October 2016, with full commercial operations beginning in January 2018. The line cuts the journey from three days by road to around 10–12 hours by rail, and carries roughly a quarter of all Ethiopian imports and exports. The CREC-CCECC consortium managed the railway for six years before handing it to the Ethiopia-Djibouti Railway Share Company (EDR) in 2024. Ethiopia owes China approximately $14 billion across all railway and infrastructure loans — about half of its total foreign debt — and renegotiated debt repayments in 2019 to extend periods from 10 to 30 years. Freight volumes remain far below original targets of 20 million tonnes annually.

Name: Adelaide Ring Road (Chinese Construction Contract)
Description: In 2025 H1, a Chinese company was awarded a AUD $2.5 billion construction contract for the Adelaide Ring Road, a major highway infrastructure project in South Australia — making it one of the largest Chinese construction contracts in Australia and one of the most significant Chinese infrastructure engagements outside the formal BRI framework. Australia is not a BRI member country and has never signed a national BRI MoU with China. The Adelaide Ring Road contract was specifically highlighted in the Green Finance and Development Center's 2025 H1 BRI Investment Report as notable Chinese engagement "outside the BRI" — alongside a $423 million Indian road project — precisely because Australia remains one of the world's most significant recipients of Chinese infrastructure investment despite its explicit non-participation in the BRI. The project illustrates China's strategy of engaging in Australian infrastructure through commercial contracting arrangements, particularly as BRI-branded investment has become politically toxic in Australia since the 2021 cancellation of Victoria's BRI agreements and ongoing controversy over the Darwin Port lease.

Name: African Union Conference Center and Office Complex
Description: $200 million USD. Construction: 3 years. Workforce: 50% Ethiopian & 50% Chinese.

Name: Al-Khairat Heavy Oil Power Plant
Description: China’s CITIC Construction has been awarded a contract to develop the first and second phases of the 3,200MW Al-Khairat heavy oil power plant in Iraq

Name: Al-Mansuriya gas field
Description: Iraq's Oil Ministry, through the state-owned Midland Oil Company, has signed a preliminary agreement with a consortium comprising the Chinese companies Jereh Group and Petro Iraq (a unit of PetroChina) to develop the Al-Mansuriya gas field in the Diyala province, in eastern Iraq.

Name: Algeria Cherchell Ring Expressway
Description: The Cherchell Ring Expressway (also known as the East–West Expressway Western Extension or the Hauts Plateaux South Expressway) is a major road infrastructure project in Algeria built with Chinese involvement. Chinese companies, particularly China Railway Construction Corporation (CRCC) and CITIC Construction, have been major contractors in Algeria's broader expressway programme — the largest in North Africa — totalling over 1,200 km of new motorway. Algeria's road infrastructure programme began in 2006 and has seen approximately $11 billion invested, with Chinese firms winning a large share of contracts. CRCC was part of the consortium that built the central and western sections of Algeria's original East–West Highway. Chinese construction companies operate extensively across Algeria's road, rail, and housing sectors, with approximately 1,000 Chinese companies active in the country. Algeria joined the BRI in 2019 and is one of China's largest African partners in infrastructure. The country is also the site of the El Hamdania Central Port, China's flagship deepwater port project in North Africa.

Name: Amador Cruise Terminal
Description: The Amador Cruise Terminal was built by China Harbour Engineering Company (CHEC), a subsidiary of CCCC, in a consortium with Belgian firm Jan de Nul. Located at the Pacific entrance of the Panama Canal on the Amador Causeway, the terminal was constructed at a cost of approximately $165 million as part of China's growing infrastructure footprint around the Panama Canal following Panama's 2017 diplomatic switch from Taiwan to China and its signing of the Belt and Road Initiative. The terminal serves cruise ships and has been noted as a strategic asset given its proximity to the canal's Pacific entrance. Reports have indicated that liquefied petroleum gas tankers have also docked at the facility.

Name: Amu Darya Oil Basin (CNPC/CAPEIC)
Description: On January 5, 2023, the Taliban regime signed a 25-year oil extraction agreement with the Xinjiang Central Asia Petroleum and Gas Company (CAPEIC), a subsidiary of China National Petroleum Company (CNPC), for oil fields in the Amu Darya basin across Sar-e-Pul, Faryab, and Jowzjan provinces in northern Afghanistan. China will invest approximately $150 million annually for the first three years, rising to $540 million per year — a total commitment estimated at over $10 billion over the 25-year contract duration. This was the first major international energy contract signed by the Taliban government and represented China's cautious re-engagement with Afghanistan following the US withdrawal in August 2021. CAPEIC had previously operated in the Amu Darya basin under a 2011 agreement with the pre-Taliban government. Afghanistan joined the BRI in May 2023, making it the most recently signed BRI member, as part of the Taliban's strategy to integrate into Chinese-led economic frameworks and access infrastructure financing.

Name: Angren–Pap Electrified Railway (Qamchiq Tunnel)
Description: The Angren–Pap Electrified Railway is a 123 km mountain railway in Uzbekistan connecting Angren in the Tashkent region to Pap in the Namangan region through the Kamchik Pass in the western Tian Shan range, at elevations of up to 2,267 metres. It was built by China Railway Tunnel Group (CRTG) under a $1.5 billion EPC contract financed by China Eximbank and inaugurated in June 2016 by Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev and Chinese President Xi Jinping. The centrepiece is the 19.2 km Qamchiq Tunnel — the longest railway tunnel in Central Asia — passing directly beneath the Kamchik Pass. Before the line opened, the journey between Tashkent and the Fergana Valley required either a lengthy detour through Tajikistan or a hazardous mountain road crossing; the railway reduced the journey from 12 hours to 2.5 hours and eliminated dependence on Tajik territory. The project included 37 bridges, 6 tunnels, 32 underpasses, and a new electrification system. It is widely cited as one of the most successful BRI infrastructure projects in Central Asia. Uzbekistan joined the BRI in June 2015 and China is its largest trading partner.

Name: Antioquia Port
Description: The only approved port project in Uraba, which is being constructed near the banana plantations of the family of Governor Anibal Gaviria, which has all but monopolized the regional economy. Receiving credit from the China Co-financing Fund for Latin America and the Caribbean, a joint initiative of the Inter-American Development Bank (IADB) and the Bank of China.

Name: Bar–Boljare Highway
Description: The Bar–Boljare Highway (North-South Expressway) is Montenegro's largest infrastructure project since independence in 2006, planned as a 169 km motorway linking the Adriatic port city of Bar to the Montenegrin-Serbian border at Boljare, providing Montenegro's primary land connection to Central Europe. Phase 1 — the 41 km Smokovac–Mateševo section through mountainous terrain with 19 bridges and 16 tunnels — was built by China Road and Bridge Corporation (CRBC) under an EPC contract. It was financed by a $943.9 million China Eximbank preferential buyer's credit at 2% interest over 20 years, signed October 2014. The section opened on July 13, 2022. The IMF and World Bank opposed the loan due to Montenegro's sovereign debt levels; Moody's downgraded Montenegro's credit rating in response. The project has been widely criticised as financially unviable — two feasibility studies declared it non-profitable before construction began — and international media mocked Phase 1 for ending 'in the middle of nowhere', connecting no major urban or commercial centres. By 2024, Montenegro still owed approximately €655 million to China Eximbank for Phase 1 alone. Phase 2 (€694 million, Mateševo–Andrijevica) was awarded in February 2026 to Chinese consortium PowerChina-Stecol, but this time financed through EU funds rather than Chinese loans.

Name: Belgrade–Novi Sad Railway (Budapest–Belgrade Line)
Description: The Belgrade–Novi Sad Railway is the first high-speed railway in Serbia and the Serbian section of the Budapest–Belgrade Railway, which is widely regarded as the Belt and Road Initiative's most important infrastructure project in Europe. The 75 km section from Belgrade to Novi Sad was reconstructed by China Communications Construction Company (CCCC) and China Railway International (CRI) for approximately $350 million (Belgrade–Stara Pazova section) funded by China Eximbank. The full Serbian section of 183 km runs from Belgrade to Subotica on the Hungarian border, with total investment approximately $2 billion. The Belgrade–Novi Sad section opened on March 19, 2022, running at up to 200 km/h and reducing the journey from 90 minutes to 30 minutes. The complete Budapest–Belgrade line stretches 350 km, with China Eximbank lending $1.3 billion to Serbia and $1.8 billion to Hungary (85% of respective costs), over 20 years. The line forms part of a planned Belgrade–Budapest–Skopje–Athens freight and passenger corridor, connecting China's COSCO-operated Port of Piraeus in Greece to Central Europe. As of April 2026, Hungarian section final testing is underway. A fatal canopy collapse at Novi Sad station in November 2024 — linked to the BRI renovation works — triggered mass protests across Serbia demanding accountability.

Name: Belgrano Cargas Railway Rehabilitation
Description: The Belgrano Cargas Railway Rehabilitation Project is a $2.1 billion freight railway modernisation programme financed by China Development Bank (CDB) and ICBC. The project covers 3,000 km of metre-gauge track spanning 14 Argentine provinces from Buenos Aires to the Bolivian and Chilean borders. The EPC contractor is China Machinery Engineering Corporation (CMEC), with CRRC Corporation supplying 107 locomotives and 2,500 carriages. Construction started in December 2014 following the signing of a buyer's credit facility during President Xi Jinping's state visit to Argentina in July 2014. The loan carries a cross-default clause with the financing for the Santa Cruz Kirchner-Cepernic dams — meaning a default on one triggers a default on the other — a provision that forced President Macri to reverse his 2015 decision to cancel the dam project. As of May 2022, the railway had reached 77.96% completion. The railway connects major agricultural provinces to ports, improving export capacity for commodities such as soybeans, minerals, and grains. Argentina joined the BRI in February 2022.

Name: Belo Monte UHV Transmission Lines (State Grid)
Description: The Belo Monte Ultra-High Voltage (UHV) Transmission Lines are two 800 kV direct-current transmission lines stretching over 4,600 km from the Belo Monte hydroelectric dam in Pará State to Brazil's industrial Southeast. Chinese state-owned utility State Grid Corporation of China built and operates both lines through its Brazilian subsidiary IE Belo Monte. The first line was won at auction in 2011 for approximately $1.5 billion; the second in 2015 for approximately $1.78 billion. For the second line, State Grid's consortium — comprising State Grid (51%), Furnas (24.5%), and Eletronorte (24.5%) — was the first to exclude Western companies entirely. The combined project represents one of the longest UHV transmission systems in the world and delivers power from Brazil's largest hydroelectric dam (11,233 MW installed capacity) to the Southeast, which accounts for nearly 70% of national energy consumption. State Grid is the largest Chinese investor in Brazil, representing 56% of total Chinese power sector investment in the country. Brazil is not a formal BRI member but is aligned with BRI principles.

Name: Biblioteca Nacional de El Salvador (BINAES)
Description: The Biblioteca Nacional de El Salvador (BINAES) is a seven-storey, 24,000 m² national library located on Plaza Barrios in the historic center of San Salvador, adjacent to the National Palace and across from the Metropolitan Cathedral. It was built as a non-reimbursable donation by the People's Republic of China, with a total value of $54 million (including equipment and books), plus a $10 million co-contribution from the Salvadoran government. The contractor was YanJian Group, a Chinese state-linked construction company. Construction began on February 3, 2022 and the library was inaugurated by President Nayib Bukele on November 14, 2023. It stands on the former site of the Francisco Gavidia National Library, which was demolished in October 2021 to make way for it. The project originated from Bukele's December 2019 state visit to China, where President Xi Jinping committed $500 million in non-reimbursable cooperation funds. BINAES is the first national library in the world to operate 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. It has a capacity for over 360,000 books and is expected to receive 5,000 daily visitors. Facilities span seven floors and include a gaming zone, robotics lab, virtual reality simulators, 3D printers, LEGO zone, auditorium, café, gift shop, art gallery, observation deck, and spaces for early childhood education. The El Salvador government classified all financial details of the project under a seven-year confidentiality agreement between the China International Economic Cooperation Agency and El Salvador's Ministry of Culture, citing national defense and public safety.

Name: Big Cypress Tree
Description: Big Cypress Tree State Park is named for the national champion bald cypress tree that once lived in the park. The tree was the largest bald cypress in the United States and the largest tree of any species east of the Mississippi River. In 1976, during a lightning storm, a strike caused the tree to die after living for more than 1,350 years.

Name: Big Hill Pond
Description: Big Hill Pond State Park is located in the southwestern part of McNairy County and encompasses 4,138 acres of timberland and hardwood bottomland. Cypress Creek and Tuscumbia River border the property. The flood plain, adjacent to the river and creek contains small oxbows and swampy areas which are desirable habitat for waterfowl, wildlife and fish.
Features: camping; birding; boat-rentals; canoe-access; hiking-trails; bike-trails; fishing; horseback-riding

Name: Bled El Hadba mine
Description: Located in Tébessa Province. One of the largest phosphates reserve: estimated reserves of 800 million tonnes of ore grading 15% Phosphorus pentoxide.

Name: Bogotá Metro Line 1
Description: Bogotá Metro Line 1 is a 23.9 km elevated metro line — the first in Bogotá's history — awarded in 2019 to a Chinese consortium comprising China Harbour Engineering Company (CHEC) and Xi'an Metro Company under a 26-year design, build, finance, operate, and maintain (DBFOM) contract. It is the largest single infrastructure project in Latin America won by Chinese companies through international competitive bidding. The line will have 16 stations connecting Portal de las Américas to Calle 72, with 10 stations connecting to Bogotá's Transmilenio BRT network. Rolling stock is supplied exclusively by CRRC Changchun — 30 fully automated, self-driving trains with an Andean condor-inspired design, each carrying up to 1,220 passengers. Chinese financing includes a $515 million package closed in November 2024: a $230 million facility from Bank of China and ICBC and a COP 1.2 trillion peso tranche from local lenders. Upon completion in 2028, the line is expected to carry 130,000 passengers daily. Colombia signed a BRI MoU in May 2025. CCECC, a subsidiary of China Railway Construction Corporation, is the general EPC contractor.

Name: Boten–Vientiane railway
Description: The Boten–Vientiane railway is an integral section of the central line on the Kunming–Singapore (Pan-Asian Railway). It is estimated to cost US$5.95 billion with 70% of the railway owned by China, while Laos's remaining 30% stake will be mostly financed by loans from China

Name: Brazil–Peru Twin Ocean Railway (Proposed)
Description: The Brazil–Peru Twin Ocean Railway, also known as the Bi-Oceanic Railway or Trans-South American Railway, is a proposed 3,000 km freight rail corridor linking Brazil's Atlantic coast (Port of Santos) to Peru's Port of Chancay on the Pacific, passing through Bolivia. The project aims to create a direct overland trade route from South America to Asia, bypassing the Panama Canal and dramatically reducing shipping times and costs for Brazilian commodities such as soybeans and iron ore. Chinese President Xi Jinping and Peruvian President Boluarte discussed the project during Xi's November 2024 state visit to inaugurate the Port of Chancay. Brazil and China signed a Memorandum of Understanding on July 7, 2025 to initiate joint technical, economic, and environmental feasibility studies, expected to take up to five years. The China Development Bank and the New Development Bank (BRICS) are identified as potential financing institutions. The estimated cost of the rail segment is $3.5 billion. Environmental groups and indigenous rights organizations have raised concerns about deforestation and displacement of communities along the proposed Amazon corridor. Brazil is not formally a BRI member but signed a cooperation alignment agreement with China in 2025.

Name: Budapest-Belgrade Railway
Description: Financed through a Chinese loan. Nonetheless, the rail project linking the capitals of Hungary and Serbia has widely been criticized for its lack of transparency, the risk of corruption, and the potential for a debt trap, although that latter has been debunked as being unsubstantiated due to limited evidence. Once completed, the railway would only serve for cargo transportation and help bring Chinese goods from the Port of Piraeus in Greece to Central Europe.

Name: Bui Dam
Description: $622 million USD. 400-megawatt (540,000 hp) hydroelectric project in Ghana. It is built on the Black Volta river at the Bui Gorge, at the southern end of Bui National Park. The project was a collaboration between the government of Ghana and Sino Hydro, a Chinese state-owned construction company. Construction on the main dam began in December 2009. Its first generator was commissioned on 3 May 2013, and the dam was inaugurated in December of the same year.

Name: CPFL Energia Acquisition (State Grid)
Description: In 2017, Chinese state-owned utility State Grid Corporation of China acquired a majority stake in Companhia Paulista de Força e Luz (CPFL), one of Brazil's largest electric utility companies, for approximately $12.2 billion — the single largest transaction by any Chinese energy firm globally at the time. CPFL operates across generation, transmission, and distribution in Brazil, with assets in hydro, wind, biomass, oil, and solar power, and a total installed capacity of approximately 4.3 GW. Through CPFL, State Grid became active in all five of Brazil's regions, with transmission lines crossing the country and distribution assets serving millions of customers. The acquisition cemented State Grid as the largest Chinese investor in Brazil and in Latin America. State Grid's total Brazilian investment represents approximately 56% of all Chinese power sector investment in the country. Brazil is not a formal BRI member but has deepened its infrastructure and energy cooperation with China under bilateral and BRICS frameworks.

Name: CRRC Mexico City Light Rail
Description: China Railway Rolling Stock Corporation (CRRC), a Chinese state-owned manufacturer and major Belt and Road Initiative participant, won the contract to supply 17 electric light rail units for Mexico City's Electric Transportation Authority (STE). The first CRRC-built light rail train, named 'Cecilia', entered public service in January 2024. The trains were designed and manufactured by CRRC Zhuzhou Electric Locomotive Co., Ltd. Each unit has a maximum operating speed of 80 km/h and a capacity of approximately 876 passengers in a four-car formation. The contract represents the first time CRRC rolling stock has served Mexico City, marking a milestone in the modernization of public transportation in the Mexican capital.

Name: Cat Linh–Ha Dong Metro, Hanoi
Description: The Cat Linh–Ha Dong Metro (Hanoi Metro Line 2A) is Vietnam's first metro line to enter commercial operation, an 13.1 km elevated light rail connecting Cat Linh station in central Hanoi to Yen Nghia in Ha Dong district across 12 stations. It is the only infrastructure project in Vietnam to have been financed by China's Export-Import Bank, through a Chinese ODA preferential loan framework signed on May 30, 2008. The original total investment was $552.86 million — $419 million from China Eximbank loans and $133.86 million from the Vietnamese government. After multiple delays and cost overruns, total investment rose to approximately $868 million. The primary contractor was China Railway Sixth Group Co. Ltd (a subsidiary of CREC). Rolling stock — 13 four-car trainsets — was supplied by Beijing Subway Rolling Stock Equipment Ltd. Construction began October 2011 with an original completion date of 2015; completion was delayed at least six times. The line finally opened commercially on November 6, 2021 — six years late. The project was plagued by construction accidents, poor safety standards, and multiple worker fatalities. Vietnam has been deeply reluctant to take on further Chinese BRI financing, preferring Japanese ODA for subsequent metro lines. Vietnam is a BRI member (signed 2017) but has kept its formal BRI engagement minimal.

Name: Central Asia–China Gas Pipeline (Turkmenistan)
Description: The Central Asia–China Gas Pipeline is the world's longest natural gas pipeline system, running approximately 1,833 km from Turkmenistan's Galkynysh gas field — the world's second-largest natural gas reserve with proven reserves of 26.2 trillion cubic metres — through Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan to China's Xinjiang region. Lines A, B, and C are operational, transporting approximately 55 billion cubic metres (bcm) of natural gas to China annually, accounting for roughly 15% of China's total gas supply. Line D, planned to run via Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan, stalled in 2016 due to financing disputes and unresolved right-of-way issues. The pipeline system is operated by Central Asia Gas Pipeline Co. Ltd (CAGP), a joint venture between CNPC and the national oil companies of Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, and Kazakhstan. China has invested over $8 billion in the pipeline. Turkmenistan joined the BRI in June 2017 and sends nearly all of its gas exports to China, making the pipeline the single most important asset in its economy and cementing its deep economic dependence on Beijing.

Name: Cheddi Jagan International Airport Expansion (CHEC)
Description: China Harbour Engineering Company (CHEC), a subsidiary of China Communications Construction Company (CCCC) and a key BRI contractor, won the contract to expand and modernise Cheddi Jagan International Airport in Guyana in 2011, at a cost of $150 million financed through the Inter-American Development Bank. The project involved the construction of a new terminal building and upgrades to the runway and facilities. However, the project took over 10 years to complete — far longer than planned — and was plagued by complaints of shoddy materials, poor quality workmanship, and environmental health and safety violations. CHEC has since become the dominant Chinese construction firm in Guyana, winning contracts for roads, bridges, hotel renovations (including a $100 million expansion of the Pegasus Hotel in Georgetown), and other public works. Guyana signed a BRI MoU with China in August 2018, and China's CNOOC entered as a 25% partner in the ExxonMobil-led oil consortium following the 2015 discovery of over 25 billion barrels of recoverable oil. As of 2023, Guyana is China's leading trade partner in the Caribbean region.

Name: Chico River Pump Irrigation Project
Description: The Chico River Pump Irrigation Project is a Chinese-financed BRI irrigation project in Kalinga and Cagayan provinces in northern Luzon, Philippines. It is one of the only Chinese BRI infrastructure projects in the Philippines to reach completion, amid broader failure of a pipeline of 'Build, Build, Build' infrastructure deals negotiated under President Rodrigo Duterte (2016–2022). The project was financed by a $62 million concessional loan from China's Export-Import Bank at 2% interest over 20 years, signed in October 2018 and is one of the two ODA loans Duterte's government secured from China Eximbank. The project was constructed by China National Machinery Industry Corporation (SINOMACH) and irrigates approximately 8,700 hectares of agricultural land across the Chico River basin, benefiting approximately 7,000 farming households. It was completed in 2021. The Philippines signed the BRI MoU in November 2017 during Duterte's state visit to Beijing. However, the Philippines' BRI engagement has been severely limited by sovereignty disputes in the South China Sea, security concerns about Chinese state entities, and constitutional constraints on foreign-financed infrastructure. Of the $24 billion worth of Chinese infrastructure projects agreed under Duterte, virtually none advanced to construction. The Chico River irrigation project stands as one of the few tangible BRI outcomes in the Philippines.

Name: China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan Railway
Description: The China–Kyrgyzstan–Uzbekistan Railway (CKU Railway) is a planned 523 km standard-gauge railway connecting Kashgar in China's Xinjiang region, through the Fergana Valley via Kyrgyzstan, to Andijan in Uzbekistan — one of the most strategically significant BRI rail projects in Central Asia. After over two decades of stalled negotiations dating back to 1997, a tripartite intergovernmental agreement was finally signed by China, Kyrgyzstan, and Uzbekistan in June 2023, with a feasibility study agreement following in May 2024. Total estimated cost is approximately $8 billion. The Kyrgyz section (~260 km) traverses the Tian Shan mountain range, requiring extensive tunnels and viaducts; China is expected to finance and build this section through policy bank loans. The line would cut China–Uzbekistan freight transit time from 7–10 days via Kazakhstan to approximately 2 days, bypassing Russia and Kazakhstan entirely. Kyrgyzstan joined the BRI in December 2013. The CKU Railway also forms a key link in the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route connecting China to Turkey and Europe.

Name: China–Nepal Cross-Border Railway (Kerung–Kathmandu)
Description: The China–Nepal Cross-Border Railway (Kerung–Kathmandu Railway) is a proposed 163 km standard-gauge electrified railway connecting Kerung (Gyirong) on the China–Nepal border in Tibet to Kathmandu, Nepal's capital, forming the core of the Trans-Himalayan Multi-dimensional Connectivity Network — one of the BRI's six official overland economic corridors. Nepal signed the BRI MoU in May 2017 and signed the 'Framework for Belt and Road Cooperation' in December 2024 during Prime Minister KP Sharma Oli's state visit to Beijing. A pre-feasibility study was completed by China Railway First Survey and Design Institute Group. A new China-funded detailed study is underway, with aerial surveys completed as of 2024; drilling and soil testing are expected in 2026. The railway would traverse some of the world's most challenging terrain, requiring extensive tunnelling through the Himalayas at elevations above 4,000 metres and crossing multiple active fault lines. If built, it would transform Nepal from a landlocked country to a land-linked transit nation connecting South Asia and China, dramatically reducing freight costs. Nepal currently relies entirely on India for surface access to global markets. The estimated construction cost exceeds $8 billion. The project faces enormous engineering, geological, and debt-sustainability challenges. Nepal insists on grant financing rather than loans, while China has proposed a mix, creating ongoing negotiation friction.

Name: China–Oman Industrial Park (Duqm SEZ)
Description: The China–Oman Industrial Park at Duqm Special Economic Zone (SEZ) is one of China's flagship BRI 'industrial park–port interconnection' projects in the Middle East. Located in Duqm on Oman's southeastern coast, the zone is being developed by Oman Wanfang, a consortium of six Chinese private companies from China's Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region. China has committed approximately $11 billion to the Duqm SEZ, which the Chinese government has designated as one of its official 'Top Overseas Industrial Parks'. Duqm is strategically located outside the Strait of Hormuz, making it a lower-risk energy export hub compared to Gulf ports. The industrial park is designed to attract Chinese manufacturers in sectors including petroleum equipment, chemicals, building materials, machinery, and light manufacturing. The port complex includes Duqm Port, a deep-water facility capable of handling Very Large Crude Carriers (VLCCs). Oman Wanfang's involvement is notable for being a private Chinese regional consortium rather than a central government SOE, driven partly by Ningxia's large Muslim Hui population and its ambition to serve as a gateway for China–Arab trade. Oman signed the BRI MoU in May 2018. The Duqm project forms one of four park–port complexes identified by China as key to its Middle East BRI strategy, alongside Khalifa Port (UAE), Jazan City (Saudi Arabia), and TEDA–Suez (Egypt).

Name: China–Venezuela Joint Fund Infrastructure Programme
Description: Venezuela received approximately $60 billion in Chinese state loans between 2007 and 2016, primarily through the China–Venezuela Joint Fund (CVJF), the world's largest commodity-backed bilateral loan programme at the time. The loans were provided by China Development Bank (CDB) and repaid through Venezuelan crude oil shipments to China at negotiated prices — a 'pre-paid oil sale' mechanism. The fund financed over 200 infrastructure and industrial projects, including metro systems in Caracas, Valencia, Los Teques, and Maracaibo; power plants including TermoCarabobo I (El Palito); highway construction; housing; cement factories; and the Tocoma hydroelectric plant. In September 2018, Venezuela signed a BRI MoU with China. However, the collapse of Venezuela's economy, the fall in oil prices after 2014, and US sanctions on PDVSA caused Venezuela to fall into severe arrears on its Chinese debt. As of 2025, Venezuela's outstanding debt to China is estimated at $10–12 billion, down from a peak of over $20 billion. Most infrastructure projects financed by the CVJF were never completed.

Name: Coca Codo Sinclair Dam
Description: The dam was constructed by Chinese engineering firm Sinohydro Corporation for $2.25 billion. The plant became fully operational in November 2016, It has a capacity of 1,500 megawatts.

Name: Coca Codo Sinclair Hydroelectric Plant
Description: The Coca Codo Sinclair Hydroelectric Plant is Ecuador's largest infrastructure project in history, located on the Coca River in Napo Province, 100 km east of Quito. It has an installed capacity of 1,500 MW and was designed to supply approximately 30–35% of Ecuador's annual electricity consumption. Built by Chinese state-owned Sinohydro Corporation under a $1.98 billion EPC contract, it was financed by a $1.68 billion loan from China's Export-Import Bank (Eximbank) at 6.9% fixed interest over 15 years, signed in June 2010. Construction began in July 2010 and the plant was inaugurated on November 18, 2016 by Presidents Rafael Correa and Xi Jinping. Total cost reached approximately $3.2 billion. The project has since become one of the most controversial Chinese infrastructure investments in Latin America: over 17,000 cracks were found in the powerhouse distributor pipes; 14 workers were killed in a 2014 tunnel collapse; Ecuador initiated international arbitration against Sinohydro in 2021 seeking $580 million in damages; and severe regressive erosion on the Coca River is advancing toward the dam. In 2024, Ecuador reached a settlement with PowerChina (Sinohydro's parent) for $400 million in compensation. Former President Lenín Moreno was charged with accepting bribes related to the project. Ecuador joined the BRI in June 2025.

Name: Corentyne River Bridge (Guyana–Suriname)
Description: Guyana and Suriname jointly selected China Road and Bridge Corporation (CRBC) — a subsidiary of CCCC — to construct a $236 million bridge over the Corentyne River, announced in December 2024. The 1.1 km bridge will link Moleson Creek in Guyana with South Drain in Suriname, and is intended to eventually form part of a broader connectivity corridor linking French Guiana and Brazil, integrating South America's northeast coastal region. Both countries are expected to share costs equally, with financing sought from the Chinese government. The bridge has a planned 100-year lifespan. Critics have raised concerns about debt sustainability for Suriname (which already owes approximately $1 billion to Chinese state banks), as well as CRBC's international track record of contractual breaches and cost overruns. The project is expected to significantly boost bilateral trade and regional integration when completed. Construction is contingent on finalising financing arrangements.

Name: Costa Rica Highway Upgrades (China Cooperation)
Description: Following Costa Rica's decision to sever ties with Taiwan in 2007 and establish diplomatic relations with China, a series of road and highway infrastructure projects were undertaken with Chinese cooperation and financing. Costa Rica became the second Central American country (after Panama) to sign a Belt and Road Initiative agreement with China in 2018. Chinese cooperation in Costa Rica's road infrastructure has included upgrades to key highway corridors. Costa Rica has also been noted as a destination for China's 'new infrastructure' investments, including technology and high-end manufacturing. The Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) has been considered as a potential financing vehicle for further infrastructure in the country. Costa Rica also signed a free trade agreement with China, which came into force in 2011, making it the first Central American country to do so.

Name: Cumberland Mountain State Park
Description: Cumberland Mountain State Park is situated on the Cumberland Plateau, a segment of the great upland, which extends from western New York to central Alabama. It is said to be the largest timbered plateau in America. Cumberland Mountain State Park began as part of the greater Cumberland Homesteads Project, a New Deal-era initiative by the Resettlement Administration that helped relocate poverty-stricken families on the Cumberland Plateau to small farms centered on what is now the Cumberland Homestead community. This 1,720-acre park was acquired in 1938 to provide a recreational area for some 250 families selected to homestead on the Cumberland Plateau.
Features: camping; cabins; hiking-trails; canoe-access; swim-beaches; bike-trails; golfing; fishing; birding

Name: Dar es Salaam Port Upgrade
Description: The Port of Dar es Salaam, Tanzania's primary Indian Ocean gateway, has undergone significant infrastructure upgrades with Chinese involvement and financing under the BRI framework. Upgrade works totalling approximately $500 million have included berth deepening and extension, new container handling equipment, expansion of container terminal capacity, and construction of roll-on/roll-off facilities. The port is the anchor of Tanzania's Central Corridor, the primary transit route for landlocked Burundi, Rwanda, Uganda, DRC, and Zambia. China Merchants Port Holdings (one of the world's largest port operators) has been involved in discussions about port management and concession arrangements in Tanzania. In 2024, Tanzania and China Merchants Group signed an agreement related to petroleum storage construction at the port. Tanzania signed the BRI MoU in 2011 and has received substantial Chinese investment across port, railway, and industrial infrastructure. Dar es Salaam Port handles approximately 95% of Tanzania's international trade and is central to the country's SGR railway integration strategy.

Name: Debrecen CATL Battery Plant
Description: CATL, or Contemporary Amperex Technology Co Ltd, announced its 7.6-billion-euro ($8.2 billion) investment in Hungary in August 2022 to build a 100 gigawatt-hour battery plant in Debrecen, the second largest city in Hungary. The project, located in the city's Southern Industrial Park, will supply battery cells and modules to European EV makers.

Name: Demerara River Bridge & East Coast Highway (CRCC)
Description: China Railway Construction Corporation (CRCC) — a Chinese state-owned enterprise that was blacklisted by the World Bank in 2019 for fraud and corruption — was awarded a $260 million contract to build a new bridge over the Demerara River in Georgetown, Guyana, in a joint venture with China Railway Construction Company and China Railway Construction Bridge Engineering Bureau Group. The project, funded through China Eximbank, replaces a century-old pontoon bridge and will dramatically improve traffic flow in and around Guyana's capital. Separately, in 2022, China Railway First Group was awarded a $184 million China Eximbank-funded contract to expand the East Coast highway and rail system. Guyana has also been negotiating up to $600 million in additional road projects with Chinese firms. Guyana signed the BRI MoU in 2018, and Chinese construction firms have become dominant players in the country's oil-boom-driven infrastructure expansion, raising concerns about quality, debt sustainability, and dual-use potential given proximity to strategic maritime routes.

Name: Dushanbe-2 Power Plant
Description: The power plant was commissioned in January 2014 after the construction of the first phase of 50 MW. The second phase of the construction added another 50 MW to the plant installed capacity and was commissioned in November 2014. The third phase of the construction added another 300 MW and was commissioned in 2016.

Name: Dushanbe-2 Power Plant
Description: The power plant was commissioned in January 2014 after the construction of the first phase of 50 MW. The second phase of the construction added another 50 MW to the plant installed capacity and was commissioned in November 2014. The third phase of the construction added another 300 MW and was commissioned in 2016.

Name: East–West Highway
Description: The Central and Western sections of the road were built by a consortium of China Railway Construction Corporation and CITIC while the Eastern section was constructed by a Japanese consortium of Kajima Corporation, Nishimatsu Construction Company, Itochu Corporation, Hazama Corporation and Taisei Corporation.

Name: Ecuador Hydroelectric Programme (China-Financed)
Description: As part of President Rafael Correa's ambitious energy transition programme to shift Ecuador away from fossil fuels, China's state-owned financial institutions financed six of eight major hydroelectric projects built between 2008 and 2018. In addition to the Coca Codo Sinclair dam, China's Export-Import Bank (Eximbank) financed the Sopladora (487 MW) and Minas San Francisco (275 MW) projects, while China Development Bank (CDB) financed Delsitanisagua (180 MW), Quijos (50 MW), and Mazar Dudas (21 MW). Chinese companies — including Consorcio CGGC (Sopladora), Harbin Electric International (Minas San Francisco), Hydrochina Corp (Delsitanisagua), and China National Electric Engineering Co. (Quijos and Mazar Dudas) — held EPC contracts for seven of the eight projects. Combined, these plants were intended to generate over 2,400 MW of clean energy and eliminate Ecuador's dependence on expensive diesel-fired thermal power. However, most projects faced delays, accidents, and engineering problems. Ecuador repaid Chinese loans partly through oil exports at a discount, with China importing up to 80% of Ecuador's oil at peak years. The loans totalled approximately $19 billion across the entire energy-for-oil programme.

Name: Edirne–Kars High-Speed Rail (Turkey–China BRI Corridor)
Description: The Edirne–Kars High-Speed Rail is a planned high-speed railway traversing the full length of Turkey from Edirne on the Bulgarian border to Kars near the Armenian-Georgian border, forming a critical component of China's Belt and Road Initiative through Turkey's Middle Corridor. The project is jointly planned by Turkey's State Railways (TCDD) and China's Ministry of Transport, with a Memorandum of Understanding signed between the two ministries. Extending approximately 3,000 km across Anatolia, the line will integrate with the Baku–Tbilisi–Kars (BTK) Railway — the 'Iron Silk Road' linking Turkey, Georgia, and Azerbaijan — and connect to the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR) onward to Central Asia and China. Turkey signed a BRI MoU in November 2015 and President Erdoğan reaffirmed his strong support for the initiative during a 2019 state visit to China, targeting bilateral trade of $100 billion. The Edirne–Kars corridor forms part of the China–Central Asia–West Asia Economic Corridor — one of the BRI's six official overland economic corridors — and would integrate with the Marmaray subsea tunnel under the Bosphorus, the Yavuz Sultan Selim Bridge, and Istanbul Airport, all of which are already operational. When complete, China–Europe container trains will be able to transit the entire Turkey corridor at high speed rather than using slower conventional tracks, dramatically cutting transit times along the emerging Central Corridor alternative to the Russian Northern Route, which has been disrupted by sanctions following the 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

Name: Egypt Suez Canal Economic Zone (Chinese Industrial Park)
Description: The Suez Canal Economic Zone (SCZone) Chinese Industrial Park is a dedicated Chinese-invested industrial zone located within Egypt's broader Suez Canal Economic Zone, strategically positioned at the junction of the Red Sea and Mediterranean trade routes. The zone, developed through cooperation between the Egypt-China TEDA Suez Economic and Trade Cooperation Zone (managed by China's TEDA Investment Holding), covers approximately 7.34 km² in Phase 1 and has attracted over 140 Chinese companies in sectors including petroleum equipment, high-voltage transmission equipment, fibreglass, textiles, and construction materials. By 2022, total investment in the zone exceeded $1.4 billion, generating over 40,000 jobs. The zone is a flagship BRI project in Egypt, and China Fortune Land Development has a $20 billion agreement with Egypt for further land development in the new administrative capital area. Egypt is one of the largest recipients of Chinese BRI investment on the African continent, with total Chinese engagement reaching $10.2 billion in 2025.

Name: El Hamdania Central Port
Description: Algeria's largest and first deep-water port and the second deep-water port in Africa.

Name: El Hamdania Central Port
Description: Algeria's largest and first deep-water port and the second deep-water port in Africa.

Name: Entebbe–Kampala Expressway
Description: The Entebbe–Kampala Expressway is a 51 km, four-lane toll highway connecting Entebbe International Airport to Kampala, Uganda's capital. It is the most prominent Chinese BRI infrastructure project in Uganda. Total project cost was $476 million, with $350 million (74%) financed by a China Eximbank preferential buyer's credit loan at 2% annual interest over 40 years, signed in November 2010. The contractor was China Communications Construction Company (CCCC). Construction began in November 2012 and the expressway was inaugurated by President Yoweri Museveni on June 15, 2018 — two years behind schedule. The highway dramatically reduced travel time between the airport and city centre from 2–3 hours to approximately 45 minutes. However, the tolling system was not operational until years after completion due to delays in passing the requisite legislation, and the expressway reportedly underperformed expectations — failing to significantly alleviate the main downtown Kampala traffic bottlenecks it was designed to address. Uganda's total debt to China across all projects was approximately $3 billion at the time of construction.

Name: Erfurt CATL Battery Plant
Description: CATL's 1st battery factory in Europe (Erfurt, Thuringia) that went into production in December 2022.

Name: Estadio Nacional de El Salvador
Description: The new Estadio Nacional de El Salvador is being built in Santa Tecla at a cost of over $100 million, financed by China as part of the $500 million Economic and Technical Cooperation Agreement signed between President Nayib Bukele and President Xi Jinping during Bukele's December 2019 state visit to Beijing. China's State Construction Engineering Corporation is the contractor. The stadium will have a seating capacity of 50,000, making it the largest stadium in Central America upon completion, scheduled for 2027. It is part of a broader package of Chinese-funded infrastructure projects that accompanied El Salvador's switch of diplomatic recognition from Taiwan to China in August 2018 and its subsequent signing of the Belt and Road Initiative in 2019.

Name: Fall Creek Falls
Description: Fall Creek Falls State Park is one of Tennessee’s largest and most visited state parks. The park encompasses more than 29,800 acres sprawled across the eastern top of the rugged Cumberland Plateau. Laced with cascades, gorges, waterfalls, streams and lush stands of virgin hardwood timber, the park beckons those who enjoy nature at her finest. Fall Creek Falls, at 256 feet, is one of the highest waterfalls in the eastern United States. Other waterfalls within the park include Piney Falls, Cane Creek Falls, and Cane Creek Cascades.
Features: waterfalls; golfing; cabins; camping; bike-trails; birding; canoe-access; fishing; hiking-trails; pools; rock-climbing; inns-lodges; restaurants

Name: Foundiougne Bridge
Description: The Foundiougne Bridge is a 1,300 metre bridge across the Saloum River in Senegal, making it the longest bridge in West Africa. It was constructed by a joint consortium of China Great Wall Industry Corporation (CGWIC) and China Henan International Cooperation Group (CHICO), both Chinese state-owned enterprises. The bridge connects the Foundiougne peninsula to the mainland and serves as a critical shortcut linking Senegal to The Gambia and the Casamance region in southern Senegal, dramatically reducing travel times for communities previously reliant on ferries. Senegal was the first country in West Africa to officially sign a BRI cooperation agreement with China, during President Xi Jinping's state visit in July 2018. The bridge formed part of China's broader infrastructure commitment to Senegal and West Africa under the BRI and FOCAC frameworks. Construction proceeded despite the COVID-19 pandemic, making it one of the notable BRI projects to maintain progress during that period.

Name: Fourth Bridge over the Panama Canal
Description: The Fourth Bridge over the Panama Canal is a $1.4 billion infrastructure project awarded in June 2018 to a Chinese consortium comprising China Communications Construction Company (CCCC) and China Harbour Engineering Company (CHEC). Then-President Juan Carlos Varela called it 'the fifth most important project in the history of the country.' The bridge is designed to connect Panama Oeste province to Panama City, speeding up daily traffic for more than 70,000 vehicles and benefiting 1.7 million people. Panama joined the Belt and Road Initiative in 2017 — the first country in Latin America to do so — after severing ties with Taiwan. The project has been beset by controversies and delays, including corruption allegations related to the contract award, but construction resumed in early 2025. Both CCCC and CHEC have histories of fraud and debarment by the World Bank in other countries.

Name: Gwadar
Description: Central Asia and South Asia, encompassing the Caspian region, Central Asian republics, Afghanistan and Iran, and the energy-rich 'lake' called the Caspian Sea, is a significant region because of its huge monetary prospective and geographically vital positioning, which has formed the region as a centre piece in the international arena.[48] Iran has also declared support for the development of Gwadar and its port.

Name: Gwadar International Airport
Description: The current airport caters mainly to the population of Gwadar. Pakistan International Airlines, the main airline flying out of the airport, connects Gwadar to Karachi, Turbat, Quetta, Peshawar, Islamabad, Lahore, Dubai, Doha, Kuwait City, Riyadh, Tehran, Mashhad, Bahrain and Muscat.

Name: Gwadar Port
Description: The Straits of Malacca provide China with its shortest maritime access to Europe, Africa, and the Middle East.[77] Approximately 80% of its Middle Eastern and African energy imports also pass through the Straits of Malacca.

Name: Hamad Port Expansion
Description: In March 2011, the steering committee awarded a $880m contract to China Harbour Engineering Company for the excavation of 58 million cubic metres of material and the construction of 8km of quay wall and 5km of breakwater.

Name: Hambantota International Port
Description: Often cited as an example of China's Debt Trap Diplomacy where the port was leased to pay off Chinese debts. However, in 2017, Sri Lanka experienced a debt distress that was unconnected to Chinese lending but instead resulted more from excessive borrowing from Western-dominated capital markets and poor domestic policy decisions. Instead of defaulting on their debts, former Sri Lankan President Mahinda Rajapaksa sought out China to lease their port to obtain foreign currency inflows. The money from China Merchant Ports was used to strengthen Sri Lanka's US dollar reserves and pay short-term foreign debts unrelated to the port

Name: Harpeth River State Park
Description: The Harpeth River State Park is a linear park that manages nine river access sites along 40 river miles. Sites include several natural, archaeological and historic areas. The park is popular for kayaking, canoeing, fishing and hiking. Canoe access areas are located at all sites (excluding archeological areas).

Name: Hofusan Industrial Park
Description: A modern industrial park jointly developed by Holley Group, Futong Group and Santos Family. Located on the north outskirts of Monterrey, capital city of Nuevo Leon, it will serve as an investment platform for global clients to explore the North America market.

Name: Hualong One Nuclear Power Plant
Description: The cost of the project is estimated to be $8 billion with China providing 85% of the costs. A key remaining hurdle, and it’s a big one, is financing Argentina’s 15% share worth $1.2 billion.

Name: Hulhumalé
Description: developing a ‘Youth City’ in the capital’s suburb Hulhumalé – both key pledges made during the 2013 presidential campaign.

Name: Hutchison Ports Mexico Network
Description: Hutchison Ports, the port division of Hong Kong-based CK Hutchison Holdings and a key operator tied to China's Belt and Road Initiative maritime strategy, operates seven terminals across five strategic Mexican ports: Manzanillo, Lázaro Cárdenas, Veracruz, Ensenada, and Altamira. Together, these terminals handle approximately 35–40% of Mexico's containerized cargo. Hutchison first acquired leases at Ensenada, Manzanillo, and Veracruz in 2001, adding Lázaro Cárdenas in 2003. China Communications Construction Company (CCCC) built new port infrastructure at both Ensenada and Veracruz for Hutchison Ports. In November 2024, Hutchison committed $189 million for a second expansion phase at Lázaro Cárdenas, and invested $125 million to extend the dock at Ensenada. The Port of Manzanillo is also undergoing a $2.7 billion expansion to become Latin America's largest maritime gateway. Hutchison's concession at Veracruz runs through 2041. The network handles a significant share of trans-Pacific trade between China and North America.

Name: Hwange Thermal Power Station
Description: In December 2015 China agreed to provide a $1.2 billion loan to add 600 MW of generating capacity to the Hwange power station with two additional units.

Name: Iran–China 25-Year Comprehensive Strategic Partnership
Description: The Iran–China 25-Year Comprehensive Strategic Partnership is China's single largest bilateral BRI commitment, signed in Tehran on March 27, 2021 by Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi and Iranian Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif. Under a draft agreement obtained by The New York Times, China is to invest approximately $400 billion in Iran's economy over 25 years — representing roughly 10% of the total BRI budget — in exchange for a steady supply of heavily discounted Iranian crude oil. The investment is structured as approximately $280 billion towards developing Iran's oil, gas, and petrochemicals sectors, and $120 billion towards upgrading Iran's transportation and manufacturing infrastructure. Key BRI-linked infrastructure components include: electrification of multiple railway lines; metro network development in Tehran and other cities; development of Chabahar and Jask deepwater ports on the Makran coast; and incorporation of Iran into multiple BRI corridors including the North–South Transport Corridor and the Chabahar–Zahedan Railway. China has also opened a consulate in Bandar Abbas as a first step toward implementation. In practice, actual Chinese investment in Iran has remained limited due to US sanctions under the 'maximum pressure' campaign, Iran's exclusion from FATF, and risk aversion among Chinese state enterprises. Despite these obstacles, China has emerged as Iran's largest trading partner, purchasing approximately 1.3 million barrels per day of Iranian crude oil as of 2023. Iran joined the BRI in November 2018 and signed full CSP status with China in 2021.

Name: Jakarta–Bandung High-Speed Railway (Whoosh)
Description: The Jakarta–Bandung High-Speed Railway, branded 'Whoosh' (Waktu Hemat, Operasi Optimal, Sistem Hebat), is the first high-speed railway in Southeast Asia and the Southern Hemisphere — and one of the flagship projects of China's Belt and Road Initiative. The 142.3 km line connects Jakarta's Halim station to Tegalluar in Bandung, reducing travel time from 3 hours to approximately 35–40 minutes at speeds up to 350 km/h. The project is developed by Kereta Cepat Indonesia China (KCIC), a 60/40 joint venture between Indonesian SOE consortium PT Pilar Sinergi BUMN Indonesia and Chinese consortium Beijing Yawan HSR Co. Ltd (comprising China Railway Group, CREC, Sinohydro, CRRC, and CRSC). Construction began in August 2018 and commercial operations launched on October 2, 2023. Total cost reached $7.3 billion — approximately $1.2 billion over the original $6.07 billion budget — with approximately 75% financed through loans from China Development Bank (CDB) at 2% on the principal and 3.4% on overrun costs. Indonesia rejected Japan's competing bid in 2015 partly because China did not initially require government budget guarantees. Cost overruns prompted a tense renegotiation with CDB and questions about debt sustainability. The KCIC operating consortium reported losses of approximately $280 million in 2024. A Surabaya extension (700 km) is under negotiation.

Name: Jorge Cepernic Dam
Description: Hydroelectric dam power station will have an installed capacity of 1,140 megawatts (1,530,000 hp). In December 2023 construction was stopped awaiting funding from China.

Name: Jupiá & Ilha Solteira Hydroelectric Dams (China Three Gorges)
Description: China Three Gorges Corporation (CTG), a Chinese state-owned hydropower giant, acquired the Jupiá and Ilha Solteira hydroelectric dams from the Brazilian company AES Tietê in 2015 for $3.7 billion, making CTG Brazil's second-largest electricity generator. Located on the Paraná River on the border of São Paulo and Mato Grosso do Sul states, the two dams have a combined installed capacity of approximately 4,000 MW. CTG has since expanded aggressively in Brazil's energy sector through its subsidiary CTG Brasil, holding stakes in over 20 hydroelectric plants in 12 Brazilian states, with a total installed capacity exceeding 6.5 GW. CTG also acquired a stake in EDP Brasil in 2011, providing further reach into generation and distribution. These acquisitions make CTG the most operationally diversified Chinese energy company in Brazil. Brazil has received more than $66 billion in total Chinese investment, with the energy sector accounting for roughly half.

Name: Kariba Hydroelectric Power Station Expansion
Description: The Kariba Hydroelectric Power Station South Bank Expansion is a $533 million project on the Zambezi River in Zimbabwe, backed by Chinese financing as a replacement for the cancelled $3 billion Sengwa coal-fired power plant. In July 2021, Chinese funders pulled support for the Sengwa coal project following President Xi Jinping's announcement that China would no longer finance new overseas coal plants. The Kariba expansion — adding two additional 300 MW generating units to bring the station's South Bank capacity from 750 MW to 1,050 MW — was subsequently supported by Chinese-backed financing. Kariba is one of the largest hydroelectric stations in Africa, and Zimbabwe relies on it for a major share of its electricity. Chinese firms are also involved in the rehabilitation of existing turbines. The project illustrates China's 2021 pivot from coal-based BRI energy projects in Africa toward hydropower and renewables. Zimbabwe joined the BRI in 2018 and has received substantial Chinese investment across power generation, mining, and infrastructure.

Name: Kenneth Kaunda International Airport Expansion
Description: Kenneth Kaunda International Airport (formerly Lusaka International Airport) in Zambia underwent a major expansion and modernization funded by a Chinese government loan and built by China Jiangxi Corporation for International Economic and Technical Cooperation (CJIC). The $360 million project, financed through China Eximbank, involved the construction of a new international terminal with a capacity of 5 million passengers per year — more than tripling the airport's previous capacity — as well as a new runway, taxiways, cargo facilities, and a new control tower. The project was completed and opened in 2015. Zambia joined the BRI in 2018, and Kenneth Kaunda Airport has become emblematic of Zambia's broader Chinese debt controversy: as of 2020 when Zambia defaulted on its Eurobond, reports emerged that the airport had been listed as collateral in Chinese loan agreements — though both Zambia and China denied this. The airport expansion is cited in debates about BRI debt sustainability in Africa.

Name: Khalifa Port CSP Terminal (COSCO)
Description: The CSP Abu Dhabi Terminal at Khalifa Port is one of China's flagship BRI Maritime Silk Road projects in the Gulf region. In 2015, COSCO Shipping Ports (CSP) — the world's second-largest terminal operator and a subsidiary of China COSCO Shipping — signed a 35-year concession agreement with Abu Dhabi Ports to develop and operate a new semi-automated container terminal at Khalifa Port, the UAE's principal marine cargo hub. China invested approximately $300 million in the terminal's construction, plus $130 million in a connected container freight station. The terminal was inaugurated in 2018, more than doubling Khalifa Port's throughput capacity and advancing it from the 89th to a top-25 global container port. Designed to handle 2.5 million TEUs annually, it was the first overseas terminal COSCO built entirely from scratch. At the inauguration, China's Deputy Minister for Transport called it 'a major achievement from China and UAE's joint efforts to implement the 21st Century Maritime Silk Road.' The terminal anchors China's broader Khalifa Industrial Zone Abu Dhabi (KIZAD) strategy, which includes a 410 km² free trade zone where 19 Chinese companies signed land-lease agreements by 2017. In 2023, leaked US intelligence documents alleged that China had been constructing a potential military facility within the port perimeter — designated 'Project 141' — though construction reportedly ceased after US diplomatic protests. The UAE signed a BRI cooperation agreement in July 2018 and has become a key Maritime Silk Road hub, with over 6,000 Chinese companies operating in Dubai.

Name: Khoemacau Copper Mine (MMG Acquisition)
Description: Khoemacau Copper Mine in Botswana is one of the world's largest undeveloped copper deposits, containing approximately 2.3 million tonnes of contained copper. In 2023, Chinese state-owned metals company MMG Limited (a subsidiary of China Minmetals Corporation) acquired Khoemacau in a $1.9 billion deal — one of the largest single Chinese mining investments in Southern Africa. MMG, which also operates the Las Bambas copper mine in Peru, purchased the mine from Canadian mining company Cuprous Capital and its financial backers. Khoemacau produces approximately 60,000 tonnes of copper concentrate per year, critical for China's electric vehicle battery and green energy supply chain. The acquisition reflects the BRI's strategic pivot toward critical mineral security, particularly copper, cobalt, lithium, and rare earth elements. Botswana joined the BRI in 2019. The mine is located in the Kalahari copper belt in western Botswana and is expected to expand to 130,000 tonnes of copper per annum with further investment.

Name: Khorgos Gateway Dry Port
Description: The Khorgos Gateway Dry Port (also Horgos-Eastern Gate) is a Special Economic Zone and inland container depot on the Kazakhstan-China border at Khorgos, the world's largest land-border dry port. It was developed as a joint Kazakh-Chinese venture under the BRI framework as a critical node on the New Eurasian Land Bridge connecting China to Europe. The project involved a $3.5 billion investment in logistics infrastructure, warehouses, rail transfer facilities, and a free-trade zone. The port handles trans-shipment of containers between China's standard-gauge rail and Kazakhstan's broad-gauge Soviet-era network. China and Kazakhstan signed their first BRI cooperation MoU in August 2015. At peak capacity, the facility processes over 100,000 TEUs annually. Khorgos is flanked by the Nurkent city project — a planned city for 100,000 residents — and the International Centre for Border Cooperation (ICBC) duty-free shopping zone. Kazakhstan is the most important BRI corridor country in Central Asia, as the New Eurasian Land Bridge passes through Almaty and Nur-Sultan (Astana) en route to Russia and Europe. China Eximbank has also financed 55 industrial projects in Kazakhstan worth approximately $24 billion, and Kazakhstan received $25.8 billion in Chinese BRI investment in 2025 alone.

Name: Kyaukphyu Deep-Sea Port & SEZ (CITIC)
Description: The Kyaukphyu Deep-Sea Port and Special Economic Zone (KPSEZ) is the centrepiece of the China–Myanmar Economic Corridor (CMEC) and one of China's most strategically significant BRI projects in Southeast Asia. Located in Rakhine State on Myanmar's western coast, the port is designed to give China direct access to the Indian Ocean, bypassing the Strait of Malacca — a critical vulnerability in China's energy supply chain. The project is led by a joint venture between China's CITIC Group (70% stake) and the Myanmar government's KPSEZ Management Committee (30% stake); the CITIC-led consortium also includes China Harbour Engineering Company, China Merchants Holdings, and TEDA Investment Holding. Originally valued at $7.3 billion, the project was renegotiated down to $1.3 billion for Phase 1 under Myanmar's NLD government in 2020. The concession was signed on November 5, 2020. Following Myanmar's military coup in February 2021, progress stalled due to political instability, armed conflict between the Myanmar junta and the Arakan Army (AA) in Rakhine State, and security concerns for Chinese workers. A supplementary agreement to expedite construction was signed in December 2023. As of early 2025, the AA controls 14 of 17 townships in Rakhine State and has surrounded Kyaukphyu — no construction progress has been made on the ground. The parallel China–Myanmar oil and gas pipelines, running 793 km from Kyaukphyu to Yunnan, are operational and carry approximately 22 million tonnes of crude oil and 12 billion cubic metres of gas annually. Myanmar joined the BRI in August 2016.

Name: La Libertad Tourist Pier
Description: Built by China Harbour Engineering Company (CHEC), a subsidiary of China Communications Construction Company (CCCC), the Tourist Pier at Puerto de La Libertad was funded through a $23 million non-reimbursable Chinese government grant. The project was part of a broader $500 million Economic and Technical Cooperation Agreement signed during President Nayib Bukele's state visit to China in December 2019, which also included a national library, national stadium, water treatment plant, and Surf City coastal development. Construction began in June 2021 and was completed in September 2023, with the pier inaugurated on November 20, 2024. El Salvador severed ties with Taiwan in August 2018 and joined the Belt and Road Initiative in 2019. The pier features a restaurant, beverage kiosk, viewing areas and recreational spaces, and is part of El Salvador's Surf City tourism strategy.

Name: Lamu Port (LAPSSET Corridor)
Description: Lamu Port is the anchor project of Kenya's Lamu Port–South Sudan–Ethiopia Transport (LAPSSET) Corridor, a $29 billion multimodal development plan connecting Kenya with South Sudan and Ethiopia via a new deep-water port, a 2,000 km standard-gauge railway, a pipeline, and a resort city. China Communications Construction Company (CCCC) and its subsidiary China Harbour Engineering Company (CHEC) were contracted to build the first three berths at Lamu Port, which were commissioned in June 2021. The overall LAPSSET project is one of Africa's most ambitious infrastructure programmes. CRBC is also involved in the LAPSSET highway corridor linking Kenya to South Sudan. Chinese financing has supported various components through China Eximbank loans. The Lamu Port is strategically significant as it opens a new Indian Ocean gateway for landlocked Ethiopia and South Sudan, reducing dependence on the Port of Mombasa. Environmental concerns have been raised regarding impacts on the Lamu Old Town UNESCO World Heritage Site and local fishing communities.

Name: Lubambe Copper Mine Acquisition (JCHX Mining)
Description: Lubambe Copper Mine is an underground copper mine in Zambia's Copperbelt Province, acquired by Chinese company JCHX Mining Management Co. Ltd in July 2024 for the nominal sum of $2 — reflecting the mine's significant outstanding debts rather than its underlying value. The mine had been placed in provisional liquidation after falling into financial distress, with outstanding liabilities of approximately $180 million. JCHX is a Chinese state-linked mining contractor that also operates other assets in Zambia and Africa. Lubambe has a production capacity of approximately 45,000 tonnes of copper per year. The acquisition exemplifies China's aggressive strategy of acquiring distressed African mining assets at minimal cost to secure critical mineral supply chains for its battery, EV, and technology manufacturing sectors. Zambia is one of the world's top copper producers and has received substantial Chinese BRI investment. Zambia defaulted on its sovereign debt in 2020 — with Chinese creditors holding a significant portion — triggering years of restructuring negotiations under the G20 Common Framework.

Name: Lusail Stadium
Description: Largest stadium in Qatar.

Name: Malaysia-China Kuantan Industrial Park
Description: Officially launched on 5 February 2013, and is strategically located in the special economic zone, East Coast Economic Region (ECER).

Name: Mambilla Hydroelectric Plant
Description: The Mambilla Hydroelectric Power Station is a proposed 3,050 MW hydroelectric plant on the Donga River in Taraba State, northeast Nigeria — which, upon completion, would be the largest power station in Africa. Chinese loans are part-funding the $4.9 billion project, with the main EPC contract awarded to a consortium led by China Gezhouba Group Corporation (CGGC) and Sinohydro. Nigeria and China signed a financing agreement in 2017 with China Eximbank providing 85% of the project cost. Construction has faced repeated delays, legal disputes (including a long-running arbitration involving a rival Nigerian contractor), land acquisition challenges, and political obstacles. As of 2025, the project remains in pre-construction stages. When complete, the plant will have an installed capacity of 3,050 MW generated by eight turbines, adding approximately 30% to Nigeria's total grid capacity. The project is central to Nigeria's ambition to end chronic power shortages, which cost the economy an estimated $26 billion annually.

Name: Manuel Piar Hydroelectric Plant (Tocoma)
Description: The Manuel Piar Hydroelectric Plant (originally Tocoma) on the Caroní River in Bolívar State is Venezuela's last major planned dam on the lower Caroní River, designed with an installed capacity of 2,160 MW. It was partly financed by the China–Venezuela Joint Fund's Long-Term Facility, with Chinese financing estimated at approximately $4.17 billion, alongside loans from the Andean Development Corporation (CAF) and the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB). Total project cost estimates range from $9.37 billion to $10.37 billion. Originally proposed by Hugo Chávez in 2002 with a planned 2012 completion, the project has faced decades of delays due to funding crises, contractor disputes, and Venezuela's economic collapse. As of the mid-2020s, the dam remains substantially incomplete. It was intended to be the fourth and final dam in the Guri–Macagua–Caruachi–Tocoma cascade on the Caroní, which together form the backbone of Venezuela's electricity system. The project illustrates the systemic failure of Chinese oil-backed loan infrastructure programmes in Venezuela.

Name: Maputo–Katembe Bridge
Description: The Maputo–Katembe Bridge is a 3 km suspension bridge across Maputo Bay in southern Mozambique, connecting the capital Maputo on the north bank with the Katembe district on the south bank. Built by China Road and Bridge Corporation (CRBC), it is the longest suspension bridge on the African continent, with a main span of 680 metres and towers rising 137 metres above sea level. Total cost was approximately $785 million — the most expensive infrastructure project in Mozambique's post-independence history — financed 95% by two loans from China Eximbank at 4% interest over 20 years (totalling $754 million), with the remaining 5% provided directly by the Mozambican government. Construction began in 2014 and the bridge officially opened on November 10, 2018. Prior to the bridge, the only crossing of Maputo Bay was by ferry, with road travel requiring a 160 km detour on unpaved, flood-prone roads. The project displaced approximately 900 families and sparked controversy over high tolls (equivalent to $2.60 per crossing), which many ordinary Mozambicans cannot afford. Mozambique defaulted on its external debt during the construction period, and by 2018 owed China approximately $2 billion across multiple projects.

Name: Masaka-Kabuga Road
Description: The 6.36-kilometre Masaka-Kabuga road was constructed under the Kigali Urban Road Upgrading Project, financed by a Chinese interest-free loan of $7.1 million (50 million RMB Yuan). The loan was provided under the agreement on economic and technical cooperation between China and Rwanda. In November 2022, China cancelled the outstanding debt as part of a broader initiative announced by Chinese President Xi Jinping at the Eighth Ministerial Conference of the Forum on China-Africa Cooperation (FOCAC) in Senegal in November 2021. China's Foreign Minister Wang Yi had also announced in August 2022 that China would waive 23 interest-free loans to 17 African countries that matured by end of 2021. The debt cancellation agreement was signed on November 28, 2022 by Rwanda's Minister for Finance and Economic Planning Uzziel Ndagijimana and Chinese Ambassador to Rwanda Wang Xuekun. The road significantly improved connectivity for local residents, reducing travel time to Kigali by up to 40 minutes. China indicated it will continue cooperating with Rwanda under the Belt and Road Initiative framework.

Name: Małaszewicze Border Hub & China–Europe Railway Express (Poland)
Description: Poland is the most important BRI transit hub in Central Europe, home to Małaszewicze border crossing station — which processes the vast majority of all China–Europe Railway Express (CRE) freight transiting between China and the EU. Located on the Belarus–Poland border, Małaszewicze is the primary gauge-change point where containers are transferred between Russian/Belarusian broad-gauge wagons and European standard-gauge wagons. Poland signed a BRI MoU in November 2015 and President Andrzej Duda met with President Xi Jinping in Beijing in June 2024, during which Xi called for enhanced bilateral cooperation under the BRI and specifically through the CRE. As of 2024, the China–Europe Railway Express has operated over 90,000 train services since launch. Lódź (Poland's second-largest city) serves as the western terminus for many CRE services and has become a major Chinese logistics hub, home to warehousing, distribution centres, and light manufacturing by Chinese firms. Chinese investment in Poland also includes Huawei's research and development centre in Warsaw (subsequently controversially shut down amid security concerns), and ZTE telecoms infrastructure. Poland's strategic value to the BRI has increased since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 disrupted the northern Trans-Siberian route, forcing CRE operators to reroute through the Middle Corridor via Kazakhstan, Caspian Sea, Azerbaijan, Georgia, and Turkey, making Gdansk and other Polish ports increasingly important as western BRI endpoints.

Name: Mecca Metro
Description: In March 2010, Serco Middle East was awarded a contract by China Railway Construction Corporation Limited (CRCC) to advise on the operation and maintenance of the Makkah Metro. CRCC had been awarded the design, build, operate and maintain contract in 2008 by the Ministry of Municipal and Rural Affairs.

Name: Meeman Shelby Forest
Description: Meeman-Shelby Forest State Park is a 12,539-acre hardwood bottomland area bordering the mighty Mississippi River 13 miles north of Memphis featuring mature Bald Cypress and Tupelo swamp. Most of the facilities are on top of the majestic Chickasaw Bluffs that rise from the bottomlands and are covered with large oaks, American beech, hickory and sweet gum. There are 10 state Champion Trees and two National Champion Trees as well as endangered and protected plants.
Features: camping; disc-golf; birding; hiking-trails; bike-trails; fishing; horseback-riding

Name: Mombasa–Nairobi Standard Gauge Railway
Description: The railway cost US$3.2bn and was Kenya's biggest infrastructure project since independence. The railway was claimed to cut the journey time from Mombasa to Nairobi from 9 hours by bus or 12 hours on the previous railway to 4.5 hours.

Name: Morocco Haite Tech City
Description: The Morocco Haite Tech City is a proposed Chinese-led technology and manufacturing park near Rabat, Morocco, to be developed by Haite Group, a Chinese private aerospace and technology conglomerate. The project is part of a broader Chinese industrial investment strategy in Morocco, which is positioned as a manufacturing hub bridging Africa, Europe, and the Gulf due to its free trade agreements with the EU and USA. In 2025, Chinese firm Boway Alloys also announced it would scrap a manufacturing plant in Vietnam and invest in Morocco instead, explicitly to take advantage of Morocco's 10% US tariff rate compared to higher Vietnamese rates — indicating China's use of Morocco as a tariff-arbitrage manufacturing location. Morocco is not a formal BRI signatory but has pursued significant Chinese investment in its industrial and renewable energy sectors. The Haite Tech City project faced delays, but reflects the broader BRI strategy of establishing Chinese technology parks and manufacturing corridors in strategically located African countries.

Name: Mutún Steel Complex
Description: The Mutún Steel Complex in Puerto Suárez, near Bolivia's border with Brazil, is a $546 million industrial project financed largely by the Export-Import Bank of China (Eximbank) through a $396 million preferential buyer's credit signed in December 2017, at 3% interest with a 15-year maturity and 5-year grace period.
