The contractor is Sinosteel Engineering and Technology, a subsidiary of Chinese state-owned Sinosteel Corporation. Construction began on January 29, 2019, and the plant was inaugurated on February 24, 2025. It produces 200,000 metric tonnes of steel annually — primarily rebar and wire mesh — sourced from the Cerro Mutún iron ore deposit, one of the world's largest reserves estimated at 40 billion tonnes. The plant is expected to meet approximately 50% of Bolivia's domestic steel demand, replace over $250 million per year in steel imports, and create around 1,000 direct jobs. The project overcame five decades of delays, including a failed contract with India's Jindal Steel & Power in 2012. Bolivia joined the BRI in 2018.

Name: Nairobi Expressway
Description: The Nairobi Expressway is a 27 km, four-lane toll highway connecting Jomo Kenyatta International Airport to Westlands in Nairobi's central business district, becoming Kenya's first toll road. It was built and is operated by China Road and Bridge Corporation (CRBC) under a build-operate-transfer (BOT) model costing approximately $600 million — meaning CRBC financed and built the road in exchange for toll revenues over the concession period. Construction began in June 2020 and the expressway opened in May 2022. More than 4,000 Kenyans were employed during construction. CRBC, a subsidiary of China Communications Construction Company (CCCC), is the same contractor that built the Mombasa-Nairobi SGR. The expressway was specifically designed to bypass Nairobi's notorious traffic congestion along Uhuru Highway, one of the most congested corridors in East Africa. Critics raised concerns about the high toll charges for ordinary Kenyans and the exclusion of public transport vehicles from certain sections.

Name: Nairobi–Naivasha SGR Extension (Phase 2A)
Description: The Nairobi–Naivasha Standard Gauge Railway (Phase 2A) is a 120 km extension of Kenya's flagship SGR project, connecting Nairobi's South Station to the Naivasha Inland Container Depot in the Rift Valley. The project cost approximately $1.5 billion, borrowed entirely from China's Export-Import Bank at approximately 3.34% interest per annum over 15 years. Construction was undertaken by China Communications Construction Company (CCCC) and was completed in October 2019. The Naivasha ICD is strategically located to serve as a transit hub for Uganda, Rwanda, and other landlocked countries in the region. The line was part of Kenya's broader Vision 2030 SGR ambition, which originally aimed to extend the railway to the Ugandan border at Malaba (another ~350 km) — a phase that stalled after China Eximbank declined to fund it due to concerns over the economic viability of the existing line. Kenya's total SGR debt to China exceeds $8 billion.

Name: Nasiriyah Smart City & Airport
Description: The Iraqi Ministry of Transportation said it signed an addendum on the contract for the construction of the Nasiriyah International Airport with China State Construction Engineering and another for the airport’s construction with Turkey’s Kiklop Design Hertz Insaat, the official Iraqi News Agency reported.

Name: New Administrative Capital
Description: A new urban community in Cairo Governorate, Egypt and a satellite of Cairo City. It is planned to be Egypt's new capital and has been under construction since 2015.

Name: New Zealand BRI Trade Cooperation MoU
Description: New Zealand signed a Belt and Road Initiative Memorandum of Understanding with China in March 2017, becoming one of the first developed Western nations to formally join the initiative. The MoU was primarily a trade and economic cooperation framework rather than a commitment to specific infrastructure projects — New Zealand's developed infrastructure meant there was no significant BRI-financed construction pipeline. Trade cooperation under the BRI framework has focused on New Zealand's agricultural exports (dairy, meat, wool) and Chinese investment in New Zealand's agrifood sector. Chinese state-owned and linked companies have invested in New Zealand's dairy industry, logistics, and real estate. New Zealand's BRI participation became politically controversial amid increasing scrutiny of Chinese influence operations in New Zealand politics, academic institutions, and media. In 2020, New Zealand declined to join the Five Eyes statement criticising Chinese human rights abuses in Xinjiang, causing diplomatic tension. As of 2025, New Zealand has not exited the BRI but has moved to increase scrutiny of Chinese investment under the Overseas Investment Act and has aligned more closely with AUKUS partners on China-related security concerns.

Name: New Zimbabwe Parliament Building
Description: The construction was funded with a US$140 million grant by the Government of China to the Zimbabwean Government.

Name: Nicaraguan Grand Canal (Proposed)
Description: The Nicaraguan Grand Canal was a proposed $50 billion mega-project to build a 278 km interoceanic canal linking the Pacific Ocean to the Caribbean Sea via Lake Nicaragua, intended to rival the Panama Canal. In June 2013, Nicaragua's National Assembly granted a 100-year concession to Hong Kong Nicaragua Canal Development Investment Company (HKND), a company controlled by Chinese billionaire Wang Jing. A groundbreaking ceremony was held in December 2014 in Brito. Plans included two ports, a free trade zone, an international airport, power plants, and a resort. However, no significant construction ever took place. Wang Jing lost approximately 80% of his net worth in the 2015-16 Chinese stock market crash, and the project stalled. HKND closed its headquarters in China in April 2018, and the concession was formally cancelled by Nicaragua in May 2024. The project raised major environmental concerns over Lake Nicaragua, Central America's largest freshwater source, and displaced thousands of rural residents along the proposed route.

Name: Nigeria Lagos–Ibadan Railway Modernization
Description: The Lagos–Ibadan Railway Modernization is a 156 km standard-gauge railway connecting Lagos, Nigeria's commercial capital, with Ibadan, the nation's third-largest city. It forms the first phase of Nigeria's broader $11.1 billion railway modernization programme under a 2006 contract with China Civil Engineering Construction Corporation (CCECC). The Lagos–Ibadan segment cost approximately $1.5 billion, financed through a China Eximbank loan. The line was officially opened in June 2021. CCECC is a subsidiary of China Railway Construction Corporation (CRCC). The broader Nigeria–China railway cooperation package totalling $6.8 billion — covering Lagos–Ibadan, Lagos–Kano, Kano–Kaduna, and the Abuja metro — represents one of the largest single-country BRI railway financing packages in Africa. As of 2019, 18 out of 19 major infrastructure loan packages in Nigeria were from China. The Lagos–Ibadan railway features 10 stations and reduces the journey time between the two cities from approximately 3 hours by road to about 2 hours by rail.

Name: Nigeria Ogidigbon Gas Revolution Industrial Park
Description: The Ogidigbon Gas Revolution Industrial Park in Ogun State, Nigeria, is a $20 billion gas processing and industrial complex being developed under a construction contract awarded to China National Chemical Engineering Co. Ltd (CNCEC) in 2025 — making it one of the single largest BRI construction contracts in Africa's history. The facility is designed to process natural gas from Nigeria's vast reserves (among the largest in Africa) into petrochemicals, fertilizers, methanol, and other value-added products. Nigeria is China's largest BRI energy engagement country in Africa cumulatively, with total Chinese BRI energy construction reaching approximately $28 billion since 2013. The project is part of Nigeria's strategy to monetize its natural gas reserves domestically rather than flaring or exporting raw LNG. CNCEC, formerly known as China Chemical Engineering Corporation, is a major Chinese state-owned enterprise specialising in chemical engineering, energy, and industrial construction. Nigeria joined the BRI in 2018.

Name: Néstor Kirchner Dam
Description: Hydroelectric dam power station will have an installed capacity of 1,140 megawatts (1,530,000 hp). In December 2023 construction was stopped awaiting funding from China.

Name: Olmeca Refinery (Dos Bocas)
Description: The Olmeca Refinery in Dos Bocas, Tabasco, is one of Mexico's largest infrastructure investments in recent decades, championed by former President Andrés Manuel López Obrador. Chinese financial institutions — the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (ICBC) and the Bank of China — invested over $600 million in the construction of the refinery, reflecting China's strategic interest in Mexico's energy sector and its alignment with Belt and Road Initiative financing objectives. The refinery is designed to process 340,000 barrels of crude oil per day and was inaugurated in 2023, though it has faced operational challenges in reaching full capacity. The project is state-run by Pemex, Mexico's national oil company. Chinese bank involvement illustrates the BRI's expansion beyond formal MoU signatories into energy infrastructure financing.

Name: PLA Support Base
Description: It is the PLAN's first overseas military base and was built at a cost of US$590 million. The facility is expected to significantly increase China's power projection in the Horn of Africa and the Indian Ocean, as well as the PLAN's blue water capabilities.

Name: PRASA Rolling Stock Programme (CRRC)
Description: In 2015, the Passenger Rail Agency of South Africa (PRASA) signed a R51 billion ($3.8 billion) contract with CRRC Corporation — the world's largest rolling stock manufacturer and a key BRI participant — for the supply of 3,600 new passenger train coaches over ten years. CRRC Electric Vehicle South Africa was established to fulfil the contract, with manufacturing to be localised in South Africa through a joint venture with South African company Gibela Rail Transport Consortium (Alstom-led, later acquired by Wabtec). However, the CRRC contract was cancelled in 2019 following an investigative report by South Africa's Public Protector, which found that PRASA CEO Lucky Montana had irregular dealings with CRRC and that the contract was unlawfully awarded. Despite the cancellation, CRRC has continued to supply diesel-electric locomotives to South Africa's Transnet through separate contracts, valued at approximately $400 million. South Africa joined the BRI in December 2015 and is one of China's most strategically important African partners, with bilateral trade reaching $38.8 billion in 2023. China is South Africa's largest trading partner.

Name: Padma Bridge Rail Link
Description: The Padma Bridge Rail Link is a 169 km railway project in Bangladesh connecting Dhaka to Jessore via the Padma Bridge, part of the broader Trans-Asian Railway network. It is financed by a $2.67 billion concessional loan from the Export-Import Bank of China at 2% interest over 20 years, with a 7-year grace period — one of the largest single Chinese loans to Bangladesh. The contractor is China Railway Group Limited (CREC). The project includes the rail connection across the Padma Bridge — the second deck of the $3.86 billion road bridge completed in June 2022 — along with new railway stations, tunnels, bridges, and viaducts. Construction on the rail link began in 2016. The project will integrate Bangladesh's southwestern regions with Dhaka and improve freight and passenger connectivity to India and beyond as part of the South Asian regional rail network. Bangladesh joined the BRI in 2016 and China is its largest development finance partner. Total Chinese BRI engagement in Bangladesh includes the Karnaphuli Tunnel, Payra Power Plant, and multiple power generation projects, making Bangladesh one of the highest-debt BRI countries in South Asia.

Name: Phnom Penh–Sihanoukville Expressway
Description: The Phnom Penh–Sihanoukville Expressway (Road E4) is a 190.6 km expressway connecting Cambodia's capital, Phnom Penh, to Sihanoukville on the Gulf of Thailand, home to the country's only deep-sea port. Built by China Road and Bridge Corporation (CRBC) on a build-operate-transfer (BOT) basis under a 50-year concession agreement signed in January 2018, it is financed through a $1.56 billion syndicated loan from China Development Bank and China Eximbank, plus an RMB 600 million ($88.5 million) grant from China's Ministry of Commerce. Total project cost is approximately $2 billion. Construction began in 2019 and the expressway opened in October 2022. It includes 89 bridges and passes through Kandal, Kampong Speu, Koh Kong, and Sihanoukville provinces. Over one million vehicles used the expressway in its first three months of operation. The route dramatically reduces the journey from Phnom Penh to Sihanoukville from 4–5 hours to approximately 2 hours. Cambodia has been one of China's closest diplomatic allies and a major BRI recipient; Sihanoukville itself has been transformed by Chinese investment and gambling tourism, raising social governance concerns. CRBC's Cambodian operations also include a new port complex and special economic zone in Kampot.

Name: Pickett State Park
Description: Pickett CCC Memorial State Park lies within the 20,887-acres Pickett State Forest and is adjacent to the massive 125,000 acre Big South Fork National River and Recreation Area. In 1933, the Stearns Coal and Lumber Company donated nearly 12,000 acres of land to the State of Tennessee to be developed as a forest recreational area. Initial development of the area by the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC) occurred between 1934 through 1942. The CCC constructed hiking trails, five rustic cabins, a recreation lodge, a ranger station, and a 12-acre lake. The park memorializes and preserves the unique work of the CCC who first developed the park.

Name: Port City Colombo
Description: Port City Colombo aims to facilitate connections to the South Asian market through investment opportunities, international business environments, world-class infrastructure, and high-quality sustainable living.

Name: Port of Annaba
Description: Improvements to the port.

Name: Port of Baku (Trans-Caspian International Transport Route)
Description: The Port of Baku (Baku International Sea Trade Port) on the Caspian Sea is a critical node in China's Belt and Road Initiative, serving as the western anchor of the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR) — also known as the Middle Corridor — linking China to Turkey and Europe via Kazakhstan, the Caspian Sea, Azerbaijan, Georgia, and Turkey. The new Baku Port facility at Alat, 65 km south of Baku, was developed with a $775 million investment and officially opened in 2018. It has a container handling capacity of 100,000 TEUs per year with plans to expand to 25 million tonnes of cargo annually. Chinese companies have participated in port modernisation and connectivity projects at Baku. The port is directly integrated with the Baku–Tbilisi–Kars (BTK) Railway — the 'Iron Silk Road' connecting Azerbaijan, Georgia, and Turkey — which became operational in October 2017. Azerbaijan President Ilham Aliyev has been among the most vocal BRI supporters, stating at the 2017 Belt and Road Forum: 'From the very beginning Azerbaijan supported the Belt and Road Initiative.' Since Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine severely disrupted the Northern Corridor through Russia, the TITR via Baku has seen a dramatic surge in cargo volumes — tripling year-on-year in 2022–2023 — dramatically elevating Azerbaijan's strategic importance as a BRI transit node. Azerbaijan signed the BRI MoU in December 2015.

Name: Port of Chancay
Description: Direct route to China with ship travel time reduction of 10 days. Ships traveling from South America to China normally take more than 45 days with stops in Central America, Mexico or the United States.

Name: Port of Chancay
Description: The Port of Chancay is a $3.5 billion deep-water megaport located 80 km north of Lima, Peru, developed by COSCO Shipping Ports (60% stake) in partnership with Peruvian mining company Volcan (40%). It is one of the flagship projects of China's Belt and Road Initiative in South America. COSCO acquired its majority stake in 2019 for $225 million, coinciding with Peru signing the BRI MoU with China. Construction began in 2020 by a consortium of China Communications Construction Company (CCCC) and China Harbour Engineering Company (CHEC). The first phase, costing $1.32 billion and featuring four docks, a two-kilometre tunnel, and automated crane systems, was inaugurated on November 14, 2024 by Chinese President Xi Jinping (via videoconference) and Peruvian President Dina Boluarte. The project was financed in part by a $975 million syndicated loan from five Chinese banks, led by the Bank of China, at 6.5% interest over 15 years. The port reduces trans-Pacific shipping time from 36 days to 24 days and is expected to generate $4.5 billion annually and 8,000 jobs. Total investment across four phases will reach $3.5 billion upon full completion in 2032, with a capacity of over 1 million TEUs annually. The port has raised U.S. security concerns over potential Chinese naval and intelligence use.

Name: Port of Darwin (Landbridge Group Lease)
Description: In October 2015, the Northern Territory Government granted Chinese company Shandong Landbridge Group a 99-year lease over the Port of Darwin for AU$506 million (approximately $320 million USD) — outbidding 32 other potential investors. Landbridge, owned by billionaire Ye Cheng, has documented close ties to the Chinese Communist Party, including an armed company militia established in 2014 with People's Liberation Army backing. The port sits adjacent to Darwin International Airport and is used by US Marines on annual rotations as part of the US pivot to Asia. US President Barack Obama publicly rebuked then-PM Malcolm Turnbull over the deal, saying Washington should have been given advance notice. China frames the Darwin Port lease as a key Belt and Road Initiative maritime asset in the Pacific. The deal triggered years of national security reviews: a 2021 review found no grounds to cancel; a 2023 review reached the same conclusion. However, during the 2025 Australian federal election, both major parties pledged to return the port to Australian ownership. As of January 2026, China's ambassador was still warning Canberra that nationalisation would harm bilateral trade and diplomatic relations. The lease remains in force.

Name: Port of Melbourne (China Investment Corporation)
Description: In September 2016, the Port of Melbourne — Australia's largest container port, handling approximately 36% of the country's container trade — was leased to the Lonsdale consortium for AU$9.7 billion (approximately $7.3 billion USD) for a 50-year lease with an optional 20-year extension, in one of Australia's largest-ever infrastructure privatisations. The consortium includes the China Investment Corporation (CIC), China's sovereign wealth fund, as a significant minority investor alongside Australiansuper, Global Infrastructure Partners, Future Fund, and others. CIC's involvement connected the Port of Melbourne to the broader Belt and Road Initiative financing architecture. The port handles over 3 million TEUs of container traffic annually, representing a critical gateway for Australia's trade with Asia, including China. The lease has not been subject to the same level of public national security controversy as Darwin and Newcastle, in part because CIC's stake is a minority shareholding within a diversified consortium. The Port of Melbourne is Australia's busiest container port and primary gateway for consumer goods, fresh food, and manufactured products.

Name: Port of Newcastle (China Merchants Group)
Description: In April 2014, the New South Wales government leased the Port of Newcastle — Australia's largest coal export facility and the world's largest coal export port — to a 50/50 consortium of Australian fund manager Hastings Funds Management and Chinese state-owned China Merchants Group for AU$1.75 billion over 98 years. The Chinese stake was later transferred to China Merchants Port Holdings Company (CMPorts), a publicly listed subsidiary of China Merchants Group. CMPorts explicitly cited Belt and Road Initiative strategy in its 2017 annual report, stating it was "seizing development opportunities arising from the 'Belt and Road' initiative" in its overseas expansion. Port of Newcastle handles approximately 40% of Australia's coal exports by volume — around 164 million tonnes per year — with 21 berths and a design capacity of 211 million tonnes. The acquisition made CMPorts the operator of strategic ports on six continents. The Chinese stake came under intense scrutiny in 2021 alongside the Darwin Port controversy. A 2018 Defence review reportedly cleared the Newcastle transaction on security grounds, though the full review remained classified. As of 2025, the Chinese stake remains in place with no announced plans for reversal.

Name: Port of Paranaguá
Description: TCP Participações operates at the Port of Paranaguá, the second-largest port in Brazil, and a port of call for most container ships operating international and cabotage lines along the Brazilian coast. In February of 2018, Advent sold its 50% stake to China Merchants Port Holdings Limited (“CMPort”), one of the world’s largest container terminal operators.

Name: Port of Piraeus
Description: The Chinese state-owned COSCO Shipping operate the port. Before COSCO took over, the port's container handling record was at 1.5 million TEUs. These figures rose to 3.692 million containers in 2017.As a result, revenue and profits soared. In 2017 the Athens stock exchange listed company (OLP) almost doubled its pre-tax profits from 11 to 21.2 million euros.

Name: Quilamba
Description: Neighborhood that serves as the administrative center of Belas Municipality and a large housing development site 30 km (18 miles) from Luanda, the capital city of Angola. It is being built by the China International Trust and Investment Corporation.

Name: Republic of Congo Oil Development (Southern Petrochemical Group Yonghua)
Description: In 2025, the Republic of Congo (Congo-Brazzaville) signed a $23 billion oil and gas development agreement with Southern Petrochemical Group Yonghua, a Chinese state-linked energy company, for the development of three oil and gas blocks: Banga Kayo, Holmoni, and Cayo. The goal of the agreement is to increase oil production from the three blocks to 200,000 barrels per day by 2030. This deal made Congo-Brazzaville the largest single recipient of Chinese BRI construction engagement in 2025, accounting for approximately $23.1 billion of the $61.2 billion total Chinese BRI engagement in Africa that year — surpassing even Nigeria's $24.6 billion in that period. The Republic of Congo is heavily indebted to China, with Chinese loans accounting for a significant proportion of its external debt, backed by oil revenues. The country's reliance on oil-backed Chinese financing has drawn comparisons to Angola's oil-for-infrastructure model and Venezuela's oil-for-loans arrangements with China.

Name: Roan Mountain State Park
Description: Located on TN Hwy 143 at the base of the majestic 6,285 Roan Mountain, Roan Mountain State Park encompasses more than 2,000 acres dominated by rich hardwood forest along rugged ridges. The cool, clear Doe River winds its way through the center of the park and supports a healthy population of trout. Wildflowers and wildlife inhabit the hollows and ridges of the Roan foothills in abundance.

Name: Salar de Atacama
Description: Salar de Atacama has become a significant hub for lithium extraction, as lithium is found in the brines of the salt flat. The Likan Antay people are the indigenous inhabitants of Salar de Atacama and its surrounding areas.

Name: Salar de Uyuni Lithium Plants (CATL/CBC)
Description: Bolivia signed a $1 billion agreement in November 2024 with CBC Investments — a Chinese consortium led by CATL (the world's largest lithium battery manufacturer, holding 66% of CBC), along with affiliates CMOC Group and Guangdong Brunp Recycling Technology — to construct two direct lithium extraction (DLE) plants in the Uyuni salt flats of Potosí Department, southwest Bolivia. Bolivian state lithium company YLB will hold a 51% stake. One plant will produce 10,000 tonnes of lithium carbonate per year and the other 25,000 tonnes of battery-grade lithium carbonate per year, for a combined annual capacity of 35,000 tonnes. Bolivia claims the world's largest lithium deposits. The DLE technology used is more efficient than traditional evaporation pond methods. An earlier January 2023 framework agreement and a January 2024 expansion added a further $90 million, expanding CBC's participation. Both agreements require approval from Bolivia's National Assembly. The deal positions Bolivia as a key node in China's global electric vehicle battery supply chain.

Name: Santa Cruz River Hydroelectric Complex
Description: The Santa Cruz River Hydroelectric Complex in Patagonia, Argentina, comprises two dams — the Néstor Kirchner (Cóndor Cliff) and Jorge Cepernic (La Barrancosa) — on the Santa Cruz River near the iconic Perito Moreno Glacier, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. It is the most expensive infrastructure project financed and built by Chinese entities outside China, with a total cost of $4.7 billion. The project is led by Represas Patagonia, a consortium in which China Gezhouba Group Company Limited holds a 70% stake alongside Argentine firms Hidrocuyo and Electroingeniería. Financing was provided via a $4.71 billion syndicated loan from China Development Bank ($2.5 billion), ICBC ($1.4 billion), and Bank of China ($800 million). Construction began in 2015, but has faced repeated delays, corruption allegations, a Supreme Court suspension in 2016 over environmental concerns, and financing freezes. When complete, the complex will have a combined capacity of 1,310 MW and generate 4.95 billion kWh annually, boosting Argentina's installed power capacity by approximately 6.5%. The project is controversially linked to the Belgrano Cargas Railway via a cross-default clause. The dams were suspended again by President Milei's government in 2024. Completion is now estimated for 2028.

Name: Shandong BaoMa Fishing Port (Punta Yeguas)
Description: Shandong BaoMa Fisheries Group, a Chinese state-linked fishing and port conglomerate with around 4,000 employees, received authorization to develop a $200 million duty-free fishing port, shipyard, and fish processing facility in Punta Yeguas, west of Montevideo, Uruguay. The project covers 28 hectares and includes an 800-metre dock capable of accommodating ships carrying up to 50,000 tonnes. As a free-trade zone, the facility would operate outside standard Uruguayan government controls. The project would allow more than 500 Chinese-flagged fishing vessels to dock, extending their expeditions in the South Atlantic. Shandong BaoMa specialises in fishing, fishmeal processing, and port terminal management. The project has attracted opposition from local residents and conservationists, who warn of threats to the South Atlantic marine ecosystem, already under severe pressure from illegal and unregulated Chinese fishing fleets. Uruguay became a BRI signatory in 2018 and has strategic importance as South America's premier deep-water Atlantic port hub.

Name: Sinamalé Bridge
Description: Opened on 30 August 2018. It was originally called the China-Maldives Friendship Bridge due to funding received from the Chinese government. It is the first inter-island bridge in the Maldives.

Name: South Cumberland State Park
Description: South Cumberland State Park is located within four different Tennessee counties: Grundy, Franklin, Marion and Sequatchie. The park is composed of approximately 30,845 acres in nine separate areas and boasts some of the best hiking and backcountry camping in the region.
Features: camping; waterfalls; birding; fishing; hiking-trails; rock-climbing

Name: South Korea BRI Digital Silk Road & Battery Supply Chain
Description: South Korea signed a Belt and Road Initiative Memorandum of Understanding with China in May 2018, becoming one of the only developed East Asian economies to formally join the initiative. Under BRI cooperation frameworks, Chinese companies have won major construction and supply contracts in South Korea's green energy transition. The most significant Chinese BRI-linked investment is CATL (Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Ltd) — the world's largest lithium battery manufacturer — which entered a joint venture with South Korean automotive company Hyundai and battery firm Stellantis to supply EV batteries for Korean-manufactured vehicles. SECO (Samsung SDI and BYD joint venture discussions) and CATL–Samsung partnerships deepened supply chain integration. Chinese state-linked firms including CRRC have also supplied rolling stock components for South Korea's metro systems, and Chinese technology companies including Huawei and ZTE secured contracts in South Korea's 5G Digital Silk Road expansion. Korea's trade relationship with China is the world's 7th-largest bilateral trade partnership. South Korea's BRI engagement has been complicated by geopolitical tensions including the THAAD missile defence deployment in 2017, which triggered Chinese economic retaliation, and growing US pressure to decouple from Chinese technology supply chains. Despite these tensions, China remains South Korea's largest single trading partner by a wide margin.

Name: Sudan Locomotives (CRRC Ziyang)
Description: In September 2020, the Sudan Railways Authority signed a contract with CRRC Ziyang — a subsidiary of CRRC Corporation, the world's largest rolling stock manufacturer and a key BRI participant — for the supply of 34 new diesel-electric locomotives. The first batch of 21 locomotives was delivered in 2021, with the remainder to follow. The locomotives are designed for freight and passenger services on Sudan's railway network, which covers approximately 4,000 km of narrow-gauge track. The contract represents a significant upgrade to Sudan's ageing colonial-era railway fleet and reflects China's growing role in supplying railway equipment to African countries under the BRI framework, even in the absence of full-scale infrastructure construction. Sudan joined the BRI in 2018. CRRC has supplied rolling stock to numerous African countries including Ethiopia, Nigeria, South Africa, Zimbabwe, and Egypt.

Name: Suriname BRI Infrastructure & Housing Programme
Description: Suriname was the first Caribbean country to sign a Belt and Road Initiative Memorandum of Understanding with China (2018) and has since received Chinese investment in road construction, bridge building, housing projects, and healthcare. Chinese company Dalian (of China) was contracted for multiple asphalt road and public housing projects in Suriname, though contract details remain largely secret. A Chinese-financed hospital was built in one of Suriname's districts under the BRI framework. Paramaribo has established a sister-city relationship with Dalian, China. Suriname's external debt reached $2.4 billion as of 2023, with approximately 17% owed to Chinese state-owned banks, and the country experienced a deep economic crisis in which it was unable to service its Chinese debt. Suriname also has 10 billion barrels of oil and gas reserves discovered offshore in 2020, attracting Chinese energy company interest. As a co-financier and prospective partner in the $236 million Corentyne River Bridge with Guyana, Suriname faces additional Chinese debt exposure. The opaque nature of Chinese infrastructure financing in Suriname has raised governance and sovereignty concerns.

Name: Tanga Cement Factory
Description: The Chinese company, Sinoma and Hengya (T) Limited, pledged to commence the construction of a Tshs.2.3 trillion ($1 billion) cement factory in the Tanga region`s Mkinga District, very soon.

Name: Tanzania Standard Gauge Railway (Dar es Salaam–Mwanza)
Description: Tanzania's Standard Gauge Railway (SGR) is a 2,561 km national rail project linking the Indian Ocean port of Dar es Salaam to Mwanza on Lake Victoria, with planned spurs to Burundi, Rwanda, Democratic Republic of Congo, and Uganda. The total project is valued at approximately $7.6 billion. Construction has been phased: the first section (Dar es Salaam to Morogoro, 300 km) was awarded to Turkish-Portuguese consortium Yapı Merkezi-MOTA-ENGIL for approximately $1.9 billion; however, subsequent sections have involved Chinese financing and contractors. In December 2022, Tanzania signed a $2.2 billion contract with a Chinese company for a later section of the line. Chinese involvement across various phases links the Tanzania SGR to the BRI framework. The SGR is designed to replace Tanzania's outdated colonial-era narrow-gauge railway and will become the backbone of the Central Corridor, connecting the coast to Central Africa. The line is part of the East African Railway Master Plan designed according to Chinese Class 2 standards.

Name: Tavan Tolgoi–Gashuunsukhait Railway
Description: The Tavan Tolgoi–Gashuunsukhait Railway is a 236 km coal export railway in southern Mongolia connecting the Tavan Tolgoi coal deposit — one of the world's largest coking coal reserves with estimated reserves of 7.4 billion tonnes — to the Gashuunsukhait border crossing with China. The line was completed and opened in August 2022, financed in part by China Development Bank. The railway dramatically cuts the cost and time of exporting coal from Tavan Tolgoi to Chinese steel mills versus the previous truck-based transport route, which was expensive and environmentally damaging. Capacity is approximately 30 million tonnes per year. The line is a centrepiece of the China–Mongolia–Russia Economic Corridor (CMREC), the BRI sub-corridor running from northern China through Mongolia to the Russian Far East. Mongolia joined the BRI in December 2013 and coal exports to China form the backbone of its export economy, with China receiving over 90% of Mongolian exports by value.

Name: Thailand–China High-Speed Rail (Bangkok–Korat)
Description: The Thailand–China High-Speed Rail project is a 220 km elevated standard-gauge railway between Bangkok (Kaeng Khoi) and Nakhon Ratchasima (Korat), forming Phase 1 of a planned 873 km corridor connecting Bangkok to the Chinese border via Nong Khai, ultimately linking to the Laos-China Railway at Vientiane. China Railway International Company Limited is the primary contractor, using Chinese railway standards and technology. The Thai government is funding the project from its own budget (not through Chinese loans) after rejecting Chinese loan terms in 2017 as too expensive. Total cost for Phase 1 is approximately THB 179 billion ($5.2 billion). Construction on the first 3.5 km section commenced in December 2017. The broader project has faced repeated delays over financing structure disputes, land acquisition, and technical disagreements — as of 2025 only initial sections are under construction. When complete, the Bangkok–Nakhon Ratchasima section will reduce travel time from 3.5 hours to about 1.5 hours. Thailand joined the BRI in December 2014 and the Bangkok–Kunming High-Speed Railway corridor is a centrepiece of China's vision for a Kunming–Singapore Railway linking all major Southeast Asian capitals to China.

Name: Tinaco–Anaco Railway (Abandoned)
Description: The Tinaco–Anaco Railway is a 468 km freight and passenger railway line through central Venezuela, connecting Anaco in Anzoátegui State to Tinaco in Cojedes State, funded through the China–Venezuela Strategic Development Fund. In 2009, China and Venezuela entered a $7.5 billion joint venture for the project, with China Railway Engineering Corporation (CREC) holding a 40% stake. The groundbreaking was held on March 22, 2009. The line was designed with 10 stations and 25 bridges and one tunnel, intended to transport 190 million tonnes of cargo and 210 million passengers annually, primarily serving the Orinoco oil belt workers and agricultural communities. Total disbursements exceeded $2.14 billion across multiple tranches from Venezuela's Economic and Social Development Bank (BANDES). However, construction stalled repeatedly — only about a third of the route was built before Chinese contractors withdrew. After Venezuelan workers and locals stripped materials from abandoned construction sites, the project was effectively abandoned. It stands as a major example of the failure of China's loans-for-oil infrastructure programme in Venezuela.

Name: Tokha–Chhahare Tunnel (Nepal–China Connectivity)
Description: The Tokha–Chhahare Tunnel is a proposed road tunnel connecting Kathmandu's northern ring road at Tokha to Chhahare in Nuwakot District, forming a strategic route connecting the Nepalese capital directly to the Chinese border at Kerung. The tunnel is part of Nepal's BRI cooperation framework and was identified as a priority connectivity project during Prime Minister KP Sharma Oli's December 2024 state visit to Beijing, where Nepal and China signed the 'Framework for Belt and Road Cooperation.' A feasibility study is pending, with Nepal requesting the study before an environmental impact assessment, while China has proposed the reverse sequence. The tunnel forms a critical first section of what would become a direct road link from Kathmandu to the Chinese border, complementing the proposed Kerung–Kathmandu Railway. It is part of a cluster of BRI-linked cross-border connectivity projects also including the Hilsa–Simikot Road (95 km, part of the Karnali Economic Corridor), and the Kimathanka–Khandbari Road and Bridge in the Koshi Corridor. Nepal joined the BRI in May 2017 and the Trans-Himalayan Multi-dimensional Connectivity Network (THMCN) is one of the BRI's six official overland corridors. Nepal's BRI engagement is strategically significant as it offers China an overland route to South Asian markets and reduces Nepal's near-total dependence on India for surface trade access.

Name: Toromocho mine
Description: China Copper holds the Toromocho Copper mine in central Peru, via its parent company Aluminum Corporation of China (Chalco), the state-owned metal giant.

Name: Tren Maya – Section 1 (CCCC)
Description: China Communications Construction Company (CCCC), a Chinese state-owned enterprise and major Belt and Road Initiative contractor, participated in the construction of Section 1 of the Tren Maya — Mexico's flagship 1,554 km intercity railway traversing the Yucatán Peninsula — with an investment of $630 million. CCCC was part of a consortium led by Portugal-based Mota-Engil, alongside Grupo Cosh and Eyasa y Gavil Ingeniería. The Tren Maya connects the states of Chiapas, Tabasco, Campeche, Yucatán, and Quintana Roo, linking major tourist destinations including Cancún, Tulum, Playa del Carmen, and Palenque across 34 stations. Construction began in June 2020 and the first section commenced operations on December 15, 2023. The total project cost is approximately $29 billion. CCCC is sanctioned by the United States government. Mexico has not formally signed a BRI Memorandum of Understanding.

Name: Uruguay BRI Partnership & Port Logistics
Description: Uruguay became the first Mercosur country and among the first in South America to sign a Belt and Road Initiative Memorandum of Understanding with China in 2018. Uruguay is a strategic BRI partner due to its status as the best deep-water harbour on the South Atlantic, its free port law (which allows goods to be re-routed to Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay, and Bolivia), and its position as the second most visited destination globally by refrigerated cargo vessels. China is Uruguay's most important trading partner, purchasing 27% of its exports — primarily beef, timber, mutton, and wool. Under the BRI framework, China and Uruguay have pursued cooperation in renewable energy infrastructure, port logistics, telecoms and digital technology, and agricultural supply chains. Key ongoing projects include energy infrastructure construction by a Chinese company and expansion of port facilities at Montevideo and Nueva Palmira. Uruguay signed over twelve bilateral agreements during President Yamandú Orsi's state visit to China in March 2026, covering science, technology, environment, and trade.

Name: Velana International Airport
Description: On 6 October 2022, a new Seaplane Terminal was opened.[22] The terminal was developed by China’s Beijing Urban Construction Group (BUCG) at a cost of US$55 million.

Name: Victoria Falls Airport Upgrade
Description: In April 2013, Exim Bank of China provided a $150 million loan to build the airport's new runway, taxiways and a new terminal to increase the airport's capacity from 500,000 to 1.7 million passengers annually.

Name: Victoria State BRI Agreement (Cancelled 2021)
Description: In October 2018, Victorian Premier Daniel Andrews signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with China's National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC) — the top economic planning body of the Chinese government — to cooperate within the framework of the Belt and Road Initiative. In October 2019, Andrews signed a more detailed Framework Agreement expanding on the MoU, without consulting the Australian federal Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT). The agreements aimed to facilitate Chinese state-owned companies tendering for Victorian infrastructure projects and enable Victorian firms to operate in China. No concrete projects were ever executed. On April 21, 2021, Australian Foreign Minister Marise Payne cancelled both agreements under Australia's Foreign Relations Act (2020), declaring them "inconsistent with Australia's foreign policy or adverse to our foreign relations" — making Australia the first country in the world to formally cancel signed BRI agreements with China. China's embassy called the move "another unreasonable and provocative" act. The cancellation was widely understood as a geopolitical signal amid a dramatic deterioration in Australia-China relations over COVID-19 investigations, Huawei bans, foreign interference concerns, and trade sanctions.

Name: Western Europe–Western China Highway (Kazakhstan)
Description: The Western Europe–Western China International Transit Corridor is an 8,445 km intercontinental highway running from St. Petersburg, Russia to the Chinese port of Lianyungang on the Yellow Sea, with 2,787 km passing through Kazakhstan. Kazakhstan invested approximately $3.5 billion in its road section under the Nurly Zhol (Bright Path) national infrastructure programme, co-financed by China Eximbank, the Asian Development Bank, and the World Bank. The corridor opened fully in 2017 and is the primary overland freight route connecting Chinese factories to European markets, reducing transit time from approximately 45 days by sea to 11–14 days by road. Kazakhstan processes approximately 4 million tonnes of transit cargo annually and earns transit fees estimated at up to $5 billion per year — making transit logistics one of the country's fastest-growing revenue streams. Kazakhstan joined the BRI in August 2015 and is the single most important transit country in the BRI's Eurasian land corridor, with the Khorgos–Eastern Gate dry port at its eastern end serving as the primary rail gauge-change hub between China and the former Soviet rail network.

Name: Indonesia Morowali Industrial Park (IMIP) – Nickel Processing Hub
Description:
The Indonesia Morowali Industrial Park (IMIP) is a flagship Belt and Road Initiative project and Asia's largest nickel processing complex, located in the Morowali regency of Central Sulawesi, Indonesia. It is the template for China's global critical minerals strategy — and has transformed Indonesia into the world's dominant nickel producer, accounting for 50% of global production as of 2024.

The project originated from a 2009 joint venture between China's Tsingshan Group (through its subsidiary Shanghai Decent Investment Group) and Indonesia's Bintang Delapan Group. The formal BRI cooperation agreement was signed in October 2013 with Xi Jinping and then-President Yudhoyono presiding over the ceremony. Construction began shortly thereafter and the first smelter opened in 2015. The industrial park now covers approximately 4,000 hectares and, as of July 2023, hosts 43 operating nickel smelters under the BRI framework.

Tsingshan — the world's largest producer of ferronickel and stainless steel, with 2024 revenues of $57.3 billion — controls approximately 66% of IMIP through Shanghai Decent. The park is also a hub for Chinese battery supply chain companies: Zhejiang Huayou Cobalt and GEM Co. operate High Pressure Acid Leach (HPAL) plants producing battery-grade nickel and cobalt; CATL has a 6% stake; and Lygend Resources (part of the CATL group) also operates in the park. Total investment across IMIP exceeds $20 billion, with Chinese banks — both policy banks in the early phase and commercial banks thereafter — providing the bulk of financing.

The park has evolved from producing nickel pig iron for stainless steel to producing battery-grade nickel chemicals for EV batteries, supplying factories that account for over 40% of global EV production. Indonesia's nickel export revenues skyrocketed from $6 billion in 2013 to nearly $30 billion in 2022. However, Chinese companies control approximately 75% of Indonesia's nickel refining capacity. The park employs over 43,000 people (approximately 38,000 Indonesian). Environmental costs have been severe: over 8,700 hectares of rainforest cleared, coal-powered captive generation capacity of approximately 5 GW, air and water pollution, and 90+ worker deaths and 100+ injuries recorded between 2015 and 2023.

Name: Indonesia Weda Bay Industrial Park (IWIP) – Nickel & EV Battery Complex
Description:
The Indonesia Weda Bay Industrial Park (IWIP) is a Chinese-led mega-scale nickel mining and processing complex in Central Halmahera Regency, North Maluku, Indonesia, billed as the world's first fully vertical — from mine to finished product — integrated EV battery and stainless steel industry complex. It is one of Indonesia's designated National Strategic Projects and a core Belt and Road Initiative investment.

The project began when China's Tsingshan Group acquired a 57% stake in Weda Bay Minerals (a joint venture with France's Eramet) in 2017, taking over responsibility for mineral processing. Construction of the industrial park commenced in April 2018; mining operations began in October 2019 and metallurgical production in April 2020. The park is managed by PT Indonesia Weda Bay Industrial Park (IWIP), owned by: Tsingshan Group (46%, through Perlux Technology), Zhenshi Holding Group (24%), Zhejiang Huayou Cobalt Group (24%), and CATL (6%). Total committed investment is approximately $15 billion, with actual investment exceeding $5 billion by 2024.

The park covers approximately 5,000 hectares and now employs approximately 70,000 workers (with a target of 100,000 by 2027), 16,400 of whom are employed directly at the Weda Bay nickel mine, with 68% originating from North Maluku province. Key industrial tenants include: PT Weda Bay Nickel (now the world's largest nickel mine, with 42 million wet metric tonnes per year permitted production); PT Huafei Nickel Cobalt (the world's largest HPAL plant, $2.3 billion investment, producing 150,000+ tonnes of battery nickel annually); PT Yashi Indonesia Investment (300,000 tonnes of ferronickel per year); and PT Youshan Nickel Indonesia. Captive coal-fired power capacity in the park exceeds 4,500 MW, making it one of the largest single coal consumers in Southeast Asia. Deforestation, flooding of surrounding villages, water contamination, and labour abuses have been extensively documented.

Name: Main Line 1 (ML-1) Railway Upgrade – Karachi to Peshawar
Description: Main Line 1 (ML-1) is Pakistan's most critical railway upgrade under CPEC and the single largest infrastructure project in the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor. The project covers the complete upgrade and dualization of Pakistan's 1,872 km main railway line from Karachi to Peshawar — a route that currently handles approximately 70% of all Pakistan Railways freight and passenger traffic. Planned upgrades include doubling the track throughout, raising maximum speeds from 60–105 km/h to 160 km/h, grade separation, new communications-based train control systems, the reconstruction of 21 major stations, and procurement of 250 new passenger coaches. The project would cut the Karachi–Peshawar journey time in half and is expected to increase Pakistan Railways' annual revenues by approximately $480 million. As of early 2024, the project's revised cost was approved at $6.76 billion across two phases. However, ML-1 has been repeatedly stalled: suspended over Pakistan's debt concerns in 2022, and still awaiting commencement of construction as of 2025. Pakistan and China agreed to proceed at the 13th JCC meeting in May 2024, with bidding to commence among eligible Chinese contractors. ML-1 is also the backbone on which any future railway extension into Afghanistan via Peshawar depends. Pakistan joined the BRI in December 2013; CPEC was officially launched during President Xi's April 2015 state visit to Islamabad.

Name: Lahore Orange Line Metro
Description: The Lahore Orange Line Metro Train is Pakistan's first mass rapid transit system and one of the most prominent urban infrastructure projects of the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC). The 27.1 km elevated and partially underground metro line runs across 26 stations through central Lahore, connecting Ali Town in the southwest to Dera Gujran in the east. It was jointly constructed by China Railway Group Co. Ltd. (CR Group) and China North Industries Corporation (NORINCO). Total cost was approximately $1.6 billion, with $1.46 billion financed by a 20-year concessional loan from China's Export-Import Bank at 2% interest. Construction began in October 2015 after a delayed start due to objections from the Supreme Court of Pakistan over cultural heritage concerns, as the line passes near 11 protected heritage buildings. The metro was inaugurated on October 26, 2020 by Prime Minister Imran Khan, five years after groundbreaking. The system uses CRRC-manufactured electric trains running at up to 80 km/h, with a designed capacity of 500,000 passengers per day across 24 elevated and 2 underground stations. As Pakistan's first electric railway transit system, it was praised as transformative for Lahore's congested traffic. However, operational costs have been a challenge, with subsidies required to keep fares affordable. Pakistan joined the BRI in December 2013.

Name: Multan–Sukkur Motorway (M-5 / CPEC PKM)
Description: The Multan–Sukkur Motorway (M-5) is a 392 km, six-lane controlled-access motorway forming the southern section of the Peshawar–Karachi Motorway (PKM) — the longest motorway in Pakistan. It was built by China State Construction Engineering Corporation (CSCEC) under CPEC, at a total cost of approximately $2.89 billion financed through a Chinese government loan via China Development Bank. Construction began in 2016 and the motorway was completed and inaugurated in November 2019. The M-5 connects Multan in south Punjab to Sukkur in northern Sindh, traversing the agricultural heartland of Pakistan along the Indus River floodplain. Before its construction, this stretch was served by an old two-lane National Highway plagued by congestion, frequent accidents, and poor road surfaces. The motorway reduces the Multan–Sukkur journey time from approximately 6 hours to 3.5 hours. As part of the broader CPEC Eastern Alignment, the PKM corridor links Karachi Port (CPEC's maritime gateway) northward through the major population centres of Punjab to Islamabad, and ultimately to the Karakoram Highway leading to China. The motorway employs smart tolling, emergency call boxes, surveillance cameras, and rest areas. Pakistan joined the BRI in December 2013 and CPEC represents over $60 billion in total committed investment.

Name: Karot Hydropower Station (Silk Road Fund)
Description: The Karot Hydropower Station is a 720 MW run-of-river hydroelectric project on the Jhelum River in Azad Kashmir and Punjab, approximately 55 km from Islamabad. It is the first investment project of China's Silk Road Fund — the $40 billion state investment vehicle established by President Xi in December 2014 specifically to finance BRI projects — making it one of the most symbolically significant CPEC energy investments. The project is owned by Karot Power Company Limited (KPCL), with China Power International Holding Ltd holding the majority stake via its subsidiary Three Gorges South Asia Investment Ltd. Construction began in 2016 and the plant achieved full commercial operation in June 2022, six months ahead of schedule. Total investment was approximately $1.7 billion. The dam is a 95-metre-high concrete-face rockfill structure impounding the Jhelum River, with an installed capacity of 6 × 120 MW Francis turbines and an average annual electricity generation of approximately 3.2 billion kWh. Karot is expected to reduce Pakistan's carbon dioxide emissions by 3.5 million tonnes per year and contributes approximately $154 million annually to Pakistan's GDP. It represents a shift in CPEC energy from coal-fired power (which dominated the 'Early Harvest' phase) toward cleaner hydropower, consistent with both countries' climate commitments. Pakistan joined the BRI in December 2013.

Name: Suki Kinari Hydropower Project (884 MW)
Description: The Suki Kinari Hydropower Project is an 884 MW run-of-river hydroelectric plant on the Kunhar River in the Kaghan Valley, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province — the largest hydropower project under CPEC and one of Pakistan's most important clean energy investments. The project is developed by SK Hydro (Pvt) Ltd, a joint venture between China Gezhouba Group Corporation (CGGC), a major Chinese state-owned hydropower developer, and Abdul Constructions Pvt Ltd. Total cost is approximately $1.73 billion, with financing from China's Export-Import Bank. Construction commenced in 2016 and the project achieved commercial operations in September 2024 after years of delays caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, difficult mountainous terrain, security threats, and construction challenges in the Kaghan Valley. At its first anniversary in September 2025, Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal highlighted the project as a turning point for Pakistan's energy security. The plant will generate approximately 3.2 billion kWh per year, avoiding approximately 2 million tonnes of CO₂ emissions annually and contributing significantly to Pakistan's grid during peak demand periods. The Kaghan Valley site is among the most scenic and seismically challenging in Pakistan's hydropower belt. Pakistan joined the BRI in December 2013; CPEC energy investment has added over 8,020 MW of new generation capacity across 16 completed projects as of 2024.

Name: Sahiwal Coal Power Plant (1,320 MW)
Description: The Sahiwal Coal Power Plant is a 1,320 MW (2 × 660 MW) coal-fired power plant in Sahiwal, Punjab, built under CPEC as one of the first major energy projects to reach completion in the 'Early Harvest' phase. It was developed by Huaneng Shandong Ruyi (Pakistan) Energy Pvt Ltd, a subsidiary of China Huaneng Group and Shandong Ruyi Group, at a total investment of approximately $1.91 billion, with financing from Chinese commercial banks. Construction commenced in May 2015 and the plant achieved full commercial operations in July 2017 — in just 26 months, a record for a project of this size. It was one of the fastest-completed power projects in Pakistan's history. The plant uses ultra-supercritical coal combustion technology, designed to run on imported coal. It directly supplies 3,700–4,000 direct jobs and generates approximately 9 billion kWh per year, equivalent to approximately 10% of Pakistan's total installed generation capacity at the time of its completion. Sahiwal Power Plant was cited by CPEC proponents as proof that Chinese investment could rapidly eliminate Pakistan's chronic electricity shortage, which had previously caused load-shedding of 12–18 hours per day in many areas. However, critics note that as an imported-coal plant, it exposes Pakistan to international coal price volatility and raises long-term debt sustainability concerns. Pakistan joined the BRI in December 2013 and CPEC energy projects have collectively added over 8,000 MW to the national grid.

Name: Mes Aynak Copper Mine (MCC/Jiangxi Copper)
Description: Mes Aynak is one of the world's largest undeveloped copper deposits, located in Logar Province, approximately 40 km southeast of Kabul, with estimated reserves of 450–700 million tonnes of copper ore. In 2007 — under the US-backed Karzai government, before the BRI era — the Afghan Ministry of Mines awarded a $2.93 billion, 30-year copper extraction contract to a consortium of two Chinese state-owned companies: China Metallurgical Group Corporation (MCC) and Jiangxi Copper Corporation. It was the largest foreign investment in Afghanistan's history at the time. The contract included commitments to build a 400 MW coal-fired power plant, a railroad connecting the mine to Pakistan and China, a copper smelter, and supporting infrastructure. However, the project has been mired in delay since award: the site is overlaid with significant Buddhist archaeological ruins (one of the largest Buddhist sites in Asia, dating to the 2nd–5th century AD), which triggered years of disputes over excavation timelines; security deteriorated as Taliban activity increased; and the Karzai and subsequent governments renegotiated contractual terms. After the Taliban takeover in August 2021, Beijing saw an opportunity to relaunch the project. In July 2024, Chinese officials held a groundbreaking ceremony for access road construction, expected to be completed in 2025. A joint China-Afghanistan market in Logar Province was announced in November 2024. Disagreements persist over power plant construction, underground vs. open-pit mining methodology, and processing plant requirements. Afghanistan joined the BRI in May 2023.

Name: Wakhan Corridor Road (Afghanistan–China Border Link)
Description:
The Wakhan Corridor Road is a proposed and partially under-construction road traversing Afghanistan's Wakhan Corridor — a narrow, 350 km-long strip of territory in Badakhshan province that forms Afghanistan's only direct land border with China (92.45 km at the Wakhjir Pass). The corridor is the missing link that could connect Afghanistan directly to China's BRI network in Xinjiang, bypassing Pakistan entirely — a strategic priority for the Taliban government, which has sought to reduce its dependence on Pakistani border crossings at Torkham and Chaman amid deteriorating Kabul-Islamabad relations.

The Taliban's Al-Emarah English stated that road construction is progressing in two stages: Stage 1 covers 50 km from Bazai Gonbad in the Little Pamir to the zero-point border with China, with 60% of construction complete as of March 2025; Stage 2 covers 71 km, targeted for completion by end of 2025. Total cost of the Afghan-funded Stage 1 is approximately $5.16 million — a fraction of what would be needed for a commercially viable route. China has so far adopted a cautious, wait-and-see posture toward the corridor, viewing it primarily as a counterterrorism security concern (a potential entry route for Uyghur militants from ETIM) rather than a commercial opportunity. The pass is accessible only five months per year due to extreme altitude and climate. Chinese discussions with the Taliban on road, rail, and pipeline connections through Wakhan continued into late 2024. Afghanistan joined the BRI in May 2023 and the Taliban views the Wakhan Corridor as its most strategic future asset for direct China engagement outside Pakistani territory.

Name: CPEC Extension to Afghanistan (China–Pakistan–Afghanistan Trilateral)
Description: In May 2023, the Foreign Ministers of China, Pakistan, and Afghanistan held the fifth China-Pakistan-Afghanistan Foreign Ministers' Dialogue in Islamabad and formally agreed to extend the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) into Afghanistan, incorporating the country fully into China's Belt and Road Initiative framework. This marked Afghanistan's official institutional entry into the CPEC framework — coming just weeks after Afghanistan joined the BRI (May 2023). On May 21, 2025, the three countries again reaffirmed their commitment to this extension at an informal trilateral meeting in Beijing. Under the proposal, CPEC would be extended northward from Peshawar into Afghanistan via the Khyber Pass and Kabul, ultimately connecting to Central Asia. Key planned elements include an extension of the Karakoram Highway from Hasan Abdal to the Afghan border, a potential Peshawar–Jalalabad railway for which Pakistan Railways and China Railway Engineering Corporation (CREC) have discussed a feasibility study, and eventual road and rail links connecting Afghanistan to the Gwadar and Karachi port complex. The project faces enormous practical obstacles: security attacks on Chinese workers in Pakistan, Taliban-Pakistan tensions over the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan, Pakistan's own CPEC debt challenges, and China's institutional risk aversion toward large-scale Afghanistan commitments. Nevertheless, as of 2025, the trilateral framework remains the central diplomatic architecture for China's engagement in Afghanistan. Afghanistan joined the BRI in May 2023.

Name: HBIS Smederevo Steel Plant (Hesteel Group Serbia)
Description: HBIS Group Serbia (formerly Hesteel Serbia) is China's most prominent BRI industrial acquisition in Eastern Europe and a flagship example of Chinese overseas capacity cooperation. In April 2016, Chinese state-owned steel giant HBIS Group (Hebei Iron and Steel Group, the world's second-largest steelmaker) acquired the Smederevo Steel Plant — a 110-year-old facility on the Danube, 70 km from Belgrade — for approximately €46 million ($56 million USD), after years of losses under US Steel (2003–2012) and subsequent state management. The acquisition was attended by President Xi Jinping during his June 2016 state visit to Serbia, cementing its symbolic BRI status. HBIS retained all 5,000 workers and the plant turned profitable within months, producing a record 1.77 million tonnes of steel in 2020. By 2024, HBIS Serbia had accumulated approximately €4.77 billion in cumulative export earnings and ranked as Serbia's largest or second-largest exporter most years, contributing approximately 1.15% of Serbia's GDP in 2023. The plant produces hot-rolled and cold-rolled steel products, primarily for the European automotive supply chain. However, significant environmental controversy surrounds the plant: local NGOs and an oncologist in Smederevo have documented a marked increase in cancer rates and heavy metal dust pollution in surrounding villages, while Serbia's Environmental Protection Agency has repeatedly issued warnings without enforcement action.

Name: Kostolac Coal Power Plant Expansion (CMEC)
Description: The Kostolac B Coal Power Plant Expansion is a major Chinese-financed BRI energy project at the Kostolac thermal power complex on the Danube River in Serbia, comprising two phases: desulphurisation upgrades to existing units B1 and B2, and a proposed new 350 MW lignite unit (Kostolac B3). Phase 1 (desulphurisation): In 2011, Serbia's state-owned electricity utility Elektroprivreda Srbije (EPS) took a €224 million loan from China Eximbank, guaranteed by Serbia's Ministry of Finance, to finance flue gas desulphurisation systems for Kostolac B1 and B2. China Machinery Engineering Corporation (CMEC) was the EPC contractor. The system was never properly put into operation despite repeated public complaints, and as of 2021, Kostolac B1 emitted more SO₂ alone than the legal ceiling for all 12 of Serbia's combined combustion plants. Phase 2 (Kostolac B3): In November 2013, EPS signed a contract with CMEC for a new 350 MW coal unit (Kostolac B3) at a cost of approximately €715 million, financed by China Eximbank. Ground preparation began in 2020 but full construction has not commenced amid ongoing scrutiny under the Espoo and Århus Conventions and the EU Energy Community Treaty. The project is non-compliant with EU Large Combustion Plant pollution standards. Serbia joined the BRI in November 2015 and is China's single most important BRI partner in the Western Balkans, having received over €7 billion in total Chinese investment.

Name: Stanari Thermal Power Plant (Dongfang Electric)
Description: The Stanari Thermal Power Plant is a 300 MW lignite-fired power plant in Stanari, Republika Srpska, approximately 70 km east of Banja Luka, built as a BRI-aligned project under the China-Central and Eastern European Countries (CEEC) 16+1 framework. It is 100% owned by UK-registered EFT Group, a private energy trading company operating across Southeast Europe. The plant cost approximately €500 million, with China Development Bank providing a €350 million loan — the largest credit facility for a private enterprise in Bosnia and Herzegovina's history. China's Dongfang Electric Corporation was the EPC contractor, constructing the facility adjacent to the Stanari coal mine (108 million tonne reserves). The plant began commercial operations in September 2016. It generates approximately 2 million MWh of electricity per year and created approximately 800 permanent jobs. Bosnia and Herzegovina joined the BRI in May 2017. The Stanari project was the first successful example of BRI-linked energy infrastructure in Bosnia, but it proceeded without a proper environmental impact assessment (EIA), triggering criminal complaints from local and international NGOs. The plant is not compliant with EU Large Combustion Plant standards, and its construction and operation have been repeatedly challenged under the Energy Community Treaty, which Bosnia has signed as part of its EU accession pathway. Critics describe the project as a template for how Chinese BRI energy investment circumvents EU environmental standards in EU-candidate countries.

Name: Tuzla Block 7 Coal Power Plant (Gezhouba – Cancelled)
Description: Tuzla Block 7 was a planned 450 MW lignite-fired power plant unit at the Tuzla Thermal Power Plant — Bosnia and Herzegovina's largest power station — designed to replace ageing units with new Chinese-built capacity. It is one of the most significant failed BRI energy projects in Europe, ultimately cancelled in 2024 after a decade of controversy. An Engineering, Procurement and Construction (EPC) contract worth €785 million was signed in August 2014 between Elektroprivreda Bosne i Hercegovine (state utility) and China Gezhouba Group Co. China Eximbank was to provide a €614 million loan, backed by a Bosnian state guarantee approved by the Federal Parliament in March 2019 despite an Energy Community Secretariat ruling that the guarantee violated EU State Aid law. General Electric withdrew as equipment supplier in 2020, and Gezhouba Group subsequently also pulled out in September 2018 amid financing disputes. By December 2023, Federal Prime Minister Nermin Nikšić confirmed the project was definitively cancelled, and in April 2024 the EPC contract was officially terminated. The project generated over 100 documented legal complaints from environmental groups across Bosnia and the region. It was projected to emit at least 2.3 million tonnes of CO₂ per year and violated multiple EU air quality standards. Bosnia and Herzegovina joined the BRI in May 2017.

Name: Kičevo–Ohrid & Miladinovci–Štip Highways (Sinohydro)
Description: The Kičevo–Ohrid Highway and Miladinovci–Štip Highway are the two major Chinese BRI infrastructure projects in North Macedonia, both built by Sinohydro Corporation (a subsidiary of PowerChina), one of China's largest state-owned hydropower and construction companies. The Kičevo–Ohrid Highway is a 57 km expressway in western North Macedonia, connecting the town of Kičevo with Ohrid on Lake Ohrid — a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Construction began in 2014 and has faced repeated delays, controversies over route changes, and complaints of damaged private property and river ecosystem destruction. The Miladinovci–Štip Highway is a 57 km expressway in the eastern part of the country. Both projects were financed through China Eximbank loans, and North Macedonia was the first country in the 16+1 framework to draw on the $10 billion credit line Beijing made available for CEE infrastructure. Sinohydro received numerous complaints for construction practices including encroachment on private land and damage to local rivers. North Macedonia joined the BRI in December 2013 and the two highways form part of Pan-European Corridor VIII, which runs east-west across the southern Balkans from Albania to Bulgaria, and are strategically important for BRI connectivity between the Aegean (Port of Thessaloniki) and Central Europe.

Name: Cernavodă Nuclear Power Plant Units 3 & 4 (CGN – Cancelled)
Description: The Cernavodă Nuclear Power Plant Units 3 & 4 project was China's most ambitious attempted BRI investment in the EU, involving an $8 billion plan to complete two partially built CANDU-6 nuclear reactors at Romania's only nuclear facility on the Danube near the Black Sea. Romania signed a Memorandum of Understanding with China General Nuclear Power Group (CGN) in November 2015 during the 16+1 summit. In May 2019, Nuclearelectrica signed a Preliminary Investors Agreement with CGN and its subsidiary CEE Investment (Romania), establishing a joint venture to develop Cernavoda Units 3 & 4, each rated at approximately 700 MW. CGN would hold a minimum 51% stake in the joint venture. After six years of negotiations from 2013, the project became the centrepiece of Romania-China BRI energy cooperation. However, in January 2020, Romania's government cancelled the CGN agreement, citing security concerns and alignment with NATO allies. In October 2020, Romania and the United States signed a draft Intergovernmental Agreement to cooperate on the project instead, with US expertise replacing Chinese technology. The cancellation reflected the broader deterioration of Chinese BRI ambitions in EU member states following US pressure, Huawei security controversies, and CGN's listing on the US Commerce Department Entity List in August 2019 for alleged nuclear weapons proliferation activities. Romania joined the BRI in June 2015 but has since significantly distanced itself from Chinese infrastructure engagement.

Name: Pelješac Bridge (CRBC – EU Funded)
Description: The Pelješac Bridge is a 2.4 km suspension bridge spanning the Mali Ston Bay on Croatia's Dalmatian coast, connecting the Croatian mainland with the Pelješac peninsula and eliminating a geographical interruption in Croatia's territory caused by Bosnia and Herzegovina's narrow 26 km coastal strip at Neum. It is the most significant BRI-linked infrastructure project completed within a European Union member state. The EPC contract was won in a fully competitive EU public procurement process in January 2018 by China Road and Bridge Corporation (CRBC), a subsidiary of China Communications Construction Company (CCCC), with a bid of €282 million — approximately €50 million less than the nearest competing bid from Austrian firm Strabag. The project is 85% co-financed by EU Cohesion Funds, with the remaining 15% from Croatian state funds; there is no Chinese financing. Construction began in July 2018 and the bridge was inaugurated on July 26, 2022, by Prime Minister Andrej Plenković and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. This project is notable as the only EU-funded project built by a major Chinese BRI contractor, and demonstrates CRBC's ability to compete and win on technical merit and cost in a fully transparent Western procurement environment. Croatia joined the BRI in May 2017.

Name: Padma Bridge Rail Link (CREC)
Description: The Padma Bridge Rail Link Project (PBRLP) is Bangladesh's largest BRI infrastructure project — and the largest infrastructure project in Bangladesh financed through Chinese loans. It involves the construction of a 172 km double-track railway from Dhaka to Jessore (via Bhanga) using the lower deck of the Padma Multipurpose Bridge, at a total cost of approximately $4.63 billion. The project is executed by Bangladesh Railway in collaboration with China Railway Group Limited (CREC), with the Corps of Engineers of the Bangladesh Army as construction supervision consultant. Financing was provided through a government concessional loan from China's Export-Import Bank (Eximbank) of approximately $2.67 billion — the largest single Chinese loan to Bangladesh. Bangladesh and China signed the loan MoU in October 2016 during President Xi Jinping's state visit to Dhaka. Phase 1, the 82 km Dhaka–Bhanga section crossing the Padma Bridge, was inaugurated on October 10, 2023. When the full 172 km line to Jessore is complete, it will cut the Dhaka–Khulna journey from six hours to three, benefit an estimated 80 million people in south-western Bangladesh, and is projected to boost GDP by approximately 1.5%. Chinese Ambassador to Bangladesh Yao Wen described it as the 'largest infrastructure project in Bangladesh using Chinese preferential loans' and a 'landmark project under the BRI.' Bangladesh joined the BRI in October 2016 during Xi's Dhaka visit.

Name: Karnaphuli Multi-Channel Tunnel (Bangabandhu Tunnel)
Description: The Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman Tunnel, commonly known as the Karnaphuli Tunnel, is South Asia's first underwater road tunnel, running 3.32 km beneath the Karnaphuli River in Chattogram (Chittagong), Bangladesh. Completed and inaugurated on October 28, 2023 by Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, the tunnel connects Chattogram city to its south bank — site of the Chinese Economic and Industrial Zone (CEIZ) and the developing Cox's Bazar corridor — and reduces a four-hour journey via road detour to approximately 20 minutes. The project was built by China Communications Construction Company (CCCC) under a $1.7 billion EPC contract, financed 85% ($1.45 billion) by a Chinese government concessional loan from China Eximbank at 2% interest over 20 years, signed in December 2014. Construction began in February 2019 and deployed China's largest TBM (tunnel boring machine) exported at the time, with a diameter of 12.12 metres. The tunnel has two tubes, each with two lanes, totalling four lanes, and is designed for a 100-year lifespan. It is strategically important for developing south Chattogram, which hosts the CEIZ — Bangladesh's dedicated Chinese economic zone with capacity for 150–200 industrial units — as well as future BRI maritime connectivity through Chittagong Port, Bangladesh's primary seaport handling 92% of the country's trade. Bangladesh joined the BRI in October 2016.

Name: Payra 1320 MW Thermal Power Plant (BCPCL)
Description: The Payra 1,320 MW (2 × 660 MW) Thermal Power Plant is Bangladesh's largest power station and one of the flagship BRI energy projects in South Asia. It was developed by Bangladesh-China Power Company Limited (BCPCL), a 50/50 joint venture between Bangladesh Power Development Board (BPDB) and China National Machinery Import and Export Corporation (CMC). The total project cost was approximately $2.48 billion, financed through a Chinese government concessional loan from China Eximbank. The EPC contractor was China National Machinery Engineering Corporation (CMEC) — a subsidiary of China's state-owned SINOMACH group — and the plant was constructed at record speed of approximately 36 months per unit. Unit 1 achieved commercial operations in May 2020 and Unit 2 in January 2021. The plant is located in Lebukhali, Kalapara Upazila, Patuakhali District, in coastal southern Bangladesh, near the newly developing Payra Port — Bangladesh's third seaport. The power plant uses ultra-supercritical coal combustion technology and runs on imported coal, primarily from Indonesia and Australia. At inauguration, it met approximately 8–10% of Bangladesh's total electricity demand, directly addressing chronic nationwide load-shedding. Bangladesh signed BRI cooperation agreements in October 2016 and the Payra plant was among the eight flagship projects signed during President Xi Jinping's state visit to Dhaka.

Name: Colombo Port City (CHEC / CCCC)
Description: Colombo Port City — officially the Colombo International Financial City (CIFC) — is Sri Lanka's most ambitious BRI project and the largest foreign direct investment in the country's history: a $14 billion development built on 269 hectares of land reclaimed from the Indian Ocean adjacent to Colombo's Central Business District. The project was launched on September 17, 2014, during a state visit by Chinese President Xi Jinping, with China Harbour Engineering Company (CHEC), a subsidiary of China Communications Construction Company (CCCC), as the developer and reclamation contractor. The investment agreement was signed between CHEC Port City Colombo (CCCC's local subsidiary) and the Sri Lankan government. Land reclamation began immediately, creating entirely new land from the sea at a cost of approximately $1.4 billion for Phase 1. Sri Lanka's Parliament passed the Colombo Port City Economic Commission Act on May 20, 2021, officially designating the 269 hectares as the country's first Special Economic Zone for service-oriented industries, governed by a presidential commission with powers to license companies, regulate operations, and attract FDI in any recognised foreign currency. The city is designed as a rival to Singapore and Dubai — envisioned as a financial, business, and residential hub for South Asia, targeting $15 billion in total international investment and 83,000 jobs. It has faced intense controversy over land rights, environmental impact, displacement of coastal fishing communities, sovereignty concerns, opacity, and accusations of entrenching Sri Lanka's dependence on China. Sri Lanka joined the BRI in 2013 and has received over $12 billion in cumulative Chinese infrastructure investment.

Name: Norochcholai Coal Power Station (CMEC)
Description: The Lakvijaya (Norochcholai) Coal Power Station is Sri Lanka's largest power station and first coal-fired plant, located in Norochcholai, Puttalam District, on the northwestern coast. It has a total installed capacity of 900 MW across three units (each 300 MW). The project was initiated in 2006 under President Mahinda Rajapaksa, financed by the Export-Import Bank of China (Eximbank) at approximately $891 million for Phase 1 (Units 1 and 2), and constructed by China Machinery Engineering Corporation (CMEC). Phase 1 was commissioned in 2011 and Unit 3 in 2014. The Norochcholai plant is China's earliest major infrastructure investment in Sri Lanka and predates the formal BRI, but is consistently cited as a BRI-precursor project that established the Chinese infrastructure financing model in the country. The plant generates approximately 30–35% of Sri Lanka's electricity and significantly reduced dependence on expensive oil-fired power. However, the plant has been plagued by repeated breakdowns, technical failures, and fuel supply bottlenecks — Sri Lanka imports coal entirely by sea, and the absence of a deep-water coal terminal at Norochcholai required costly offshore transshipment.
