The plant's SO₂ and particulate emissions have been linked to threats to the Sri Maha Bodhi tree in Anuradhapura — considered the world's oldest historically documented tree — triggering significant environmental controversy. Sri Lanka is among China's most important Indian Ocean BRI partners, given its location on the Maritime Silk Road between the Strait of Malacca and the Suez Canal.

Name: Mattala Rajapaksa International Airport
Description: Mattala Rajapaksa International Airport (MRIA), located near Hambantota in southern Sri Lanka, was built as part of the broader Chinese BRI-linked infrastructure programme under President Mahinda Rajapaksa. It was constructed by China Machinery Engineering Corporation (CMEC) at a cost of approximately $209 million, financed through a Chinese government concessional loan from China Eximbank. The airport opened on March 18, 2013, and is Sri Lanka's second international airport. From its inception, MRIA was mocked internationally as 'the world's emptiest airport' — it is located 240 km from Colombo, near the already-troubled Hambantota Port, serves only a handful of domestic flights, and at various points operated with almost zero international passenger traffic. Single-digit weekly flights, bats roosting in the terminal, and elephants wandering the grounds became emblematic of China's 'white elephant' BRI projects. The airport's poor commercial performance contributed directly to Sri Lanka's debt crisis: unable to service its Chinese loans, the government in 2017 was compelled to hand over the nearby Hambantota Port to China Merchants Port Holdings on a 99-year lease in exchange for $1.12 billion in debt relief. MRIA has since been offered for lease or management to various international parties. The project remains one of the most cited examples globally of BRI 'debt trap' infrastructure, despite academic pushback on that specific framing. Sri Lanka joined the BRI in 2013 and has received approximately $13 billion in cumulative Chinese infrastructure investment.

Name: Sinamalé Bridge (China–Maldives Friendship Bridge)
Description: The Sinamalé Bridge — officially the China–Maldives Friendship Bridge — is the Maldives' first inter-island sea-crossing bridge, a 1.39 km prestressed concrete viaduct connecting the capital Malé to Hulhulé Island (site of Velana International Airport) and continuing to the reclaimed island of Hulhumalé. It is the flagship BRI infrastructure project in the Maldives and among the most symbolically significant projects on China's 21st Century Maritime Silk Road. The bridge was built by China Harbour Engineering Company (CHEC), a subsidiary of CCCC, at a total project cost of approximately $210–222 million. Financing comprised a $126 million grant from China's Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM), a $68 million government concessional loan from China Eximbank at 2% interest over 20 years, and a $12–14 million contribution from the Maldivian government. Construction officially began in February 2016 and the bridge opened on August 30, 2018 — completed in 33 months, ahead of the original schedule. The 20.3-metre-wide structure carries two car lanes, two motorcycle lanes, a bicycle lane, and a pedestrian path. Before the bridge, travel between Malé and the airport on Hulhulé required a 15-minute ferry journey, often with long queues; the bridge reduced this to minutes and transformed daily life for hundreds of thousands of people. The Maldives joined the BRI in 2014 under President Abdulla Yameen — one of the first South Asian countries to do so — and Chinese investment during Yameen's presidency totalled approximately $1.5 billion, raising significant debt sustainability concerns. The bridge is maintained free of charge by CCCC and as of 2025 remains in excellent condition per Chinese inspection teams.

Name: Pokhara International Airport (CAMC/SINOMACH)
Description: Pokhara International Airport (PIA) is a $216 million international airport in Pokhara, Nepal's second-largest city and primary tourism hub, built by China CAMC Engineering Co. Ltd. — the construction arm of China's state-owned SINOMACH group — and financed by a $215.96 million government concessional loan from China's Export-Import Bank (Eximbank). The agreement was signed with CAMC in 2013; construction proceeded from 2018, and the airport was inaugurated on January 1, 2023 by Prime Minister K.P. Sharma Oli. China's ambassador to Nepal declared it a 'flagship BRI project,' though the Nepali government formally contests this, as the airport contract predates Nepal's 2017 BRI accession. Despite its prominent inauguration as a gateway to the Annapurna Circuit and Nepal's western tourism corridor, PIA has since become one of Asia's most controversial BRI-associated white elephants. As of early 2025, the airport has no regular scheduled international flights — only occasional charter services from Kunming — due to the absence of ICAO certification, missing radar systems, terrain restrictions limiting narrowbody payload, and Indian airlines' reluctance to operate there given its Chinese BRI association. Nepal's anti-corruption agency CIAA filed the country's largest-ever corruption case in December 2025, charging 55 individuals (including five former ministers) and CAMC with inflating costs by at least $74 million through fake invoices, overbilling, substandard materials, and evasion of $16 million in contractual taxes. Nepal has asked China to convert the loan into a grant; China has not agreed. The debt repayments commenced in 2026.

Name: YASREF – Yanbu Aramco Sinopec Refinery
Description: The Yanbu Aramco Sinopec Refining Company (YASREF) is China's single largest investment project in Saudi Arabia and a flagship BRI industrial cooperation project, linking China's largest oil refiner (Sinopec) with Saudi Arabia's national oil company (Aramco) in a strategic downstream energy partnership. YASREF is a 400,000 barrel-per-day full-conversion oil refinery located in Yanbu Industrial City on Saudi Arabia's Red Sea coast, covering approximately 5.2 million square metres. The joint venture is structured as Aramco (62.5%) and Sinopec (37.5%), with a total investment of approximately $8.6–10 billion. Construction commenced in 2010 and the refinery entered formal commercial operations on January 20, 2016 — inaugurated jointly by Chinese President Xi Jinping and Saudi King Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud during Xi's state visit to Riyadh, cementing its symbolic BRI significance. YASREF processes Arabian heavy crude oil to produce ultra-low sulphur diesel (263,000 bpd), gasoline (105,000 bpd), petroleum coke (6,200 tonnes/day), sulphur, benzene, propane, and butane for both Saudi domestic markets and international export. The refinery won the S&P Global Platts 'Construction Project of the Year' at the 2015 Global Energy Awards. YASREF is the anchor project in Yanbu Industrial City and part of Saudi Arabia's Vision 2030 industrial diversification strategy. In April 2025, Aramco and Sinopec signed an expansion agreement for the Yanbu complex worth an additional $10 billion, including a 1.8 million tonnes/year steam cracker and 1.5 million tonnes/year aromatics complex. Saudi Arabia joined the BRI in January 2016 and signed a BRI-Vision 2030 synergy agreement in 2022. China is Saudi Arabia's largest trading partner, purchasing approximately one in six barrels of Saudi crude oil exports.

Name: Haramain High Speed Railway (CRCC)
Description: The Haramain High Speed Railway (HHR), also known as the Western Railway or the Two Holy Mosques Railway, is a 449.2 km high-speed rail line connecting the holy cities of Mecca (Makkah) and Medina (Al Madinah) via Jeddah King Abdulaziz International Airport, Jeddah City, and King Abdullah Economic City (KAEC). It is operated at speeds up to 300 km/h by Spanish company Renfe and Spanish/Chinese rolling stock. China Railway Construction Corporation (CRCC), through its subsidiary CRCC–South Asia Investment Ltd, was one of the primary contractors in the civil works packages of the project, particularly for the sections of elevated viaduct and earthworks in the Makkah–Jeddah alignment. Construction of the railway began in March 2009. The Chinese-built sections were completed and opened in stages from 2018, with full operations commencing in October 2018. The railway can carry approximately 60 million passengers annually during the Hajj and Umrah pilgrimage season, dramatically reducing the Mecca–Medina journey from approximately 4–5 hours by road to just 2 hours by rail. Total cost of the full project was approximately $16.5 billion. The project exemplifies China's growing role in Saudi infrastructure under the BRI-Vision 2030 alignment, alongside other Chinese construction contracts in Riyadh (Mukaab Square City earthworks by CCCC) and Jeddah (CRCC/CHEC contracts worth $3.2 billion, announced 2024). Saudi Arabia joined the BRI in 2016.

Name: Noor Ouarzazate CSP Solar Complex (SEPCO III / PowerChina)
Description: The Noor Ouarzazate Concentrated Solar Power (CSP) Complex is the world's largest operational concentrated solar power facility, located in the Draa-Tafilalet region near Ouarzazate in southern Morocco — 'the gateway of the Sahara Desert.' Chinese state-owned construction firm SEPCO III (Shandong Electric Power Construction No. 3 Engineering Company Ltd), a subsidiary of Power Construction Corporation of China (PowerChina), built the two Chinese-constructed phases of the four-phase complex: Noor II (200 MW, parabolic trough, the world's largest parabolic trough plant) and Noor III (150 MW, solar tower, at 248 metres the world's tallest solar power tower when built). Total CSP complex capacity across all four phases (Noor I–IV) is 580 MW, making it the world's largest multi-technology solar complex. Overall investment in the full complex exceeds $2 billion, financed by a consortium including the World Bank, African Development Bank, European Investment Bank, KfW, and the government of France. Construction of Noor II and III began in May 2015; Noor II entered commercial operation in 2018 and Noor III achieved first grid connection in 2018. The complex generates over 1 billion kWh per year, powering over one million Moroccan households and reducing CO₂ emissions by approximately 522,000 tonnes annually. Morocco signed its BRI MoU with China in November 2017 — the first African country to do so. In January 2022, Morocco and China signed a formal BRI implementation plan, and King Mohammed VI and President Xi Jinping held a summit in November 2022. The complex is cited as the first overseas new energy CSP construction project by a Chinese company, representing the BRI's flagship renewable energy achievement in North Africa.

Name: Mohammed VI City of Tanger Tech (CCCC)
Description: Mohammed VI City of Tanger Tech (also known as Tangier Tech City or Cité Mohammed VI Tanger Tech) is a planned Chinese-Moroccan industrial park and smart city project adjacent to the Tanger Med Port Complex — Africa's largest and the Mediterranean's number one port by container throughput. Launched in 2018 as a joint project between CCCC (China Communications Construction Company) subsidiary and the Moroccan government, the project was announced with a total investment of approximately $10–11 billion over multiple phases, covering over 2,000 hectares. The city is designed to attract over 200 Chinese high-tech and manufacturing companies in sectors including automotive, aeronautics, electronics, robotics, and battery materials. Its strategic position near Tanger Med — less than 14 km from Spain across the Strait of Gibraltar, and five shipping days from North America's Atlantic coast — makes it a critical BRI gateway for Chinese goods targeting European and North American markets. As of 2023–2025, major Chinese manufacturers operating or under construction include: BTR New Material (battery anode materials gigafactory), Shinzom and Hailiang (lithium battery materials), Sentury Tire, Bonsing, and electric vehicle manufacturer XEV. The cluster is part of Morocco's Industrial Acceleration Plan and aligns with its ambition to be Africa's leading electric vehicle manufacturing hub. Morocco signed its BRI MoU in November 2017 and formalized a joint BRI implementation plan in January 2022. As of 2025, Morocco is the top destination for Chinese greenfield investment in Africa according to The Economist.

Name: Doraleh Multipurpose Port & Djibouti International Free Trade Zone (China Merchants Group)
Description: The Doraleh Multipurpose Port (DMP) is the core Chinese BRI infrastructure investment in Djibouti and the largest single Chinese-financed project in East Africa at the time of its construction. Located on the Doraleh littoral 12 km west of Djibouti City, at the southern entrance to the Red Sea and overlooking the Bab-el-Mandeb Strait, the port was developed by Port de Djibouti S.A. (PDSA) — 23.5% owned by China Merchants Port Holdings (a subsidiary of China Merchants Group, CMG) and 66.5% by the Djibouti Ports and Free Zones Authority (DPFZA). Construction was contracted to China Civil Engineering Construction Corporation (CCECC) and China Construction Harbour and Channel Engineering Bureau Group. Total investment was approximately $590 million, with $405 million financed by China Eximbank. Construction began in August 2014 and the port was inaugurated on May 24, 2017. Phase 1 includes six berths along 1,200 metres of quayside with 16–18 metre draft, handling bulk cargo, containers, roll-on/roll-off, crude oil, and break-bulk. The DMP is designed as the maritime terminus for the Addis Ababa–Djibouti Railway, forming a critical node in China's 'port–park–city' development strategy for the region. Adjacent to the DMP is the Djibouti International Free Trade Zone (DIFTZ), developed by a Chinese consortium led by CMG (Phase 1 investment $370 million, China Development Bank loan $250 million), inaugurated in 2018 and planned to be Africa's largest free trade zone at completion. The PLA Navy's first overseas military base is located adjacent to the DMP, operational since 2017. Djibouti joined the BRI in November 2014 and China had invested approximately $14 billion in infrastructure finance in the small nation by 2020, raising significant debt sustainability concerns given Djibouti's limited revenue base.

Name: Khartoum Refinery & Greater Nile Oil Pipeline (CNPC)
Description: The Khartoum Refinery (Al-Jaili Refinery) is China's most strategically significant BRI-precursor investment in Africa's energy sector — a project that transformed Sudan from a petroleum importer to an exporter and served as the model for Chinese overseas oil refinery investment across the continent. In 1996, China National Petroleum Corporation (CNPC) and Sudan's Petroleum Corporation jointly established the Khartoum Refinery Co. Ltd (KRC), a 50/50 joint venture. Total project cost was approximately $640 million ($320 million financed by a CNPC supplier's credit). Construction commenced in 1998 and the refinery came online in May 2000 — completed in just 20 months. Located on the east bank of the Nile, approximately 70 km north of Khartoum at Al-Jaili, the refinery was expanded in 2006 to 100,000 barrels per day capacity, including the world's first delayed coking unit (DCU) for processing heavy Fula crude oil. The refinery made Sudan self-sufficient in refined petroleum products and enabled it to become a net exporter. In 2019, CNPC reduced its ownership stake from 50% to 10%. CNPC also built the 1,506 km Greater Nile Oil Pipeline connecting South Sudan and Sudan's oil fields to Port Sudan on the Red Sea, and a 1,500+ km Petrodar Pipeline running from the Melut Basin in South Sudan to Port Sudan — both operated by CNPC-led consortia. Together, these projects form China's largest oil infrastructure network on the African continent. Sudan joined the BRI in September 2015. The civil war that erupted in April 2023 severely disrupted oil operations, with the Greater Nile Pipeline suffering multiple ruptures and force majeure declarations. CNPC remains active in Sudan's oil sector through continued maintenance and operational support.

Name: Tunisia BRI Infrastructure Programme (Hospitals, Port Zarzis, Bridges)
Description: Tunisia signed a Belt and Road Initiative Memorandum of Understanding with China in September 2018, making it one of the last Maghreb countries to join the BRI framework. However, unlike Morocco and Algeria, Tunisia's BRI engagement has produced relatively few completed large-scale infrastructure projects, due to political instability, governance weaknesses, lack of a legal framework for public-private partnerships, and cautious attitude toward Chinese loans. The most significant confirmed Chinese-built infrastructure in Tunisia includes: the Sfax University Hospital ($56 million, Chinese grant, begun 2016 and completed 2020); a $23 million diplomatic academy inaugurated in April 2022; and the Bizerte Bridge. During the 2018 FOCAC Summit in Beijing, Tunisia signed agreements for development of the Port of Zarzis into an economic and trade hub, a 140 km railway linking Gabès to Zarzis, a bridge connecting Djerba Island to Djorf, and a SAIC Motor car assembly plant — none of which had advanced to construction as of 2025. China has expressed interest in developing deep-water ports at Bizerte, Enfidha, and Zarzis. Chinese telecom giant Huawei is active in Tunisia's digital infrastructure. Tunisia is strategically located at the centre of the North African Mediterranean coast, between Algeria and Libya, offering proximity to European markets and access to Sahel trade routes. China views Tunisia as a potential Mediterranean and trans-African logistics hub linking BRI's Maritime Silk Road with Sub-Saharan Africa.

Name: Jordan BRI Industrial & Transport Projects (Aqaba / Zarqa Light Rail)
Description: Jordan signed a BRI Memorandum of Understanding with China in September 2017 and China is one of Jordan's most significant sources of infrastructure investment and construction contracts. The most prominent Chinese BRI-linked projects in Jordan include the Aqaba Special Economic Zone industrial infrastructure and several highway and road projects. In January 2022, Jordan and China signed an updated BRI framework agreement in Beijing during PM Bisher Al-Khasawneh's visit. Key Chinese construction activities in Jordan include: The Ma'an Development Area / Aqaba Industrial Estate corridor, where Chinese firms have been involved in logistics and industrial zone development adjacent to Jordan's Red Sea port at Aqaba; the National Phosphate Company (JPMC) infrastructure, where Chinese companies are involved in mining logistics; the Jordan-China Industrial Parks under the Special Economic Zone Authority (ASEZA) in Aqaba; and highway and road construction contracts won by Chinese state-owned firms including CRBC and CHEC. In 2021, Chinese firms won a $600 million contract for the Al-Hashemiyah–Zarqa Light Rail, Jordan's first metro link. The project was financed through a China Eximbank loan at 2% interest. Jordan receives approximately 20% of its imports from China — its largest single import source — and annual bilateral trade exceeds $4 billion. Jordan's strategic location on the Ancient Incense Route between the Arabian Peninsula and the Mediterranean makes it a key node in China's BRI land and maritime connectivity through the Levant.

Name: Kenya Standard Gauge Railway (SGR) – Mombasa to Naivasha
Description:
The Kenya Standard Gauge Railway (SGR) is one of East Africa's most significant BRI infrastructure projects and the largest infrastructure investment in Kenya since independence. It consists of two completed phases: Phase I (Mombasa–Nairobi, 609 km, $3.6 billion) and Phase IIA (Nairobi–Naivasha, 120 km, $1.5 billion). The prime contractor for Phase I was China Road and Bridge Corporation (CRBC), a subsidiary of China Communications Construction Company (CCCC); CCCC served as main contractor for Phase IIA. Both phases were financed 90% by China Eximbank concessional loans with the Kenyan government contributing the remainder. Construction of Phase I began in October 2014 and the Madaraka Express passenger service opened on June 1, 2017 — completing in just 2.5 years, ahead of schedule. Freight services commenced January 1, 2018. The SGR replaced the British colonial metre-gauge Uganda Railway (1901), cutting the Mombasa–Nairobi journey from over 10 hours to 4.5 hours for passengers and from 2 days to 8 hours for freight. Phase IIA to Naivasha opened in October 2019, linking to a new inland container depot serving landlocked East African countries.

Construction created over 65,000 jobs and features innovative wildlife crossings allowing animals to pass beneath the elevated viaducts through Tsavo National Park. However, the SGR has been deeply controversial: CRBC secured the contract without international competitive tender — ruled illegal by Kenya's Court of Appeal in 2020; Kenya defaulted on China Eximbank SGR loans in 2022 and again in 2024 (with $167.5 billion KES in missed payments); and the rail's operating costs have made it economically marginal. Planned extension to Malaba on the Ugandan border (Phase IIB, ~267 km, $5.49 billion) and ultimately to Kampala remain unfunded and stalled. Kenya joined the BRI in 2017.

Name: Nigeria Standard Gauge Railway Programme – Lagos–Kano (CCECC)
Description:
Nigeria's standard gauge railway modernisation programme under the BRI represents China's largest and most complex railway investment in West Africa, comprising multiple phases of the planned Lagos–Kano corridor built by China Civil Engineering Construction Corporation (CCECC), a subsidiary of China Railway Construction Corporation (CRCC). Three major completed BRI segments define the project:

Abuja–Kaduna (186 km): Nigeria's first standard gauge railway, connecting the capital Abuja (Idu) with Kaduna's commercial centre. Cost: $876 million (financed by $500 million China Eximbank concessional loan). Groundbreaking February 2011; inaugurated July 26, 2016. Now carries 3,700+ daily passengers in a corridor previously plagued by kidnappings on the Abuja–Kaduna highway. CCECC operates the line and has established a training centre for Nigerian staff.

Lagos–Ibadan (156 km): The first double-track standard gauge line in West Africa, connecting Nigeria's commercial capital Lagos with Ibadan. Cost: $1.5 billion (financed by $1.3 billion China Eximbank loan). Construction began March 2017; inaugurated June 10, 2021. In November 2024, CCECC became the first company licensed to operate standard-gauge rail freight in Nigeria.

Kaduna–Kano (203 km): Signed in late 2024 with $1.02 billion China Development Bank financing (85% of total cost). Connects Nigeria's two most important northern cities and forms the final link in the original Lagos–Kano plan. Nigeria joined the BRI in 2018. The full Lagos–Kano corridor is estimated to cost $11.1 billion when complete.

Name: Benguela Railway Reconstruction (CRCC / Angola)
Description: The Benguela Railway Reconstruction is China's most significant BRI-era infrastructure investment in Angola, and the historical foundation of what is now the US/EU-backed Lobito Corridor. The 1,344 km Benguela Railway connects the port of Lobito on Angola's Atlantic coast eastward through Huambo and Kuito to Luau near the border with the Democratic Republic of Congo, where it links to the Congolese rail network. Originally built by the British-financed Benguela Railway Company between 1902 and 1931 to export Central African copper and cobalt to the Atlantic, it was almost entirely destroyed during Angola's 27-year civil war (1975–2002). After the war ended, reconstruction began in 2006 under a $2 billion oil-for-infrastructure credit agreement between Angola and China, with China Railway Construction Corporation (CRCC) as the primary EPC contractor. Reconstruction employed approximately 100,000 Angolans and was completed in stages: reaching Huambo in 2011, Kuito in 2012, and Luau at the Congolese border in 2013–2014. The formally reconstructed line was inaugurated in 2015. The railway has 67 stations and 42 bridges and is designed for a capacity of 20 million tonnes of cargo and 4 million passengers annually. Angola joined the BRI in 2015. In 2023, a Western-backed consortium (Trafigura, Mota-Engil, Vecturis) won a 30-year concession on the line as the Lobito Atlantic Railway (LAR), making the Chinese-rebuilt Benguela Railway the foundation of the US/EU's flagship Lobito Corridor counter-BRI initiative — a rare case where BRI-built infrastructure became a Western geopolitical asset.

Name: Sicomines Copper-Cobalt Mine (Sinohydro/CREC – Minerals for Infrastructure)
Description: The Sicomines (Sino-Congolaise des Mines) agreement is the largest and most strategically consequential Chinese resource-for-infrastructure deal in Africa, and a defining example of China's BRI model in the Democratic Republic of Congo. The original agreement was signed in 2007–2008 between the DRC government and a Chinese consortium led by Sinohydro Corporation and China Railway Engineering Corporation (CREC), in partnership with DRC's state mining company Gécamines. Under the deal, the Chinese consortium received a 68% stake in the Sicomines joint venture — granting access to copper and cobalt deposits near Kolwezi in southeastern DRC estimated to contain 10 million tonnes of copper and 600,000 tonnes of cobalt (valued at approximately $93 billion) — in exchange for a commitment to invest $3 billion in DRC infrastructure (roads, hospitals, schools) financed from mine revenues, plus approximately $3 billion in mining development. The Sicomines mine began operations around 2015 and by 2018 DRC crossed 100,000 mt/year in cobalt production, with Chinese firms controlling approximately 80% of the DRC's cobalt output across 24 of 33 cobalt exporters. However, infrastructure spending fell far short: by 2021 independent audits found China had earned nearly $10 billion in profits while delivering only $822 million in infrastructure. President Tshisekedi demanded renegotiation; in January 2024 a fifth amendment raised the infrastructure commitment to $7 billion, though details and enforcement mechanisms remain disputed. The DRC joined the BRI in 2021. Sicomines continues to operate and is exempt from taxes until 2040 under the renegotiated terms.

Name: TAZARA Railway Rehabilitation (CCECC – Tanzania-Zambia)
Description:
The TAZARA (Tanzania-Zambia Railway Authority) is the oldest and most historically resonant Chinese infrastructure project in Africa, and is now undergoing a major BRI-era rehabilitation. The 1,860 km single-track Cape-gauge railway runs from Dar es Salaam on Tanzania's Indian Ocean coast southwestward to Kapiri Mposhi in Zambia's Copperbelt — spanning 975 km in Tanzania and 885 km in Zambia. It was originally built between 1970 and 1975 with an interest-free Chinese government loan of approximately $406 million (RMB 988 million) at the request of Presidents Julius Nyerere and Kenneth Kaunda, who wanted an export route for Zambian copper that bypassed white-minority-ruled Rhodesia and South Africa. Construction involved approximately 50,000 Chinese and African workers. It opened commercially in 1976 and in its 1973 peak carried 3.3 million tonnes of cargo. Over decades, TAZARA fell into severe disrepair due to funding shortfalls, deteriorating rolling stock (much of it original 1970s equipment), and seasonal flooding. China provided periodic maintenance loans ($39 million in 2010, $42 million in 2012) but the line operated far below its 5 million tonne capacity.

In September 2024, at the FOCAC summit in Beijing, China, Tanzania, and Zambia signed a Memorandum of Understanding for a $1.4 billion rehabilitation programme to be executed by CCECC (China Civil Engineering Construction Corporation). In November 2025, a formal ceremony in Lusaka launched the project. CCECC received a 30-year operating concession; the investment covers 34 new locomotives, 760 wagons, 18 passenger coaches, and full track, bridge, signalling, and station upgrades, targeting cargo capacity of 2.4 million tonnes by Year 3. China's Zijin Mining and CMOC Group, which control major copper and cobalt operations in the DRC and Zambia, hold equity stakes in the CCECC-led JV, making the rehabilitation a critical minerals supply chain project as much as an infrastructure investment. Tanzania joined the BRI in 2013.

Name: Ghana Sinohydro Bauxite-for-Roads Infrastructure Programme
Description: Ghana's Sinohydro-for-bauxite infrastructure programme is one of the most significant BRI resource-for-infrastructure deals in West Africa. In August 2018, Ghana and China's Sinohydro Corporation (a subsidiary of PowerChina) signed a $2 billion Master Project Support Agreement (MPSA) under which Sinohydro would finance and build Ghanaian road infrastructure in exchange for a guaranteed supply of refined bauxite (alumina) from the Awaso bauxite deposits in the Western Region. The programme — structured as a commodity-backed financing arrangement using the Ghana Bauxite Company and Sinohydro Resources Limited — was the first of its kind in sub-Saharan Africa since Angola's oil-for-infrastructure deals. Under Phase 1 ($646 million), Sinohydro delivered approximately 580 km of road construction and rehabilitation across Ghana. This included the Accra–Kumasi dualization, the Obosomase–Apedwa section of the Eastern Corridor, sections of the Western Corridor highway, and several rural feeder roads. Construction commenced in 2019 and was largely completed by 2022. In return, Ghana's Mineral Income Investment Fund supplied alumina to China from Awaso. The programme created approximately 12,000 jobs and is widely cited in Ghana as one of the most successful Chinese BRI-linked programmes in the country. A proposed Phase 2 ($2 billion) for additional roads was under discussion as of 2025. Ghana joined the BRI in September 2018.

Name: Maputo Ring Road (CRBC/CHEC)
Description: The Maputo Ring Road (also known as the Maputo Circular Highway or Maputo Bypass) is a 98 km four-lane expressway encircling Mozambique's capital Maputo, built by China Road and Bridge Corporation (CRBC) and China Harbour Engineering Company (CHEC), both subsidiaries of China Communications Construction Company (CCCC). The project was financed through a concessional loan from China Eximbank at approximately $785 million (combined with the adjacent Maputo–Katembe Bridge totalling approximately $800 million). Construction was carried out between 2014 and 2018 and the ring road opened alongside the Maputo–Katembe Bridge. The ring road connects the Maputo–Katembe Bridge and South Africa’s N4 highway, linking Mozambique’s capital with the border at Ressano Garcia, and completing the Southern African regional transport corridor. It was designed to relieve severe traffic congestion in central Maputo and facilitate cross-border goods movement. In addition to the ring road, CRBC and CHEC also rehabilitated the Maputo–Catembe ferry service corridor and associated access roads. Mozambique's total Chinese debt reached approximately $2 billion during the construction period. Mozambique joined the BRI in 2018.

Name: Kribi Deep Water Port (CHEC)
Description: The Kribi Deep Water Port is Cameroon's most significant BRI-era infrastructure project and a flagship Chinese-financed port development in Central Africa. Located in Kribi, Océan Department, approximately 150 km south of Douala on the Atlantic coast, the port was built by China Harbour Engineering Company (CHEC), a subsidiary of CCCC. Phase 1 included two container berths (350 m) and one multipurpose berth, with a total handling capacity of 350,000 TEUs and 750,000 tonnes per year. Total Phase 1 investment was approximately $567 million, with $367 million financed by China Eximbank and $200 million from the Cameroonian government. Construction began in 2011 and the port was inaugurated on March 2, 2018. Kribi Port was designed to become the primary export gateway for Cameroon's oil, timber, and agricultural commodities, and a transit hub for landlocked Chad and Central African Republic. Phase 2 is currently under construction and will add a bulk terminal, an oil terminal, and additional container capacity, more than doubling the port’s throughput. As of 2024, Kribi is Cameroon's second major port after Douala and handles an increasing share of the country’s external trade. Cameroon joined the BRI in November 2018. China is Cameroon’s largest source of construction financing, with CHEC and CRBC active in road, bridge, and hydropower projects across the country.

Name: Great Stone China-Belarus Industrial Park
Description: The Great Stone Industrial Park (GSIP) — formally the China-Belarus Industrial Park — is the largest Chinese-developed special economic zone (SEZ) in Europe and one of the most significant BRI cooperation projects outside of Asia. Located 25 km east of Minsk in the Smolevichi District, directly on the Northern Corridor of the New Silk Road, the park covers 112.5 km² (roughly one-third the area of Minsk itself) and is designed as a high-tech manufacturing hub, logistics node, and planned eco-city of 250,000–300,000 residents. The project originated from a bilateral agreement in September 2011, ratified in January 2012; the Joint Development Company (IPDC) was incorporated in August 2012 with ownership split between Sinomach (32%), China Merchants Group (20%), CAMCE (13.71%), Harbin Investment Group (2.29%), and the Government of Belarus (32%). Infrastructure construction began in 2014, financed partly by a $110 million China Development Bank loan and additional China Eximbank facilities totalling around $1.5 billion; Phase 1 (8.5 km²) was commissioned in October 2017. Total estimated project cost is $6 billion with a long-term investment potential of up to $30 billion. The park offers resident companies a 10-year income-tax holiday (reduced to 9% thereafter), free customs access to the 183 million-person Eurasian Economic Union market, zero VAT, and access to Minsk National Airport, which is integrated into the park's territory. As of 2024, the park hosts over 130 resident companies across advanced manufacturing, electronics, telecommunications, new materials, biopharmaceuticals, logistics, and e-commerce, including 49 Chinese-invested enterprises. German port operator Duisburger Hafen AG (duisport) acquired a 1% stake in IPDC in 2018, establishing a rail terminal linking Great Stone to Duisburg. Belarus joined the BRI in 2015; China considers GSIP the model BRI industrial park for Europe.

Name: Russia Power of Siberia Gas Pipeline (CNPC/Gazprom)
Description: The Power of Siberia (Sila Sibiri) is Russia's most important BRI energy project and the first direct natural gas pipeline connecting Russia with China, representing a defining pillar of the Sino-Russian energy partnership. The pipeline runs approximately 3,000 km from gas fields in eastern Siberia — the Chayandinskoye field in Yakutia and the Kovykta field in Irkutsk Oblast — through Russia's Far East to the Chinese border at Blagoveshchensk/Heihe, continuing into northeast China to supply consumers in the Beijing region and beyond. The project is operated by Gazprom on the Russian side and China National Petroleum Corporation (CNPC) on the Chinese side under a 30-year supply contract signed in May 2014 worth an estimated $400 billion over its lifetime — one of the largest single commercial agreements in history. The deal was signed during President Putin's visit to Shanghai against the backdrop of deteriorating Russia-West relations over Ukraine and Crimea. Construction on the Russian side began in September 2014; President Putin and President Xi jointly inaugurated the pipeline on December 2, 2019, marking the first-ever pipeline delivery of Russian gas to China. Annual contracted delivery volumes rise progressively to 38 billion cubic metres (BCM) per year at full capacity — equivalent to roughly 10% of China's annual gas consumption. A second line, Power of Siberia 2, was under negotiation as of 2025, which would carry up to 50 BCM/year through Mongolia. Russia joined the BRI framework in 2015 and the pipeline is a centrepiece of the China-Russia energy corridor within the BRI's New Eurasian Land Bridge.

Name: Georgia Anaklia Deep-Sea Port (CCCC / China Harbour)
Description: The Anaklia Deep-Sea Port is Georgia's most strategically significant and geopolitically contested infrastructure project — a planned $2.5 billion deep-water port on the eastern Black Sea coast designated as the crown jewel of the Middle Corridor, the BRI's trans-Caspian route linking China to Europe while bypassing Russia. Located in the town of Anaklia in Samegrelo-Zemo Svaneti region, the port is designed to accommodate Panamax and Post-Panamax vessels (draft up to 17 metres), with an initial capacity of 100 million tonnes of goods per year by 2030 and a planned 15 container berths. Construction of the port was first proposed in 2012 and a $2.5 billion contract was awarded to a US-Georgian consortium (TBC-Conti) in 2016, but cancelled by the Georgian government in 2020 amid political controversy. On May 29, 2024, Georgian Economy Minister Levan Davitashvili announced that a Chinese-Singaporean consortium — led by China Communications Construction Company (CCCC) and its Singapore subsidiary China Harbour Investment Pte. Ltd., with China Road and Bridge Corporation (CRBC) and Qingdao Port International as subcontractors — had submitted the sole valid bid and would be declared the winner. Construction formally commenced in October 2024 with Belgian dredging firm Jan De Nul awarded the marine construction contract; the port is targeted for initial container traffic by 2029. CCCC is blacklisted by the US Department of Commerce (since August 2020) for building artificial islands in the South China Sea for military purposes. Critics, including the US Embassy in Tbilisi, the EU, and Georgian civil society, have raised concerns about debt-trap risk, sovereignty, and Georgia's Euro-Atlantic orientation. Georgia signed its BRI MoU in 2015 and a China-Georgia strategic partnership agreement in 2023.

Name: Azerbaijan Baku International Sea Trade Port – Alat (Middle Corridor)
Description: The Baku International Sea Trade Port Complex at Alat is the most critical maritime node in the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route (TITR, also known as the Middle Corridor) — the BRI's alternative Eurasian land bridge that bypasses Russia by routing cargo from China through Kazakhstan, across the Caspian Sea to Azerbaijan, then via Georgia and Turkey to Europe. Located on the Absheron Peninsula's southern Caspian coast, approximately 70 km south of Baku near the town of Alat, the port replaced the old Soviet-era port in central Baku. The port's construction was initiated by Azerbaijan in 2007 — six years before BRI was announced — as part of the country's economic diversification strategy. Phase 1 was completed in 2018; Phase 2 and 3 are ongoing. In its current configuration the port handles 15 million tonnes of bulk cargo per year and 100,000 TEUs of containers, with roll-on/roll-off and ferry terminal facilities linking directly to Kazakhstan's ports of Aktau and Turkmenbashi for trans-Caspian connections. China has contributed approximately $70 million in grants and $2 million in equipment to the port under BRI cooperation. Azerbaijan signed its BRI MoU in 2015 and formalized a China-Azerbaijan strategic partnership in July 2024. The port is integral to the Baku-Tbilisi-Kars (BTK) railway — opened in October 2017 — which is the only rail link connecting Azerbaijan, Georgia and Turkey and serving as the westward terminus of Middle Corridor rail cargo. Transit traffic between Azerbaijan and China surged 86% in 2024 to 378,000 tonnes; 287 block trains were dispatched from China to Azerbaijan via the Middle Corridor in 2024. The Alat Free Economic Zone was established adjacent to the port to attract manufacturing and logistics companies from China and elsewhere.

Name: Poland Małaszewicze–Łódź China-Europe Railway Express Gateway
Description: Poland is the single most important European gateway for the China-Europe Railway Express (CRE) — the BRI's flagship overland freight rail network — serving as the transhipment hub where China-bound and Europe-bound trains transition between the Chinese/European standard gauge (1,435 mm) and the Russian/Belarusian broad gauge (1,520 mm). Approximately 90% of all China-Europe Railway Express trains transit or are transshipped in Poland, making it structurally indispensable to BRI rail connectivity. The Małaszewicze border crossing (Polish-Belarusian border) is the primary gauge-change facility, processing the majority of cross-continental container freight between China and the EU. Łódź is designated the most strategically important BRI rail terminal city in Poland and one of the earliest, hosting the Chengdu–Łódź freight corridor (first train 2013), which was the first China-Europe BRI freight rail connection and the largest completed BRI project in Poland. As of 2025, the CRE network from China transits Poland to reach approximately 50 European cities in 25 countries; total trips surpassed 90,000 as of mid-2024. Freight volumes cut transit time from China to Europe by 75% vs. sea (approximately 15 days vs. 30–40 days), at roughly one-fifth the cost of air freight. Poland signed its BRI MoU in November 2015. The Ukraine war (February 2022) disrupted the Russia-Belarus transit route; Poland has expanded alternative capacity through the China-Kyrgyzstan-Tajikistan-Uzbekistan-Iran-Turkey-Bulgaria corridor (southern Middle Corridor) to compensate, highlighting Poland's role as a bottleneck and adaptation point for BRI's European rail strategy.

Name: Bulgaria Belene Nuclear Power Plant (CNNC – China General Nuclear)
Description: The Belene Nuclear Power Plant is Bulgaria's long-running and controversial nuclear energy project on the Danube River in Pleven Province, which became a significant BRI-linked energy investment when China General Nuclear Power Group (CGN) and China National Nuclear Corporation (CNNC) entered negotiations as strategic investors. The Belene site was originally selected in 1981 during the Soviet era; construction was abandoned in 1990, restarted with Russian firm Atomstroyexport in 2008, then again halted in 2012 after Germany's RWE withdrew as strategic investor, leaving €600–700 million in sunk costs. In 2019, Bulgaria's NPPB (Natsionalna Elektricheska Kompania subsidiary) relaunched the project and received a Non-Binding Letter of Interest from China National Nuclear Corporation (CNNC). In October 2019, the Bulgarian Energy Ministry announced Chinese companies as the preferred bidders for a strategic investor role; negotiations with China National Nuclear Corporation continued through 2020–2023 for a two-unit VVER-1000 plant with an estimated cost of €10 billion. As of 2025, the project remains under negotiation. Bulgaria's National Assembly voted in favour of proceeding in 2021, but financing and strategic investor terms remain unresolved, complicated by EU state-aid rules and geopolitical pressure from the US against Chinese nuclear involvement. Bulgaria signed its BRI MoU in November 2015. If completed, Belene would be the first Chinese-financed nuclear power plant in the EU.

Name: Mongolia–China Railway: Zamyn-Üüd–Erenhot Corridor
Description: Mongolia is one of China's most strategically important BRI partners, located at the physical centre of the China-Mongolia-Russia Economic Corridor (CMREC) — one of the six official BRI economic corridors — and serving as the primary land bridge between China and Russia. The Zamyn-Üüd (Mongolia)–Erenhot (China) border crossing is the busiest land port on the China-Mongolia border and one of the most important overland freight arteries on the New Eurasian Land Bridge, processing the majority of bilateral and transit trade. Chinese investment in Mongolia's railway infrastructure under the BRI includes: the electrification and modernisation of the Ulaanbaatar Railway (of which China holds a stake through a joint venture); the Tavan Tolgoi coal export railway — connecting the world's largest untapped coking coal deposit in southern Mongolia to the Chinese border at Gashuunsukhait (660 km, completed 2022) financed by China's TBEA and built by Chinese contractors, enabling direct coal export to China without road transport; and broader track upgrade programmes. China is Mongolia's largest trading partner, accounting for over 90% of Mongolian exports, primarily coal, copper, and iron ore. Mongolian coal exports to China via the Gashuunsukhait–Ganqimaodao border crossing surpassed 50 million tonnes in 2023. Mongolia signed its BRI MoU with China in 2014; CMREC was formalised at the 2016 trilateral summit between Xi, Putin, and Mongolian President Elbegdorj. Power of Siberia 2, the proposed $55 billion gas pipeline from Russia to China via Mongolia, would represent the single largest BRI infrastructure investment in the country if completed.

Name: Croatia Pelješac Bridge (China Road and Bridge Corporation)
Description: The Pelješac Bridge is Croatia's most important modern infrastructure project and one of the most high-profile BRI construction contracts awarded to a Chinese company within the European Union. The bridge connects the Croatian mainland to the Pelješac Peninsula across the Neretva Channel, bypassing the narrow strip of Bosnian coastline at Neum that had historically interrupted the continuity of Croatia's Adriatic highway network. China Road and Bridge Corporation (CRBC), a subsidiary of CCCC (China Communications Construction Company), won the international tender in 2018 with a bid of €282.6 million — significantly below European competitors — to design and build the 2.4 km cable-stayed bridge with a 55-metre navigation clearance for large vessels. The EU co-financed 85% of the total cost (approximately €420 million) through Cohesion Fund grants, while Croatia funded the balance. Construction commenced in 2018; the bridge was formally opened on July 26, 2022, by Croatian Prime Minister Andrej Plenković and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. The project created approximately 900 jobs and employed local Croatian subcontractors for about 30% of works. The Pelješac Bridge is significant as the only major Chinese-built infrastructure project within a core EU member state on Croatian soil, demonstrating that Chinese contractors can win competitive EU-funded tenders. However, it also sparked controversy about allowing a US-sanctioned Chinese SOE (CRBC's parent CCCC is blacklisted by the US DoD) to build strategic EU infrastructure. Croatia signed its BRI MoU in 2017 and joined the EU in 2013.

Name: Ivory Coast Abidjan Port Expansion (CHEC)
Description: The Abidjan Autonomous Port Expansion and Modernisation Project is the largest single Chinese investment in West African port infrastructure and one of the most strategically significant BRI port projects on the continent. West Africa's busiest port by throughput, the Port of Abidjan handles approximately 90% of Côte d'Ivoire's seaborne trade and serves as the primary maritime gateway for landlocked Burkina Faso and Mali. The expansion was contracted to China Harbour Engineering Company (CHEC), a subsidiary of CCCC, under a $933.4 million EPC contract signed on January 11, 2013. China Eximbank provided an $851 million preferential buyer's credit loan (85% of the contract value) at 2% interest over 20 years with a 7-year grace period; the Government of Côte d'Ivoire financed the remaining 15% ($140 million). Afreximbank also arranged a €250 million syndicated bridge loan in 2014. The project involved widening and deepening the Vridi Canal entrance channel (from 14.5m to 16m depth and from 150m to 250m width), constructing a second container terminal, and building a new roll-on/roll-off terminal, targeting an expansion of annual capacity from approximately 750,000 TEU to 2.25 million TEU. Construction commenced in 2013 and the expanded terminal became operational by 2019–2020. Côte d'Ivoire signed its BRI MoU with China in 2019. President Alassane Ouattara described the Abidjan port expansion as the symbol of Sino-Ivoirian cooperation. The project is a key node in the BRI's Maritime Silk Road connecting West Africa to Asia, and CHEC has been active in additional Ivorian road and bridge contracts since, including a lagoon bridge in Abidjan awarded in 2018 to China State Construction Engineering for 109 billion CFA francs ($191 million).

Name: Namibia Walvis Bay Container Terminal Expansion (CHEC)
Description: The Walvis Bay New Container Terminal is Namibia's largest infrastructure project since independence in 1990 and a flagship BRI port development for southern Africa. Located on the Atlantic coast approximately 400 km west of the capital Windhoek, Walvis Bay is the deepest natural harbour on the southern African Atlantic coast and a critical transit gateway for landlocked SADC countries including Zambia, Angola, the DRC, Botswana, and Zimbabwe. The terminal was built by China Harbour Engineering Company (CHEC), a subsidiary of CCCC, funded jointly by the Namibian government and the African Development Bank, at a total cost of approximately $280 million. Construction began in 2014–2015 and the terminal was inaugurated on August 2, 2019 by President Hage Geingob. The project involved reclaiming 40 acres (16 hectares) of land from the sea — making Namibia one of a handful of countries to use reclaimed sea land for port expansion — and constructing two new container berths along a 600-metre quay wall, capable of accommodating vessels up to 8,000 TEU. The expansion tripled annual container capacity from approximately 350,000 TEU to 750,000 TEU, with potential to exceed 1 million TEU. CHEC also built the National Oil Storage Facilities at Walvis Bay as a second concurrent project. The project created over 2,000 local jobs and 600 trained skilled workers; CHEC also funded two Namibian engineers to study Marine Harbour Engineering in China on full scholarships. Namibia signed its BRI MoU in September 2018. The Chinese ambassador cited the project as a benchmark for China-Namibia cooperation under BRI. Analysts have noted Walvis Bay's strategic significance for potential future PLA Navy operations in the South Atlantic, though China has denied such intentions.

Name: Guinea Simandou Iron Ore Mine and Trans-Guinean Railway (Winning Consortium)
Description: The Simandou iron ore project is Africa's largest greenfield integrated mine and infrastructure project, and one of China's most strategically consequential resource investments globally — designed to diversify China's iron ore imports away from near-total dependence on Australia and Brazil. The Simandou deposit in southeastern Guinea, located approximately 600 km from the coast between the prefectures of Beyla and Kérouané, contains estimated reserves exceeding 4 billion tonnes of high-grade hematite iron ore (average grade >65%), making it potentially the world's largest undeveloped high-quality iron ore deposit. Total project investment is approximately $20 billion across four blocks, making it the largest infrastructure investment in Guinean history and one of the largest in Africa. The project involves two parallel development tracks: Blocks 1 and 2 are developed by the Winning Consortium Simandou (WCS) — a Chinese-led consortium including Winning Shipping, United Mining Suppliers (UMS), Shandong Weiqiao Aluminum, and CIOH — which holds a 100% mining stake (with 15% eventual government participation). Blocks 3 and 4 are held by Rio Tinto Simfer (45.05% Rio Tinto, 41.3% Chinalco/Chalco, 7.5% Government of Guinea, 6.15% IFC). A critical shared infrastructure element is the Trans-Guinean Railway, a 650+ km railway including 206 bridges and 4 tunnels cutting through challenging rainforest and mountain terrain from the Simandou range to a new deepwater port at Morebayah/Matakong on Guinea's Atlantic coast. Construction began in 2022 and mining officially launched on November 11, 2025. The first commercial shipment of Simandou ore departed Guinea on December 2, 2025 and arrived at China Baowu's Majishan port in Zhejiang on January 17, 2026. Full production capacity is targeted at approximately 120 million tonnes per year, which would make Simandou the world's second-largest iron ore exporting complex and fundamentally restructure the global iron ore market. Guinea signed its BRI MoU in 2017.

Name: Togo Lomé Container Terminal (China Merchants / China Development Bank)
Description: The Lomé Container Terminal (LCT) is West Africa's most strategically important deep-water port terminal and a critical BRI Maritime Silk Road node, developed with Chinese financing and operated by China Merchants Port Holdings. Togo's capital Lomé hosts the only natural deep-water port on the entire West African coast, with a 16.6-metre draft that can accommodate Post-Panamax and Ultra-Large Container Vessels — a unique advantage on a coastline where most ports require dredging to handle large ships. The LCT was developed under a 35-year BOT concession awarded in December 2011 to the special purpose vehicle Lomé Container Terminal S.A. (LCT), co-owned by China Merchants Port Holdings (CMPort, 50% — a subsidiary of China Merchants Group) and Terminal Investment Limited (TiL, MSC subsidiary, 50%). China Development Bank (CDB) provided a $46.64 million loan for the project's construction phase. Total investment in the greenfield terminal was approximately $400–450 million. The terminal features 1,050 metres of quayside across 3–5 berths, 9 ship-to-shore gantry cranes, 24 rubber-tyred gantry cranes, and a 50-hectare storage yard with designed annual capacity of 2.2 million TEU. LCT has become the dominant gateway for landlocked Mali, Niger, and Burkina Faso, as well as northern Nigeria, serving as a transshipment hub across the entire West African coast. In 2023 the Port of Lomé handled approximately 1.9 million TEU, making it the busiest port in West Africa and ranked 93rd globally. Military analysts have noted that CMPort's 50% stake and Lomé's deep-water specifications make it one of the three West African ports most likely to serve future PLA Navy access needs. Togo signed its BRI MoU in 2018.

Name: Gabon Belinga Iron Ore Mine and Railway (CMEC)
Description: The Belinga iron ore project in Gabon is one of China's earliest and most ambitious African resource-for-infrastructure deals, granting Chinese firms access to what was then described as the world's largest known untapped iron ore deposit in exchange for a $3 billion infrastructure investment package. The Belinga deposit is located approximately 500 km east of Libreville in Ogooué-Ivindo Province. In April 2005, China Machinery Engineering Corporation (CMEC) announced a $3 billion package comprising: development of the Belinga iron ore mine; construction of a 560 km railway from Belinga to the Transgabonais national railway; a new deep-water mining export port at Santa Clara; two hydroelectric dams (including one at Kongou Falls in Ivindo National Park); and a steel mill. In 2006, the Gabonese government awarded the mining rights to a Chinese consortium led by CMEC, establishing Compagnie Minière de Bélinga (Comibel S.A.) as the joint venture, with Chinese investors holding 85% and the Gabonese government 15%. China Eximbank agreed in principle to finance the project. However, the project encountered major obstacles from 2008 onward: Gabon's civil society groups raised serious concerns about deforestation, dam impacts on Ivindo National Park, corruption, and lack of transparency; China Eximbank withdrew financing in 2009 pending environmental assessments; and an amicable renegotiation agreement was signed in Paris in November 2013. As of 2025, the Belinga mine remains undeveloped — representing one of BRI's most prominent stalled projects and a cautionary case study on the tension between Chinese resource extraction ambitions, environmental governance, and host-country politics. Gabon signed its BRI MoU in 2015.

Name: Malawi China BRI Road Infrastructure Programme (CRBC/CCCC)
Description: Malawi has been one of China's most active BRI road construction recipients in Southern Africa, with China Road and Bridge Corporation (CRBC) — a CCCC subsidiary — serving as the dominant contractor across multiple road rehabilitation and construction contracts financed by China Eximbank concessional loans. Key projects include: the M1 Blantyre–Lilongwe Road Rehabilitation (450 km, one of Malawi's main north-south arteries), financed in part by a $200+ million China Eximbank loan; the Nacala Road Corridor (Malawi section), which links the landlocked country to Mozambique's deep-water Nacala Port; and ongoing highway rehabilitation in the Northern, Central, and Southern Regions. Malawi signed its BRI MoU with China in September 2019, and China is one of Malawi's largest bilateral infrastructure lenders. Chinese firms have been involved in a broad portfolio of construction including bridges, government buildings, and stadium construction. China Eximbank loans to Malawi raised debt sustainability concerns highlighted by the IMF; by 2022 Malawi was in debt distress with external debt comprising over 50% of GDP, with Chinese loans accounting for a significant share. Despite political tensions — including Malawi's 2023 decision to decline a Chinese offer to build a $35 million parliament building following pushback over sovereignty conditions — Chinese infrastructure contractors remain active in Malawi's road sector. Malawi is among the poorest countries in Africa, with over 70% of the population in poverty, making infrastructure investment a high-priority development need.

Name: South Sudan China Oil Infrastructure (CNPC/SUDD Petroleum)
Description: South Sudan hosts one of China's most complex and high-stakes BRI resource investments in Sub-Saharan Africa — a multi-decade oil extraction and infrastructure partnership centred on CNPC's extensive operations in the country's oilfields. China National Petroleum Corporation (CNPC) entered Sudan (undivided) in 1995 and retained its stakes after South Sudan's independence in July 2011. CNPC holds equity in multiple oilfield blocs in South Sudan, including: Block 1/2/4 (through GNPOC — Greater Nile Petroleum Operating Company — where CNPC holds 40%); Block 3/7 (through Petrodar, where CNPC holds 41.28%); and additional exploration blocs. Together these fields produced over 250,000 barrels per day before the civil war began in 2013, representing the primary source of government revenue. China also financed and built the key export infrastructure: the 1,506 km Greater Nile Oil Pipeline (GNOP) from oilfields to Port Sudan (originally built 1997–1999, operated by CNPC-led consortium); and the 1,500+ km Petrodar Pipeline from the Melut Basin to Port Sudan. CNPC invested approximately $8 billion in South Sudan's oil sector through 2013. The 2013–2018 civil war devastated oil production, dropping output to under 130,000 bpd. South Sudan signed its BRI MoU in September 2018. Post-conflict, CNPC committed to resuming operations and exploring a new alternative export pipeline via Ethiopia and Djibouti to bypass Sudan, which was proposed in 2024. In January 2024, South Sudan awarded CNPC a new drilling contract for an estimated $1 billion to resume production in Block 1/2/4. China remains South Sudan's dominant oil partner and largest financier, with its loans and oil infrastructure creating deep structural dependency.

Name: Liberia Freeport of Monrovia Expansion (CHEC)
Description: The Freeport of Monrovia Rehabilitation and Expansion Project is Liberia's most significant BRI infrastructure investment and the country's primary seaport development, located in the capital Monrovia on the Atlantic coast. China Harbour Engineering Company (CHEC), a CCCC subsidiary, was awarded contracts for rehabilitation and expansion works at the Freeport, which handles approximately 95% of Liberia's seaborne trade. Works financed under Chinese BRI-linked financing have included: rehabilitation of the quay structure and container terminal berths; expansion of roll-on/roll-off facilities; harbour dredging to accommodate larger vessels; and upgrades to port operations infrastructure. China Eximbank and China Development Bank have provided concessional financing for port and road infrastructure in Liberia since the post-civil war reconstruction period beginning in 2005, with CHEC and CRBC as primary contractors. Total Chinese-financed infrastructure in Liberia from 2000–2020 exceeds $800 million according to AidData. The Freeport of Monrovia serves as the maritime gateway for all of Liberia's imports (primarily food, fuel, and manufactured goods) and exports (iron ore, rubber, timber). It is also critical for humanitarian logistics and UN peacekeeping resupply operations. Liberia signed its BRI MoU with China in 2018. China is Liberia's second-largest source of infrastructure financing after the World Bank. The port is strategically located on the West African Atlantic coast and has hosted Chinese naval vessels. Chinese firms are also active in Liberia's road sector, including the Monrovia-Ganta Highway and Buchanan Port rehabilitation.

Name: Turkey Yavuz Sultan Selim Bridge & North Marmara Highway (China Merchants Consortium)
Description: The Yavuz Sultan Selim Bridge — Turkey's third Bosphorus bridge, the world's widest suspension bridge and one of the tallest at 322 metres — became a major BRI acquisition project when a six-company Chinese consortium agreed to purchase a 51% controlling stake in ICA (IC İçtaş-Astaldi Consortium), the concession holder for both the bridge and the adjacent Northern Marmara Highway. The consortium was led by China Merchants Expressway Network & Technology Holdings (CMET, 31% of the JV) — a subsidiary of China Merchants Group — alongside CMU (China Merchants Union, 20%), Zhejiang Expressway (17.5%), Jiangsu Expressway (17.5%), Sichuan Expressway (7%), and Anhui Expressway (7%). The agreed purchase price was $688.5 million. Turkey's competition authority approved the transfer in early 2020. The Yavuz Sultan Selim Bridge was opened in August 2016, connects Europe to Asia across the northern Bosphorus near Istanbul's new third airport, and carries over 100,000 vehicles per day. The bridge was built under a public-private partnership with a Turkish government minimum revenue guarantee of $464 million/year; however, actual toll revenues of $135 million in 2017 fell far short, leaving the original Italian-Turkish consortium (Astaldi and IC İçtaş) under financial pressure — creating the opening for Chinese buyers. The Northern Marmara Highway (Kuzey Marmara Otoyolu) is a 260+ km toll road accompanying the bridge. Note: Bloomberg reported in August 2021 that talks had stalled after IC Yatırım Holding halted discussions. As of 2025, the concession operational status and full completion of transfer remains subject to negotiation. Turkey signed its BRI MoU in 2015 and is a key Middle Corridor node linking Asia to Europe.

Name: Turkey Hunutlu Coal Power Plant (Shanghai Electric)
Description: The Hunutlu Coal Power Plant (also known as the Adana Power Plant or EMBA Power Plant) is China's largest single energy investment in Turkey and a flagship BRI energy infrastructure project on the Mediterranean coast. Located in the Karataş district of Adana Province in southern Turkey, the plant is a 1,320 MW supercritical coal-fired thermal power station (two 660 MW units) developed as a joint venture between Shanghai Electric Power (a subsidiary of Shanghai Electric Group) and Turkish energy company Avic International. Total project investment is approximately $1.7 billion, making it the largest Chinese greenfield investment in Turkey at the time of construction. Shanghai Electric holds a 78% stake with the remaining 22% held by Avic International. Financing was provided primarily by the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (ICBC) and Bank of China, with additional support from Chinese policy banks. Construction commenced around 2018–2019. The plant is designed to supply approximately 3% of Turkey's total electricity needs. The project is significant as one of the few BRI coal power projects built in a NATO member and EU candidate country, raising sustainability and diplomatic questions. TBEA (Tebian Electric Apparatus) supplied transformer and electrical equipment. Turkey signed its BRI MoU with China in 2015 and designated the Hunutlu plant as part of BRI energy cooperation during the Second Belt and Road Forum (2019).

Name: Georgia Baku–Tbilisi–Kars (BTK) Railway – Georgian Section
Description: The Baku–Tbilisi–Kars (BTK) Railway is the most strategically important land transport corridor in the South Caucasus and a central artery of the BRI's Trans-Caspian Middle Corridor, linking the Caspian Sea to Turkey and onward to Europe while bypassing Russia and Iran. The BTK railway was inaugurated on October 30, 2017 in Baku by the presidents of Azerbaijan, Georgia, and Turkey. The Georgian section of the BTK runs approximately 159 km from the border with Azerbaijan (Red Bridge / Gardabani) through Tbilisi and westward to the Turkish border at Akhalkalaki–Kartsakhi. Georgia rehabilitated and electrified its section of the BTK using a $775 million low-interest loan from Azerbaijan (2% over 25 years), with construction and rehabilitation carried out primarily by Turkish and Georgian contractors. In May 2024, Azerbaijan and Georgia jointly completed a five-phase modernisation of the BTK's Georgian section, upgrading 61 km of track, 98 km of contact network, 172 km of 10kV cable, and 338 km of fibre-optic cable, increasing annual capacity from 1 million to 5 million tonnes. The BTK directly connects to China's Middle Corridor via the Caspian ferry link from Baku's Alat port to Kazakhstan's Aktau port and onwards to China. As of 2024, 287 block trains ran from China to Azerbaijan via the Middle Corridor, with transit traffic up 86% year-on-year. Georgia signed its BRI MoU in 2015 and the BTK is central to Georgia's strategy to position itself as a Eurasian transit hub. China's involvement is primarily as the origin and destination for cargo flows rather than direct project financing of the Georgian section.

Name: Uzbekistan China-Central Asia Gas Pipeline (CNPC/Uzbekneftegaz)
Description: Uzbekistan is a critical transit country for the Central Asia–China Gas Pipeline (CACGP), which is China's flagship energy infrastructure project in Central Asia and the world's longest transnational gas pipeline system. The pipeline crosses approximately 529 km of Uzbek territory as part of Lines A, B, and C — the three parallel operational lines running from the Turkmen-Uzbek border at Gedaim eastward through central Uzbekistan and southern Kazakhstan to Horgos in China's Xinjiang. Lines A, B, and C have a combined designed capacity of 55 billion cubic metres per year (BCM/year); in addition, Uzbekneftegaz has committed to supplying 10 BCM/year of Uzbek gas to China under a purchase-and-sale agreement with CNPC signed in June 2010. The pipeline has been one of the main drivers of Chinese debt accumulation in Uzbekistan: as of 2023, Uzbekistan owed China approximately $3.775 billion, with the China Development Bank as the third-largest single creditor at $2.2 billion. Beyond transit, Uzbekistan is also a participant in the planned Line D (see Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan entries) — a 966 km fourth pipeline line under construction via Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, and Kyrgyzstan to add 30 BCM/year. The Uzbek section of Line D involves a JV between CNPC and Uzbekneftegaz signed in August 2014. Additionally, China Energy Engineering Corporation (CEEC), PowerChina, and other Chinese companies have signed over 5,000 MW in new solar and wind energy contracts in Uzbekistan since 2023, marking a pivot from fossil fuels to renewables. Uzbekistan signed its BRI MoU in 2015.

Name: Turkmenistan Galkynysh Gas Field Development (CNPC)
Description: The Galkynysh Gas Field (formerly South Iolotan) in southern Turkmenistan is the world's second-largest natural gas field with estimated reserves of between 13.1 and 21.2 trillion cubic metres — and China National Petroleum Corporation (CNPC) is the primary developer, financer, and offtaker, making it China's most strategically consequential upstream energy investment globally. In 2009, China Development Bank provided a $4 billion loan to Turkmenistan's state gas company Turkmengaz to develop South Iolotan/Galkynysh, to be repaid through gas deliveries to China at below-market prices. A further $8.1 billion in Chinese loans were extended subsequently for field development and pipeline capacity. CNPC operates the Bagtyyarlyk gas fields on the right bank of the Amu Darya — a contract area of approximately 3,500 km² — which supplies Lines A and B of the Central Asia–China Gas Pipeline. Gas from Galkynysh supplies Lines A, B, C, and is planned for Line D. Turkmenistan's total annual gas export to China via the three operational pipeline lines is approximately 40 BCM/year under a quota stated by the Turkmenistan Ministry of Foreign Affairs in 2023, representing over 90% of Turkmenistan's total export earnings. The Chinese financing arrangement has created profound structural dependency: Turkmenistan sells gas to China at prices set by CNPC that critics describe as well below market, and debt repayments are made in-kind via gas deliveries under a take-or-pay structure. The Galkynysh development and pipeline system together constitute the single largest Chinese BRI investment in any individual country by value, estimated at $20–30 billion cumulatively. Turkmenistan signed its BRI MoU with China in 2013.

Name: Tajikistan Dushanbe–Kulma Highway & BRI Road Network (CRBC)
Description: China Road and Bridge Corporation (CRBC), a CCCC subsidiary, is the dominant infrastructure contractor in Tajikistan and has built the most extensive Chinese-financed road network of any Central Asian country relative to GDP. Key completed projects include: the Dushanbe–Kulma Highway, a 1,293 km strategic road connecting the Tajik capital to the Chinese border at the Kulma Pass (Murghab, 4,362 m), passing through the eastern Pamirs and integrating Tajikistan's most remote Gorno-Badakhshan region into regional connectivity; multiple sections of the Shahritus–Nizhny Panj highway connecting Tajikistan to Afghanistan; the Dushanbe–Chanak Highway; the Vahdat–Yavan Railway Tunnel; and the Chormazak Tunnel. In 2019 alone, CRBC built 728 km of roads in Tajikistan for $779 million. Between 2017 and 2021, Chinese companies won tenders worth approximately $154.3 million in Tajikistan under ADB and World Bank programmes in addition to China Eximbank-financed direct contracts. Total Chinese infrastructure lending to Tajikistan has made China Eximbank Tajikistan's single largest creditor at approximately $900 million as of early 2024 (down from $1.4 billion at peak) — representing 27.8% of total external debt and approximately 27% of GDP. The grace periods on multiple China Eximbank loans end in 2025, sharply increasing annual debt service obligations. China also built Tajikistan's South–North 500 kV Power Transmission Line (TBEA, $237 million) connecting the northern and southern electricity grids, and the $350 million Dushanbe-2 Thermal Power Plant (already in CMS). Tajikistan signed its BRI MoU in 2014.

Name: Kyrgyzstan Datka–Kemin Power Transmission Line (TBEA)
Description: The Datka–Kemin 500 kV Power Transmission Line is the most transformative Chinese BRI energy project in Kyrgyzstan, fundamentally reshaping the country's energy sovereignty. Prior to its construction, Kyrgyzstan's northern and southern electricity grids were completely disconnected from each other, forcing the northern regions (including the capital Bishkek) to import electricity from Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan — making the country politically and economically vulnerable to pricing pressure and supply disruptions from neighbours. The 428 km high-voltage transmission line was built by TBEA (Tebian Electric Apparatus Stock Co. Ltd), a Chinese state-linked electrical equipment and EPC company headquartered in Xinjiang, at a total cost of approximately $400 million, financed by a China Eximbank concessional loan. Construction ran from 2012 to 2015 and the line was commissioned in 2015. The Datka–Kemin line connects the Datka substation in the south (Jalal-Abad Province) to the Kemin substation in the north (Chui Province), passing through mountainous terrain at elevations up to 3,400 metres with 19 river crossings. A key component is the Datka 500/220 kV substation and the Kemin converter substation. The project directly ended Kyrgyzstan's dependence on transit electricity from Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan and allowed the country to export surplus hydropower eastward. It is consistently cited as one of BRI's most successful infrastructure projects in Central Asia. Kyrgyzstan signed its BRI MoU in 2015. Kyrgyzstan's total outstanding Chinese loans represent approximately 40% of GDP — the highest ratio in Central Asia — creating ongoing debt sustainability concerns.

Name: Laos Nam Ou River Cascade Hydropower Project (PowerChina/Sinohydro)
Description: The Nam Ou River Cascade Hydropower Project is a series of seven hydroelectric dams spanning 350 km of the Nam Ou River — the seventh-largest Mekong tributary — in the provinces of Phongsaly and Luang Prabang in northern Laos. It is the first and only overseas project in which PowerChina has taken full basin-wide planning and development responsibility under a Build-Operate-Transfer (BOT) model, and is presented by PowerChina as a flagship BRI project. The masterplan was signed between Sinohydro (later merged into PowerChina) and the Lao government in April 2011, with a total investment of $2.73 billion. The seven dams — Nam Ou 1 through 7 — span a range of dam types (concrete gravity, rockfill, gate dams) suited to varying terrain and geological conditions. Phase 1 (Nam Ou 2, 5, and 6) became operational in October 2016; Phase 2 (Nam Ou 1, 3, 4, and 7) was completed in September 2021. Combined installed capacity is 1.272 GW, making the cascade one of the largest Chinese-built hydropower complexes in Southeast Asia. Financing was provided by China Development Bank (Phase 1, ~$1 billion) and China Eximbank and China Construction Bank (Phase 2). The project was developed through two SPV subsidiaries of PowerChina Resources Limited (PCR): Nam Ou River Basin Hydropower Company Limited (PCR 85%, Électricité du Laos 15%) for Phase 1, and Nam Ou Power Company Limited (PCR 100%) for Phase 2. PCR holds a 29-year BOT operating concession. The cascade powers northern Laos and supplies electricity for the China-Laos Railway corridor. It has attracted significant controversy: over 2,300 families (12,600 people) — predominantly Khmu, Akha, Hmong, and other ethnic minority groups — were relocated, with widespread complaints of inadequate compensation, substandard resettlement villages, and loss of agricultural land and riverine livelihoods. The Nam Ou was previously one of the healthiest rivers in Laos; the cascade has fundamentally altered its ecology and sediment regime.

Name: Vietnam Lao Cai–Hanoi–Hai Phong Standard Gauge Railway (CREC)
Description: The Lao Cai–Hanoi–Hai Phong–Ha Long Standard Gauge Railway is Vietnam's largest and most geopolitically significant BRI infrastructure commitment, approved by the Vietnamese National Assembly on February 19, 2025 by an overwhelming vote of 455 to 4. The 427 km standard gauge (1,435 mm) railway will replace a century-old French-built metre-gauge line, connecting the Vietnam–China border at Lao Cai–Hekou (linking to China's Kunming–Hekou railway in Yunnan Province) through Hanoi to the major port city of Hai Phong and onward to Ha Long City. Total project cost is $8.37 billion, financed primarily through a concessional loan from the Chinese government via the Export-Import Bank of China. Phase 1 will construct a single-track standard gauge line with a design speed of 160 km/h for both passenger and freight; Phase 2 will upgrade to double-track capable of 200 km/h. Construction was targeted to begin by end of 2025, with completion by 2030. The project is the centrepiece of Vietnam's participation in BRI under the 'Two Corridors, One Belt' connectivity framework aligned with China, agreed during high-level summits between General Secretary Tô Lâm and President Xi Jinping (August 2024) and confirmed via an inter-governmental agreement signed in December 2024. Two additional cross-border rail lines — Dong Dang–Hanoi (Lang Son) and Mong Cai–Ha Long–Hai Phong — are planned under the same framework, with Vietnam considering a total of three new standard gauge links to China. China Railway No. 6 Engineering Group (CREC subsidiary) has been identified as a key technical partner. The railway will dramatically improve trade logistics: Hai Phong hosts factories for Samsung, Foxconn, and Pegatron heavily dependent on Chinese component supply chains. Once operational, Vietnamese goods can connect to Europe via the China–Europe freight train network, potentially reducing transit time and cost significantly. Vietnam signed its BRI MoU with China in 2017.

Name: Cambodia Sihanoukville Special Economic Zone (SSEZ)
Description: The Sihanoukville Special Economic Zone (SSEZ) is Cambodia's largest, best-known, and most strategically consequential Chinese-built industrial zone, situated 20 km northeast of the Sihanoukville Autonomous Port — Cambodia's only deep-water seaport — in Preah Sihanouk Province on the Gulf of Thailand. It is the first SEZ jointly recognised by both the Cambodian and Chinese governments, and is consistently cited as a model BRI project by Chinese officials, including during President Xi Jinping's 2022 state visit to Cambodia. The SSEZ covers 11.13 km² and was developed by a joint venture between Cambodia's WorldBridge Land and China's CCIG Group (Union Development Group's Jiangsu subsidiary). Development began in 2008, predating the BRI's formal announcement, and has been incorporated into the BRI framework since 2013. As of 2025, the zone hosts 327 enterprises from China, the US, Europe, and Southeast Asia employing approximately 46,750 Cambodian workers, with over $1.3 billion in total enterprise investment and annual wages exceeding $150 million. Key industries include garments, electronics, automobile parts, building materials, medical devices, and food processing. The zone benefits from Cambodia's zero-tariff access to the EU under EBA (Everything But Arms) and preferential US and ASEAN market access. Cambodia is deeply strategically tied to China: in 2021 Prime Minister Hun Sen declared 'If I don't rely on China, who will I rely on?' The SSEZ sits at the intersection of China's BRI and Cambodia's industrial development strategy, but has also attracted controversy: Chinese criminal networks exploited the broader Sihanoukville development boom from 2016–2019, turning the city into a centre for online scam operations and human trafficking before a government crackdown. The SSEZ itself remains an active and growing legitimate industrial zone. Cambodia signed its BRI MoU in 2017.

Name: Myanmar Sino-Myanmar Oil & Gas Pipelines (CNPC/PipeChina)
