Description: The Sino-Myanmar Oil and Gas Pipelines are China's most strategically critical energy infrastructure project in Southeast Asia — twin pipelines running ~800 km from Myanmar's Bay of Bengal coast through the heart of Myanmar to Yunnan Province, China. They are central to China's strategy to reduce its 'Malacca Dilemma': the vulnerability of its oil supply to potential blockade of the Strait of Malacca. The parallel oil and gas pipelines both originate near Kyaukphyu in Rakhine State. The natural gas pipeline (793 km in Myanmar, extending to Guigang, Guangxi, for a total of 2,806 km) was completed in June 2013 and began delivering gas from the offshore Shwe gas field (Blocks A-1 and A-3) operated by Daewoo/POSCO/MOGE. Design capacity is 12 billion cubic metres per year. The crude oil pipeline (771 km in Myanmar) was completed in 2014 but delayed in opening until April 2017 after protracted negotiations over transit fees; it terminates at CNPC's Yunnan Petrochemical refinery in Kunming. Design capacity is 22 million tonnes per year (~440,000 barrels/day). CNPC (now PipeChina holds a majority stake) holds 50.9% of the oil pipeline operating consortium (SEAOP); Myanmar Oil and Gas Enterprise (MOGE) holds 49%. China Development Bank financed the gas pipeline via a €452.75 million loan. Total combined project cost was approximately $2.54 billion (oil: ~$1.5B, gas: ~$1.04B). The pipelines pass through Rakhine, Magway, and Mandalay regions before crossing Shan State to Ruili, Yunnan. Four gas off-take stations in Myanmar divert less than 20% of total gas volume for domestic use. The project has faced persistent controversy over land confiscation without adequate compensation, environmental damage, lack of public participation, and the fact that most of Myanmar's own population lacks reliable electricity access. Since the February 2021 military coup, the pipelines have remained operational but ongoing civil war poses escalating security risks to Chinese energy interests. Myanmar signed its BRI MoU in 2018.

Name: Thailand Laem Chabang Port Phase 3 Expansion (CHEC)
Description: The Laem Chabang Port Phase 3 expansion is Thailand's largest port infrastructure project and a key node of the Eastern Economic Corridor (EEC) — the Thai government's flagship special economic zone on the Gulf of Thailand — within the BRI's Maritime Silk Road framework. Laem Chabang is Thailand's main commercial port and one of Southeast Asia's busiest container ports, handling approximately 80% of Thailand's container trade. Phase 3 adds three new container terminals (Terminal F, G, and H) and a new service lane, expanding the port's annual capacity from approximately 11 million TEU to 18 million TEU. China Harbour Engineering Company (CHEC), a subsidiary of CCCC, won the Phase 3 F Terminal infrastructure contract — the centrepiece of the expansion — which covers the construction of new berths, quay walls, dredging, and terminal infrastructure. Total Phase 3 investment is estimated at approximately $3 billion (around 100 billion baht). CHEC was confirmed as the Phase 3 contractor in a deal that involved state-owned Port Authority of Thailand (PAT). The Phase 3 expansion directly connects to BRI-linked projects: the Council on Foreign Relations noted that the Funan Techo Canal in Cambodia is projected to boost freight traffic to Laem Chabang; the Thai Ministry of Transport has also linked Phase 3 to the proposed Thai Land Bridge (formerly Kra Canal) project backed by China. Construction commenced around 2022–2023, with completion targeted for the late 2020s. Thailand signed its BRI MoU with China in 2017. The EEC zone surrounding Laem Chabang hosts heavy Chinese industrial investment in automotive, electronics, and petrochemical sectors.

Name: Malaysia East Coast Rail Link (ECRL) – CCCC
Description: The East Coast Rail Link (ECRL) is Malaysia's largest infrastructure project and China's biggest single overseas construction contract, a 665 km standard gauge double-track railway connecting Port Klang on the Strait of Malacca to Kota Bharu in northeast Peninsular Malaysia. The project links the relatively underdeveloped East Coast states of Kelantan, Terengganu, and Pahang to the economic heartland of the Klang Valley — intended to reduce regional economic disparity, open new trade corridors, and serve as a key link in the Pan-Asia Railway network connecting China to Singapore via Malaysia. China Communications Construction Company (CCCC) is the engineering, procurement, construction, and commissioning contractor; Malaysia Rail Link Sdn Bhd (MRLSB), fully owned by Malaysia's Ministry of Finance, owns the rail assets and will operate the line in a 50:50 joint venture with CCCC. The project was signed in November 2016 for RMB 72.8 billion (RM 46 billion) with China Eximbank providing a preferential buyer's credit at 3.25% interest, 20-year maturity, 7-year grace period. Construction began in August 2017 but was suspended in 2018 after the new Mahathir government raised concerns about cost inflation and corruption links to the 1MDB scandal. After renegotiation, the contract was restructured in April 2019 at a revised cost of RM 44 billion (~$11B), with a further upward revision to RM 50.27 billion by 2025 (total project cost RM 74.96 billion including land, design, and support costs). As of April 2025 the project is 82.45% complete, with all 41 tunnels excavated (including the challenging 16 km Genting Tunnel through the Titiwangsa mountains) and operations expected January 1, 2027. The first CR200J passenger trains and HXD3CA freight locomotives began production at CRRC Dalian in November 2025. The ECRL's 20 stations include 10 combined passenger-freight stations and 3 interchange stations; it will reduce travel time from Kota Bharu to Kuala Lumpur from 8 hours by road to approximately 4 hours by rail. Malaysia signed its BRI MoU with China in 2016.

Name: Indonesia Nusantara New Capital City (IKN) Chinese Investment
Description: Indonesia's Nusantara New Capital City (Ibu Kota Nusantara, IKN) is the Indonesian government's ambitious $35 billion project to relocate the national capital from Jakarta to East Kalimantan on Borneo by 2045, and Chinese firms are among the most active investors in its construction and infrastructure under the BRI framework. The IKN project — formally established by Law No. 3 of 2022 and driven by President Joko Widodo — involves constructing a new purpose-built city of approximately 256,000 hectares, ultimately intended to house 1.9 million people, in a forested area in East Kalimantan. Chinese companies have secured or are pursuing multiple major contracts within IKN, including: China Railway Engineering Corporation (CREC) and China Communications Construction Company (CCCC) bidding on road and bridge infrastructure; Chinese solar and renewable energy firms contracted for IKN's smart city energy systems; Chinese conglomerate Powerchina and other SOEs engaged in land preparation and construction; and Huawei contracted to build IKN's digital backbone and smart city IT infrastructure. President Joko Widodo visited Beijing in July 2023 and secured Chinese investment commitments for IKN. China is Indonesia's largest trading partner and a leading investor in its manufacturing and infrastructure sectors. The IKN project also ties into broader Chinese BRI interest in East Kalimantan, which hosts significant Chinese nickel, coal, and palm oil investments. Indonesia signed its BRI MoU with China in 2018 and is the largest recipient of BRI investment in Southeast Asia, with Chinese-financed projects covering energy, metals processing, railways, and digital infrastructure.

Name: Kuwait Mubarak Al-Kabeer Port (CCCC)
Description: The Mubarak Al-Kabeer Port on Bubiyan Island is Kuwait's most significant infrastructure project in decades and the largest Chinese port construction contract signed in the Middle East in 2025. On December 22, 2025, Kuwait's Ministry of Public Works and China Communications Construction Company (CCCC) signed a $4.164 billion Engineering, Procurement and Construction (EPC) contract — confirmed by Kuwait's State Audit Bureau at 1.28 billion Kuwaiti dinars — for the first phase of the port. The signing ceremony was attended by Kuwaiti Prime Minister Sheikh Ahmad Abdullah Al-Ahmad Al-Sabah, senior cabinet ministers, and Chinese officials who described the project as a key pillar of the BRI's Maritime Silk Road. Bubiyan Island, located at the northern tip of the Arabian Gulf in Jahra Governorate, is currently largely uninhabited. The first phase involves construction of a 1,200-metre container terminal with an annual handling capacity of 2.7 million TEU. Phases 2 and 3 will add 14 further container berths, bringing total capacity to over 8 million TEU; all phases are targeted for completion by 2026. Kuwaiti officials noted that roughly 50% of Phase 1 had already been completed under earlier contracts, meaning the new $4.1B CCCC EPC contract covers completion of remaining marine and civil works. CCCC confirmed this will be its first Middle East port project partially constructed to Chinese standards from inception. The port is a centrepiece of Kuwait's Vision 2035 economic diversification strategy, designed to reduce oil dependency by establishing Kuwait as a regional commercial and logistics hub serving the underserved northern Gulf, including Iraq. Kuwait signed its BRI MoU with China in 2023.

Name: Sri Lanka Sinopec Hambantota Oil Refinery
Description: The Sinopec Hambantota Oil Refinery is Sri Lanka's largest-ever foreign direct investment and China's flagship BRI energy project in the Indian Ocean in 2025. In January 2025, Sri Lanka's Foreign Minister Vijitha Herath announced that both countries had signed an agreement to fast-track the $3.7 billion project; in October 2025, a delegation led by Sinopec Senior Vice President Lü Liang visited Colombo and reached an 'immediately launch' consensus with senior Sri Lankan officials. The refinery will process 200,000 barrels of crude oil per day and is to be located adjacent to the Hambantota Port — itself built and operated under a 99-year lease by China Merchants Port Holdings. The project is structured as foreign direct investment (FDI) rather than a loan, a deliberate departure from the debt-financed model that led to Hambantota Port's 2017 debt-for-equity swap and global scrutiny of BRI 'debt trap' dynamics. Key commercial terms agreed: Sinopec will sell up to 40% of refinery output on the domestic Sri Lankan market (up from the initially proposed 20%), with the remainder exported. The facility is expected to generate $6–8 billion in annual revenues and create tens of thousands of direct and indirect jobs. It incorporates advanced carbon capture and cleaner production technologies. Sri Lanka is entirely dependent on imported refined fuel costing billions annually; the refinery could meet approximately 20% of domestic needs while generating hard currency through exports. The refinery's proximity to Hambantota Port enables bunkering services that could transform the port into a genuine Indian Ocean logistics hub. Construction is expected to take approximately three years from groundbreaking. Sri Lanka signed its BRI MoU with China in 2017. According to the Griffith/GFDC BRI 2025 annual report, Sri Lanka saw a 1,590% surge in Chinese BRI engagement in 2025, largely attributable to the Sinopec deal.

Name: Kazakhstan East Hope Green Aluminum Industrial Complex
Description: The East Hope Group Green Aluminum Industrial Complex is the single largest Chinese BRI investment in Kazakhstan in 2025 and one of the biggest overseas industrial investments by a Chinese private company globally. China's East Hope Group — a private industrial conglomerate controlled by billionaire Liu Yongxing, ranking among China's wealthiest individuals — committed $12 billion to develop a vertically integrated 'green aluminum' industrial park in Kazakhstan, spanning the full production cycle from raw material extraction and alumina refining to electrolysis and aluminum processing. In 2025, Kazakhstan's Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov met with East Hope Chairman Liu Yongxing to finalise details. Phase 1 involves construction of an ore processing plant with annual capacity of 2 million tonnes of aluminum oxide and an electrolysis plant producing 1 million tonnes of aluminum per year. The 'green' designation refers to the use of renewable or low-carbon energy sources for the energy-intensive electrolysis process, reducing the carbon intensity of aluminum versus Chinese domestic production. The strategic logic is threefold: rising US tariffs on Chinese aluminum (raised from 10% to 25%) make direct Chinese exports less competitive, so producing in Kazakhstan allows Chinese firms to bypass tariffs and access US and EU markets; Kazakhstan offers strategic resource security with abundant bauxite and energy inputs; and China's domestic aluminum overcapacity makes overseas processing investment attractive. Kazakhstan was the single largest recipient of Chinese BRI investment in 2025, receiving $25.8 billion in total, of which East Hope's aluminum complex comprised the largest share. An additional $7.5 billion in Chinese copper investments was committed to Kazakhstan in 2025, making the country the dominant BRI destination by investment. Kazakhstan signed its BRI MoU in 2015.

Name: Nigeria LONGi Green Hydrogen & Methanol Complex
Description: The LONGi Green Hydrogen & Methanol Complex is one of the most ambitious Chinese renewable energy investment agreements globally in 2025 and Nigeria's largest-ever clean energy deal. In February 2025, Chinese solar power giant LONGi Green Energy Technology — the world's largest solar PV manufacturer — signed a preliminary €7.6 billion agreement (approximately $8.3 billion) with the Nigerian government to develop a giant green hydrogen-to-methanol complex in Nigeria. The facility is designed to produce approximately 1.2 million tonnes per year of green methanol — a transportable green fuel — from green hydrogen produced via electrolysis powered by Nigeria's abundant solar and wind resources. LONGi has secured a 10-year power purchase agreement, providing revenue visibility. The project is integrated with Nigeria's broader clean energy architecture: it aligns with Nigeria's 2023 Electricity Act, the Energy Transition Plan (targeting universal electricity access by 2030 and net-zero by 2060), and sits alongside Longi's role in advancing green hydrogen as a pathway for Nigeria to monetise its solar endowment rather than fossil fuels. The deal reflects a structural shift in BRI investment: LONGi is a private company, not a Chinese SOE, and its investment — along with those of CALB, East Hope Group, and Xinfa Group — marks the growing dominance of Chinese private sector firms in BRI engagement in 2025. According to the Griffith/GFDC BRI 2025 report, Nigeria was the top recipient of Chinese BRI construction contracts in 2025 ($24.6 billion), driven by the LONGi hydrogen deal and the Ogidigbon Gas Revolution Park. Nigeria signed its BRI MoU in 2018.

Name: Republic of Congo Yonghua $23B Oil & Gas Development (Banga Kayo / Holmoni / Cayo)
Description: The Congo-Yonghua $23 Billion Oil and Gas Development Agreement is the largest Chinese energy investment deal in Sub-Saharan Africa in 2025 and fundamentally transforms the Republic of Congo (Brazzaville)'s oil sector. In August 2025, the Republic of Congo's Minister of Hydrocarbons Bruno Jean-Richard Itoua, Minister of State Jean-Jacques Bouya, and Xiao Lianping, President-General of Southern Petrochemical Group Yonghua Company (also known as Wing Wah), signed a $23 billion agreement for the integrated development of three oil and gas permits: Banga Kayo, Holmoni, and Cayo. The agreement targets increasing Congo's national oil production from approximately 250,000 barrels per day to 200,000 barrels per day (from the three new blocks alone) by 2030, with cumulative production across the three permits targeted to exceed 1.3 billion barrels by 2050. Yonghua/Wing Wah has already established its presence in Congo through existing operations at Banga Kayo, which has approximately 237–250 wells drilled with current daily production of ~45,000 barrels. The new $23B agreement expands this via a revised Production Sharing Contract (PSC) framework. Beyond crude extraction, the deal emphasises comprehensive utilisation of associated gas to advance energy independence and eliminate routine flaring. It includes an integrated gas monetisation component — LNG, LPG, butane, and propane production capacity for both domestic use and exports — and a training centre to build Congolese workforce capacity and increase local content at all skill levels. This deal is distinct from the CMS's existing entry for Republic of Congo which covers historical Southern Petrochemical Group Yonghua operations at earlier-stage production. The 2025 $23B agreement represents the largest expansion of Sino-Congolese energy cooperation ever and is a core element of Congo's national economic and financial strategy. Congo signed its BRI MoU in 2015.

Name: Portugal CALB EV Battery Factory
Description: The China Aviation Lithium Battery (CALB) EV Battery Factory in Portugal is one of the largest Chinese manufacturing investments in the European Union in 2025 and a flagship BRI technology and manufacturing deal in Europe. CALB — China Aviation Lithium Battery Co., Ltd., a major Chinese EV battery manufacturer backed by state aerospace conglomerate AVIC and one of China's top-five lithium battery producers — committed $2.1 billion to construct an electric vehicle battery factory in Portugal. The investment was recorded as one of the top BRI technology-sector deals of 2025 H1 in the Griffith/GFDC BRI Investment Report. The facility reflects several converging strategic rationales: European Union rules of origin requirements for battery manufacturing (under the EU Battery Regulation and EU EV tariff frameworks) necessitate that batteries installed in EVs sold in Europe be substantially manufactured within the EU to qualify for preferential treatment; Portuguese labour costs and energy access are competitive for battery production; and Portugal's critical mineral supply — particularly its significant lithium reserves, among Europe's largest — provides potential upstream supply chain integration. The project aligns with China's broader BRI strategy of embedding Chinese technology and manufacturing into European value chains to circumvent trade barriers, a pattern also seen in CATL's Hungarian gigafactories (already in CMS). CALB's Portugal factory joins a growing cluster of Chinese battery investments in Europe (CATL in Erfurt/Debrecen, SVOLT in Germany) that collectively represent China's effort to secure European EV market access under local-content frameworks. Portugal signed its BRI MoU with China in 2018.

Name: Saudi Arabia Harbin Electric Rumah 2 & Nairyah 2 Gas Power Plants
Description: The Harbin Electric Rumah 2 and Nairyah 2 Gas Power Plants represent the largest Chinese EPC contract in Saudi Arabia's power sector in 2025 and a flagship BRI energy deal in the Gulf. In March 2025, Siemens Energy announced a $1.6 billion project in which Harbin Electric International Co., Ltd. — a subsidiary of Harbin Electric Group, a major Chinese state-owned power equipment and engineering company — serves as the Engineering, Procurement and Construction (EPC) contractor for the Rumah 2 and Nairyah 2 gas-fired combined-cycle power plants in Saudi Arabia. The two plants together add 3.6 GW to Saudi Arabia's national grid — equivalent to powering approximately 1.5 million homes. Located in the western and central regions of the Kingdom, these are among the world's largest combined-cycle gas power plants employing H-class and J-class gas turbine technology with efficiency exceeding 60% and hydrogen co-firing capability, positioning them for Saudi Arabia's long-term net-zero trajectory. The plants replace aging oil-fired generation, reducing CO₂ emissions by up to 60% compared to oil-based power. They include long-term maintenance agreements spanning 25 years. Siemens Energy supplies key turbine and technology components; Harbin Electric handles full EPC execution. The project sits within Saudi Arabia's Vision 2030 energy diversification programme and its ambitious targets to reduce domestic oil burn for power generation. Saudi Arabia was the third-largest recipient of Chinese BRI construction contracts in 2025 ($19.8 billion total engagement), with Harbin Electric's power plant deal among the most prominent. Saudi Arabia signed its BRI MoU with China in 2017.

Name: Egypt Xinyi Glass Solar PV Glass Production Base
Description: The Xinyi Glass Solar PV Glass Production Base is a $700 million Chinese private-sector BRI manufacturing investment in Egypt in 2025, representing a new model of Chinese industrial investment in North Africa — focused on high-tech export manufacturing rather than infrastructure or resource extraction. Xinyi Glass Holding Co., Ltd. — a major Chinese private-sector company and one of the world's largest glass manufacturers, known for float glass, solar PV cover glass, and automotive glass — committed $700 million to build a solar photovoltaic glass production facility in Egypt. The project was identified as one of the most notable BRI technology and manufacturing deals of 2025 H1 in the Griffith/GFDC BRI Investment Report. Solar PV cover glass is a high-volume, specialist product: each solar panel requires one sheet of ultra-clear tempered glass, creating enormous demand as global solar deployment accelerates. Egypt offers strategic advantages for this investment: low-cost natural gas as an energy input for glass manufacturing, low labour costs, geographic access to European and Middle Eastern solar markets, and Egypt's existing position as a major Chinese manufacturing investment destination. Egypt was the second-largest recipient of Chinese BRI investment in 2025 ($10.2 billion total), behind only Kazakhstan. The Xinyi facility complements existing Chinese BRI infrastructure in Egypt, particularly the Suez Canal Economic Zone (already in CMS), which hosts multiple Chinese industrial investments. Egypt signed its BRI MoU with China in 2016.

Name: Uganda Karuma Hydroelectric Power Station (Sinohydro/PowerChina)
Description: The Karuma Hydroelectric Power Station is Uganda's largest power plant, a flagship BRI project on the Victoria Nile, and the centerpiece of Uganda's energy transformation strategy. The 600 MW station is located in Kiryandongo District, approximately 270 km north of Kampala and 110 km downstream of Lake Kyoga, built across Karuma Falls on the Victoria Nile. The $1.7 billion project was financed 85% by China Eximbank ($1.44 billion) and 15% by the Ugandan government. Sinohydro Corporation Limited — a subsidiary of PowerChina — was awarded the EPC contract, selected by presidential directive in 2013. Construction began in August 2013. The power station features six underground turbine units of 100 MW each, housed in a cavern beneath the Nile riverbed, representing a technically demanding underground hydropower construction. Uganda Electricity Generation Company Limited (UEGCL) is the Ugandan state entity overseeing the project. The first turbine was connected to the national grid in October 2022; the sixth and final turbine was synchronized in February 2024, marking full 600 MW capacity. Annual power generation is approximately 4.07 billion kWh, expected to reduce Uganda's average electricity price by about 17.5% and eliminate chronic power shortages in Northern Uganda and West Nile regions. Karuma more than doubles Uganda's previously installed generation capacity and is expected to raise the country's total installed capacity to approximately 2,000 MW. The project is central to Uganda's 2040 development vision. However, it has generated controversy: reports of construction defects emerged alongside Uganda's start of loan repayments; concerns were raised about procurement irregularities, and a Senate hearing revealed Chinese contractors overstated costs. Uganda signed its BRI MoU in 2018.

Name: Philippines Kaliwa Dam / New Centennial Water Source (CEEC)
Description: The New Centennial Water Source – Kaliwa Dam Project is the Philippines' most significant Chinese BRI infrastructure commitment, designed to solve Metro Manila's chronic water supply shortage, which already affects over 18 million people. Metro Manila relies almost entirely on the Angat Dam in Bulacan, which was designed for a population of just 7 million. The Kaliwa Dam, straddling the Rizal–Quezon provincial boundary 60 km east of Manila in the Sierra Madre mountains, will create a 57 million cubic metre reservoir supplying 600 million litres of water per day to Metro Manila, Rizal, and Quezon provinces. The project involves a 60-metre concrete dam, a 27.7 km conveyance tunnel through the Sierra Madre, and two water treatment plants. Total project cost is approximately PHP 15.3 billion (~$255 million, after revision). Financing is 85% via a $211.2 million preferential buyer's credit from China Eximbank at 2% interest, 20-year maturity, 7-year grace period; the remaining 15% is provided by the Philippine government. The EPC contract was awarded to China Energy Engineering Corporation (CEEC), a Chinese state-owned firm, signed during Chinese President Xi Jinping's state visit to Manila in November 2018. Construction began in January 2020. As of December 2024, the project was 24.8% complete after repeated delays; NEDA approved a cost increase and extended the implementation period in April 2025, with the dam now expected to be operational in 2027. The project is contentious: the Dumagat and Remontado indigenous peoples, whose ancestral land the reservoir will flood, have sustained protests; environmental groups oppose forest clearing in the Sierra Madre; and the Commission on Audit flagged apparent irregularities in the bidding process. The Philippines signed its BRI MoU under President Duterte in 2018, though the Marcos Jr. government cancelled three BRI railway projects in November 2023 amid South China Sea tensions.

Name: Pakistan Diamer-Bhasha Dam (PowerChina/FWO)
Description: The Diamer-Bhasha Dam is Pakistan's largest and most strategically vital infrastructure project, and a defining test of BRI partnership: the world's tallest roller-compacted concrete (RCC) dam, rising 272 metres on the River Indus in Gilgit-Baltistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, 315 km upstream of the Tarbela Dam and 40 km downstream of Chilas. The project was first proposed in 1980 and approved in 2008, but languished for a decade without financing as the World Bank, ADB, and Western governments refused to fund it due to India's objection — the dam site falls within the disputed Kashmir region. Pakistan pivoted to China under CPEC/BRI. In May 2020, the construction contract was awarded to a joint venture of Power Construction Corporation of China (PowerChina) and Pakistan's Frontier Works Organization (FWO). Financing is provided by Pakistan's government through a domestic public financing model, supplemented by Chinese EPC capacity and technology. Installed hydropower capacity will be 4,500 MW (6 turbines of 750 MW each in two underground powerhouses), generating approximately 18,100 GWh annually — enough to supply a substantial share of Pakistan's entire electricity needs. The 10 billion cubic metre reservoir will provide 8.1 million acre-feet of water storage, supporting agriculture, drinking water, and flood mitigation; and is expected to extend Tarbela Dam's life by 35 years by reducing upstream sedimentation. The crest length exceeds 1 km and the reservoir will submerge 110 km of the Karakoram Highway, requiring full road realignment. At 272 m, the dam will set the world record for tallest RCC dam. Construction is expected to take approximately 9 years from 2020. The project has generated controversy over forced displacement of indigenous communities and destruction of Buddhist petroglyphs and inscriptions in villages to be inundated. Pakistan signed its BRI MoU in 2015 and CPEC is the BRI's most developed land corridor.

Name: UAE Masdar–Silk Road Fund Green BRI Renewable Energy Partnership
Description: The Masdar–Silk Road Fund Strategic Renewable Energy Partnership formalises the UAE's growing co-investment relationship with China's BRI in global clean energy, and is the most significant UAE-China BRI energy agreement to date. At COP29 in Baku, Azerbaijan in November 2024, Masdar (the Abu Dhabi Future Energy Company, owned by ADNOC, TAQA, and Mubadala) and the Silk Road Fund — China's $40 billion state-owned investment vehicle created specifically to support BRI projects — signed a Memorandum of Understanding committing the Silk Road Fund to invest up to 20 billion yuan (~$2.8 billion) alongside Masdar in renewable energy projects in BRI countries across the Middle East, Central Asia, Southeast Asia, and Africa. Masdar CEO Mohamed Jameel Al Ramahi and Silk Road Fund chairwoman Zhu Jun formalised the partnership, which Zhu Jun described as testament to both countries' commitment to 'the Green Silk Road.' Masdar has a global portfolio of 83 renewable energy projects in 40+ countries with 22 GW installed capacity, targeting 100 GW by 2030, and is already working with multiple Chinese energy companies including China Resources, PowerChina, and Huawei Digital Power. The Silk Road Fund's renewable portfolio already exceeds 7 GW in BRI regions. This partnership represents a structural shift in BRI energy investment: the UAE's sovereign clean-energy champion and China's principal BRI investment fund are jointly targeting the green energy transition in emerging markets, combining Masdar's project development experience with the Silk Road Fund's capital deployment firepower. The UAE has been an active BRI partner since signing its MoU with China in 2018, with a $10 billion China-UAE joint investment fund for BRI projects in East Africa previously established.

Name: Zambia Kafue Gorge Lower Hydropower Project (Sinohydro/HELI)
Description: The Kafue Gorge Lower Hydropower Project is Zambia's largest power infrastructure project in decades and one of Africa's biggest Chinese-financed hydropower developments, adding 750 MW to Zambia's national grid on the Kafue River in Southern Province. Zambia faces a severe electricity deficit — over 50% of the population lacks reliable grid access, and the country is prone to load-shedding crises exacerbated by droughts affecting existing Kafue Gorge Upper and Kariba hydropower stations. The Kafue Gorge Lower (KGL) station is built 4.5 km downstream of the existing Kafue Gorge Upper station, and connected to it via a shared penstock. The project was developed by ZESCO (Zambia Electricity Supply Corporation) in partnership with a consortium of Chinese companies led by Sinohydro and HELI China Overseas Engineering Group. China Eximbank provided $1.7 billion in financing (approximately 85% of the total project cost), with the Zambian government providing the remainder. Construction was contracted in 2015; the project was officially inaugurated and first power was generated in August 2021, with all five turbines (150 MW each) fully commissioned by 2022. The station features five underground Francis turbine generators and associated infrastructure including a 750 MW switchyard and transmission facilities. KGL increases Zambia's total installed hydropower capacity by roughly 40%, providing critically needed baseload power. However, the project contributed significantly to Zambia's debt distress: by 2020 Zambia became the first African country in the COVID era to default on its external debt, with Chinese loans (primarily from China Eximbank for energy projects including KGL) representing a major share. In 2023 Zambia reached a debt restructuring agreement under the G20 Common Framework, with China participating alongside Paris Club creditors to reduce and extend repayments. Zambia signed its BRI MoU with China in 2018.

Name: Ethiopia Addis Ababa Outer Ring Road (CCCC)
Description: The Addis Ababa Outer Ring Road is one of Ethiopia's most significant Chinese BRI urban infrastructure investments, a 43.6 km four-lane divided highway forming a full orbital ring around the Ethiopian capital Addis Ababa, connecting all the major radial roads leading out of the city. The project was financed by China Eximbank and constructed by China Communications Construction Company (CCCC) subsidiaries under a series of contracts. The ring road is divided into multiple sections and was developed across several phases from approximately 2012 onward, with later sections completed under BRI cooperation frameworks. The project is a core component of Addis Ababa's broader urban infrastructure upgrade, connecting the Bole International Airport road in the east with the Sululta industrial area to the north and Kaliti in the south, and linking to the Addis Ababa–Adama Expressway — itself a Chinese-built toll road. The ring road is designed to drastically reduce traffic congestion in Addis Ababa by allowing circumferential movement without passing through the city centre, and to support freight and logistics access to industrial parks (including the Chinese-built Eastern Industrial Zone at Dukem). With a population exceeding 5 million and among the fastest-growing cities in Africa, Addis Ababa's transport infrastructure was wholly inadequate before the ring road's construction. Associated projects include Chinese-built interchanges at key junctions and Chinese financing for the broader Addis Ababa Integrated Development Corridor. Ethiopia was the country with the fastest-growing BRI engagement in 2025 (+4,827% per the Griffith/GFDC BRI report), reflecting renewed Chinese infrastructure activity post-conflict. Ethiopia signed its BRI MoU with China in 2018.

Name: Colombia Puerto Antioquia (Antioquia Port Complex – CHEC)
Description: The Antioquia Ports Complex (Puerto Antioquia) near Turbo on Colombia's Gulf of Urabá, Caribbean coast, is one of the most significant Chinese BRI port investments in South America, designed to become Colombia and Northwestern South America's Pacific Gateway via a proposed overland corridor. The deep-water port was developed by a consortium featuring Chinese port operator China Harbour Engineering Company (CHEC, a CCCC subsidiary), which holds a significant equity stake. The Urabá region is Colombia's fastest-growing banana, palm oil, and industrial export corridor. Puerto Antioquia, inaugurated in 2022, can handle vessels up to Panamax class, operates container berths and bulk commodity terminals, and is linked to a highway connecting Turbo to Medellín (Antioquia's capital) and beyond. The Chinese strategic interest in Puerto Antioquia is its position as the Colombian entry point for a potential bioceánico route — a proposed road-rail corridor crossing the continent to Pacific ports such as Buenaventura or a new Pacific terminal, connecting Caribbean and Pacific trade flows. This mirrors Chinese interest in the proposed Nicaragua Canal and Peru's Chancay Port as components of a BRI trans-American connectivity strategy. Colombia signed its BRI MoU with China in 2023 under President Gustavo Petro, making it one of the most recent large Latin American BRI additions. Chinese companies have also been active in Colombian energy, mining, and telecommunications sectors.

Name: Iran Chabahar Free Trade Zone & Chinese Investment Programme
Description: The Chabahar Free Trade and Industrial Zone (CFTIZ) and Chinese Investment Programme represents China's most strategically significant BRI engagement in Iran, connecting the Persian Gulf, the Indian Ocean, and Central Asia at Iran's southeastern tip on the Gulf of Oman. Chabahar is Iran's only ocean port, located in Sistan-Baluchestan Province near the Pakistani and Afghan borders. Under the Iran–China 25-Year Comprehensive Strategic Partnership signed in March 2021 (already in CMS), China committed $400 billion over 25 years in infrastructure and energy investment in exchange for discounted oil supplies. The Chabahar CFTIZ is the centrepiece of the infrastructure component: Chinese investments have been directed at port expansion, oil refinery construction, petrochemical complex development, and the creation of a special economic zone for Chinese manufacturing and re-export. The Chinese interest in Chabahar is primarily strategic: the port provides access to the Indian Ocean without passing through the Strait of Hormuz, creates a logistics corridor to Central Asia (bypassing Pakistan's Gwadar), and enables China to circumvent US sanctions pressure by using Iran as a supply chain hub. Key Chinese firms include CNOOC (oil field development), Sinopec (refinery), and CCCC (port infrastructure). The CFTIZ is a 200 km² zone designed to attract Chinese industrial production and re-export activity. US sanctions complicate the scale of Chinese investment, as major Chinese banks risk secondary sanctions exposure; in practice, Chinese engagement has been more limited than the $400B headline figure suggests, but Chabahar remains one of the most geopolitically sensitive BRI nodes globally, particularly given competing Indian investment in the same port. Iran signed its BRI cooperation framework within the 25-Year Partnership in 2021.

Name: Nigeria Brass Industrial Park & Methanol Complex (CRBC/BFPCL)
Description: The Brass Industrial Park and Methanol Complex is a $3.3 billion Chinese-Nigerian joint venture on Brass Island in Bayelsa State, in the Niger Delta. The project was formalised on 4 September 2024 when the China Road and Bridge Corporation (CRBC) — a CCCC subsidiary — signed Project Agreements with Brass Fertilizer and Petrochemical Company Limited (BFPCL) for the Brass Industrial Park, Gas Gathering Pipelines and Associated Facilities, and the Methanol Complex Project. The agreements were signed on the sidelines of the 2024 Forum on China-Africa Cooperation (FOCAC) in Beijing, during President Tinubu's state visit to China. BFPCL is a joint venture between DSV Engineering Limited, the Nigerian National Petroleum Corporation (NNPC), and the Nigerian Content Development and Monitoring Board (NCDMB). The project site covers a 667.5-hectare plot at the eastern end of Brass Island, near the St. Nicholas River, bounded to the south by the Atlantic Ocean. The development includes: a gas supply network connecting gas fields, wells, and pipelines; a natural gas processing plant; a methanol production and refining facility targeting approximately 3,600 tonnes per day; product export terminals; and supporting utilities and infrastructure. Additional Chinese investors including Bohai Chemical Industries Group (BCIG) and the China Africa Development Fund (CADFund) committed to participate in the methanol project's financing. COSCO Shipping Lines Co. Ltd. signed a Shipping Vessels Acquisition and Joint Venture Agreement for 16 new 50,000 MT methanol-powered vessels (valued at approximately $900 million) to transport methanol globally. The Brass Oil and Gas City project, of which this is a component, had attracted $3.5 billion in total committed investment as of late 2024 and aims to position Nigeria as Africa's leading hub for petrochemical, fertilizer, refinery, and hydrocarbon processing. Construction is projected to create 30,000 direct and indirect jobs, with 5,000 permanent operations-phase jobs. Financial close was targeted for December 31, 2024. Nigeria signed its BRI MoU with China in 2018.

Name: Nigeria Port Harcourt–Maiduguri Eastern Railway Rehabilitation (CCECC)
Description: The Port Harcourt–Maiduguri Eastern Narrow Gauge Railway Rehabilitation and Reconstruction is Nigeria's most extensive rail infrastructure project, a $3.02 billion programme to rehabilitate, reconstruct, and extend the 1,443 km colonial-era narrow gauge (1,067 mm) railway running from Port Harcourt on the Atlantic coast of Rivers State to Maiduguri in Borno State in the far northeast, traversing 14 states. The project was groundbroken by President Muhammadu Buhari on 10 March 2021 in Port Harcourt. The EPC contract was awarded to China Civil Engineering Construction Corporation (CCECC) Nigeria Limited on 16 October 2020. Financing is 85% from a syndicate of Chinese financiers and 15% Nigerian government counterpart funding. The project rehabilitates and reconstructs the existing 1,443 km mainline and adds new branch lines to Owerri (Imo State) and Damaturu (Yobe State), extending the total network to approximately 2,044 km. Design speeds are 80–100 km/h for passenger trains and 60–80 km/h for freight. Associated components include the Bonny Deep Sea Port and a Railway Industrial Park in Port Harcourt, co-developed by Chinese partners. Track laying on the first Port Harcourt to Aba section (62.8 km) was completed by CCECC by January 2024; commercial passenger operations commenced April–May 2024; the section was formally handed over to the Nigerian Railway Corporation (NRC) in November 2024, with five-days-per-week services running. As of August 2025, the Aba–Enugu section (181 km) remained under construction with progress stalled due to funding gaps and security concerns. President Tinubu has repeatedly committed to completing the full Port Harcourt–Maiduguri corridor. The line spans Rivers, Abia, Imo, Enugu, Ebonyi, Anambra, Benue, Nasarawa, Plateau, Kaduna, Bauchi, Gombe, Yobe, and Borno states, reconnecting the southern seaports to the northern and northeastern hinterland.

Name: Nigeria Kano–Katsina–Jibiya–Maradi Railway (CCECC/Mota-Engil)
Description: The Kano–Katsina–Jibiya–Maradi Railway is a 284 km standard gauge railway connecting Kano, Nigeria's largest northern city, to Maradi, Niger Republic's second-largest city — the first cross-border rail link between the two countries. The Federal Executive Council approved the project in September 2020. A Memorandum of Understanding was signed with Mota-Engil Engenharia E Construcao Africa (MEECA) in January 2021 under what was described as the largest contract in the company's history ($1.8 billion). A formal groundbreaking took place in February 2021. The railway passes through Kano, Jigawa, and Katsina states before crossing into Niger Republic, traversing territory inhabited by over 80 million people. Infrastructure includes 80 overhead bridges, 34 railway bridges, 9 underpasses, 74 culverts, locomotive depots, freight yards, and integrated maintenance centres. It will transport approximately 9,300 passengers and 3,000 tonnes of freight daily. Financing is structured with 85% from a consortium led by the China Civil Engineering Construction Corporation (CCECC), with 15% from the Nigerian government alongside the African Development Bank (AfDB) and Africa Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank). Nigeria announced it had secured the full $1.3 billion in CCECC-led construction financing in March 2024. The AfDB separately committed $350 million in October 2024. In January 2025, China Development Bank released $254.76 million for the related Kano–Kaduna segment. President Tinubu announced a 2026 completion target; the Kano–Daura first section was targeted for 2025. Note: while CCECC leads financing (85%) and handles earthworks, Mota-Engil (Portugal) is the primary construction contractor. Niger's post-2023 coup political instability has complicated environmental and social studies on the Niger side of the border. Nigeria signed its BRI MoU with China in 2018.

Name: Nigeria Lekki Deep Sea Port (CHEC / China Development Bank)
Description: The Lekki Deep Sea Port is Nigeria's first deep-water container port and the largest by design capacity in West Africa, built by China Harbour Engineering Company (CHEC), a CCCC subsidiary, and financed by China Development Bank (CDB). Located in the Lekki Free Trade Zone on Lagos's Atlantic coastline, approximately 65 km east of the chronically congested Apapa and Tin Can Island ports, the port was officially inaugurated by President Muhammadu Buhari on 23 January 2023. Total project cost is approximately $1.5 billion. The port is operated as a joint venture: the Nigerian government holds 20% through the Nigerian Ports Authority and Lekki Port LFTZ Enterprise; Singapore-based Tolaram Group holds 30%; and CHEC/China-Africa Lekki Investment holds 45%, with 5% held by Lagos State. The port features a 16.5-metre draft channel capable of accommodating Ultra-Large Container Vessels (ULCVs), three container berths with 680 metres of quayside, 13 ship-to-shore gantry cranes, 24 rubber-tyred gantry cranes, and an annual designed capacity of 2.5 million TEU expandable to 4.5 million TEU. CDB described it as Nigeria's first deep-sea port at inauguration. The port is designed to end the diversion of West African cargo to rival ports in Togo (Lomé) and Morocco (Tanger Med), retaining trade revenues within Nigeria. In May 2025, Nigeria's Federal Executive Council approved a $652 million China Eximbank loan for the Lekki Port Access Road, linking the port directly to the Dangote Refinery and southern states to streamline logistics. The port is a centrepiece of the broader Lekki Free Trade Zone, which hosts Chinese industrial investment across manufacturing and petrochemical sectors. Nigeria signed its BRI MoU with China in 2018.

Name: Nigeria Super Grid Electricity Transmission Project (China Eximbank – Proposed)
Description: The Nigeria Super Grid Transmission Project is a proposed national electricity super grid for which Nigeria is in advanced negotiations with China's Export-Import Bank (China Eximbank) for a $2 billion concessional loan. The plan was confirmed on 7 October 2025 by Nigeria's Minister of Power, Adebayo Adelabu, who described it as 'part of plans to decentralise power generation in Nigeria' and to attract heavy commercial users back to the national grid after years of chronic instability. Nigeria's national electricity grid experienced dozens of partial or total collapses in recent years, with multiple blackouts recorded in 2024 alone, attributed to inadequate generation capacity, transmission constraints, and technical faults. The new super grid is designed to create a high-capacity transmission backbone linking multiple new generation sources — gas, solar, and wind — to industrial zones across eastern and western Nigeria, reducing dependence on the existing single-spine network managed by the Transmission Company of Nigeria (TCN). Nigeria's Federal Executive Council has already approved the financing framework. Talks with China Eximbank were described as 'progressing positively' as of October 2025 and reported by Bloomberg on 6 October 2025. The $2 billion loan, if finalised, would complement Nigeria's broader power sector reforms: electricity distribution company revenues rose 70% in 2024 following tariff adjustments for urban consumers, with further 41% growth projected to reach N2.4 trillion ($1.6 billion) in 2025, improving the sector's debt service capacity. Note: as of early 2026 this project remains at the financing negotiation stage and has not yet reached financial close or commenced construction. Nigeria signed its BRI MoU with China in 2018.

Name: Nigeria Lagos Blue Line Metro (CCECC / LAMATA)
Description: The Lagos Blue Line is Nigeria's first urban metro rail system and one of Sub-Saharan Africa's most significant Chinese-built urban transit projects, built by China Civil Engineering Construction Corporation (CCECC) — a subsidiary of China Railway Construction Corporation (CRCC) — for the Lagos Metropolitan Area Transport Authority (LAMATA). The Blue Line runs along the Lagos-Badagry Expressway corridor from Mile 2 on the mainland to Lagos Marina on Lagos Island, eventually extending 27 km to Okokomaiko. Phase 1 (13 km, 5 stations: Marina, National Theatre, Orile Iganmu, Suru Alaba, Mile 2) was formally commissioned by President Muhammadu Buhari on 24 January 2023 and opened for commercial passenger operations on 4 September 2023 by Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu. The line is fully electrified, running CRRC Dalian-built Class 210 trains based on Chinese Type B stock. Phase 1 cost approximately $1.17 billion, funded entirely by the Lagos State Government. The two-line Blue and Red system combined is estimated at $1.4 billion. In its first year of operation (ending September 2024) the Blue Line carried approximately 2 million passengers; as of September 2025 LAMATA reported a cumulative 5 million passengers. Frequency was increased from 54 to 72 daily services in August 2024. Phase 2 (Mile 2 to Okokomaiko, ~14 km) is under construction. A third Green Line (68 km, Marina to Lekki Free Trade Zone) was awarded to China Harbour Engineering Company (CHEC) and MOFI in September 2024, with construction commencing April 2025. Conceived as early as 1983 under Governor Jakande, the project was revived in 2002 by then-Governor Bola Tinubu and construction was awarded to CCECC in 2009 after a 2012 contract formalisation, making the 2023 opening more than a decade overdue. More than 2,000 Chinese workers were deployed on the project. Nigeria signed its BRI MoU with China in 2018.

Name: Nigeria Lagos Red Line Railway (CCECC / LAMATA)
Description: The Lagos Red Line is the second urban rail line in Lagos and Nigeria's first heavy rail suburban metro service, running 27 km from Agbado in Ogun State to Oyingbo in Lagos, sharing track with the Lagos–Kano Standard Gauge Railway. Like the Blue Line, construction was contracted to China Civil Engineering Construction Corporation (CCECC), with the contract awarded in 2021. The Red Line was inaugurated by Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu and President Tinubu in a ceremony on 29 February 2024, but regular commercial passenger services commenced on 15 October 2024. Phase 1 covers 27 km with 8 stations: Agbado, Iju, Agege, Ikeja, MMIA Domestic Airport, Oshodi, Mushin, Yaba, and Oyingbo. The Phase 1 construction cost is approximately $135 million. The line operates with Diesel Multiple Units (DMUs) sharing track with the NRC Lagos–Ibadan Railway, unlike the electric-powered Blue Line. It is operated under a 25-year concession by First Metro Infrastructure Limited (FMIL). Designed daily capacity is 250,000 passengers, scalable to 500,000. Phase 2 (Oyingbo to Marina, ~10.5 km, 3 additional stations including Ebute Metta, Iddo, and Ebute Ero) is currently under construction and will create an interchange with the Blue Line at Marina/National Theatre. The Red Line connects to the future Purple Line at Agege and will eventually link to MMIA International Airport. As of February 2025, the Red Line operated 9 services daily (5 morning, 4 evening), with a journey time of approximately 50 minutes end-to-end. The combined Blue and Red Lines represent the realisation of a 40-year Lagos transit vision, and make Lagos one of only a handful of Sub-Saharan African cities with operational metro rail. Nigeria signed its BRI MoU with China in 2018.

Name: Nigeria Eko Atlantic City – Land Reclamation (CCCC / South Energyx)
Description: Eko Atlantic City — officially the Nigeria International Commerce City — is Africa's most ambitious urban development project: a planned city of 10 km² built entirely on land reclaimed from the Atlantic Ocean, adjacent to Victoria Island in Lagos. China Communications Construction Group Ltd (CCCC) served as one of the primary marine dredging and landfill contractors for the land reclamation works, alongside Belgian firm DEME which carried out dredging operations from December 2009 to May 2019. The project is 100% privately funded by South Energyx Nigeria Limited, a subsidiary of the Lebanese-Nigerian Chagoury Group, in strategic partnership with the Lagos State Government (which acts as a facilitating partner but provides no direct financing). The project is not formally a BRI-financed development, but CCCC's role as a primary construction contractor places it within the broader ecosystem of Chinese construction engagement in Nigeria. The coastal defence centrepiece is the 'Great Wall of Lagos' — an 8.5 km rock revetment designed by Royal Haskoning to withstand 1,000-year storm waves — protecting the reclaimed land and adjacent Victoria Island from Atlantic Ocean surges. As of 2023, approximately two-thirds of the land (6.52 million m² of the planned 10 million m²) had been reclaimed, with 75 million m³ of sand deposited. When complete, the city will host 10 districts across 10 km², provide homes for up to 300,000 residents, and accommodate 200,000 daily commuters. Key developments include Eko Pearl Towers, the Rugby School Nigeria, the Eko Atlantic Free Zone (with 100% foreign ownership and zero withholding tax on dividends), and the new $537 million US Consulate General (groundbreaking 2024). The project originated in 2003 as a solution to severe coastal erosion at Bar Beach — which was losing 8–14 metres annually — and was formally launched in 2008. The land reclamation area is the 'sand-filled' site visible from aerial views of Lagos referenced in many international media and social media discussions of Nigerian development. Nigeria signed its BRI MoU with China in 2018.

Name: Zambia Sinomine Kitumba Copper Mine & Processing Plant
Description: The Sinomine Kitumba Copper Mine and Integrated Processing Plant is one of the most significant Chinese BRI mining investments in Zambia and Sub-Saharan Africa in 2025–2026, representing a landmark step in China’s strategy to secure upstream copper supply for its electric vehicle, renewable energy, and data centre industries. Located in the Mumbwa district of Zambia’s Central Province, the Kitumba project is an undeveloped open-pit copper deposit with a JORC-compliant mineral resource estimate of 27.9 million tonnes of copper-bearing material, holding a mining licence valid from November 2014 to November 2039. In March 2024, Beijing-based Sinomine Resource Group (SHE: 002738) — a leading Chinese minerals and mining company — invested $58.5 million to acquire a 65% controlling stake in the project vehicle, Sinomine Kitumba Minerals Company Limited. In December 2024, Sinomine approved a full project investment of $563 million (revised to approximately $600 million in subsequent disclosures) to develop a fully integrated open-pit mine, beneficiation plant, and copper smelter on site. Construction commenced with stripping operations (removal of surface soil and rock to expose the ore body) in April 2025, with copper production targeted for September–December 2026. The integrated facility will include: an open-pit mine; an ore beneficiation plant with annual raw ore processing capacity of 3.5 million tonnes producing copper sulfide and copper oxide concentrates; a copper smelter with annual production capacity of 60,000 tonnes of cathode copper and 110,000 tonnes of sulfuric acid as a by-product; a 100 MW solar power plant (of which a 50 MW Mumbwa phase is a near operational by 2026) to power operations and supply surplus electricity to Zambia’s national grid; community development infrastructure including roads, schools, and workforce training. Based on three-year average market prices, Sinomine projects annual profits of approximately $155 million once at full capacity, with a total investment payback period of 5.1 years including construction. Sinomine’s chairman Wang Pingwei has stated the company will accelerate construction and conduct additional exploration drilling to potentially expand the resource base. The project is part of Zambia’s broader copper expansion strategy: in 2025 Zambia’s mining sector grew from a -2.8% contraction to a 6.4% GDP growth rate, partly driven by ramping copper production. The Kitumba mine is projected to make a major contribution to Zambia’s stated goal of reaching 3 million tonnes of annual copper production by 2031. In a parallel announcement in December 2024, Sinomine also committed $223 million to build a rare metals recovery facility at its Tsumeb smelter in Namibia, creating a multi-metal recycling hub in South-Central Africa. Zambia signed its BRI MoU with China in 2018 and is the world’s seventh-largest copper producer.

Name: Nigeria Dangote Petroleum Refinery (Chinese EPC Contractors / XCMG)
Description: The Dangote Petroleum Refinery is the world's largest single-train oil refinery, the largest refinery in Africa, and one of the most consequential industrial projects on the continent in the 21st century — built on a 2,635-hectare site at the Lekki Free Trade Zone in Lagos, adjacent to the Dangote Fertilizer Plant and the Chinese-built Lekki Deep Sea Port. While the refinery is privately owned and funded — not a Chinese state BRI project — Chinese engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) contractors were indispensable to its realisation. Aliko Dangote, the refinery’s founder and Africa’s wealthiest person, explicitly credited Chinese contractors at the Africa Finance Corporation conference in Nairobi in April 2026: “The case between Africa and China is like where everybody abandoned you and somebody tells you, ‘Fine, you know what, let us partner with you.’ We will get credit lines from China and deliver on time.” At peak construction, 3,250 Chinese workers were deployed on site alongside over 30,000 Nigerians and 6,400 Indian workers, with Chinese firms handling significant EPC packages across the refinery’s processing units. The refinery was officially commissioned on May 22, 2023 by President Bola Tinubu; diesel and aviation fuel production began in January 2024; and Premium Motor Spirit (petrol) production commenced in September 2024. By February 2026 the refinery had reached its full nameplate capacity of 650,000 barrels per day (bpd), making it the world’s largest single-train refinery — surpassing every European single-site refinery and rivalling large US facilities — at a total construction cost of approximately $20 billion. The facility produces 50 million litres of Euro-V quality petrol and 17 million litres of diesel daily, as well as aviation fuel, LPG, and polypropylene. It has transformed Nigeria from a chronic importer of refined fuel into a net exporter: by 2025–2026 the refinery was supplying Ghana, Cameroon, Togo, Tanzania, and other African markets, as well as exporting to Europe and Asia, during the global fuel supply shock triggered by US-Israel military operations against Iran that disrupted flows through the Strait of Hormuz. In February 2026, Dangote signed a $400 million deal with China’s XCMG Construction Machinery for equipment to support the first phase of an expansion targeting 1.4 million bpd — which, if realised, would make it the world’s largest refinery by any measure, surpassing India’s Jamnagar complex (1.24 million bpd). In January 2026, Engineers India Limited renewed a $350 million contract as Project Management and EPCM Consultant for the expansion. In May 2025, Nigeria’s Federal Executive Council approved a $652 million China Eximbank loan for the Lekki Port Access Road directly connecting the Dangote Refinery to the deep-sea port, cementing Chinese infrastructure involvement in the refinery’s logistics chain.

Name: Rwanda Masaka Hospital Renovation & Expansion (Chinese Government Grant)
Description: The Masaka Hospital Renovation and Expansion Project is China's most significant healthcare infrastructure investment in Rwanda and one of the largest Chinese-funded hospital projects in Sub-Saharan Africa, officially handed over to the Rwandan government on August 28, 2026. Located in Kicukiro District, Kigali, the hospital was originally built by China in 2011 as a district hospital with 127 beds and a floor area of 6,398 m². The China-aided renovation and expansion project was launched in 2022, with a formal groundbreaking ceremony held on March 30, 2023, attended by Chinese Ambassador Wang Xuekun and Rwandan Prime Minister Dr. Edouard Ngirente. The project was designed by IPPR International Engineering and funded by the Chinese government as a grant — not a loan — under the Forum on China-Africa Cooperation (FOCAC) framework. Upon completion, the hospital's total floor area expanded from 6,398 m² to 56,957 m² — a nearly ninefold increase — and the number of beds rose from 127 to 837, making it the largest hospital in Rwanda by bed capacity. The facility now holds daily outpatient capacity of 2,000 visits and features 22 operating theatres, an outpatient and emergency building, a medical technology building, inpatient wards, paediatric and infectious disease departments, an administrative block, a helicopter pad, and a connecting corridor system engineered to accommodate the site's challenging terrain with a 32-metre height difference across the complex. A total of 13 buildings were constructed. The expanded hospital will become the new home of the University Teaching Hospital of Kigali (CHUK), which is expected to relocate to Masaka by end of 2026. Rwanda's Minister of Health Dr. Sabin Nsanzimana described it as the largest hospital in Rwanda, noting the previous largest had 500 beds. Prime Minister Ngirente said at the 2023 groundbreaking that upon completion Masaka would be 'a vital medical centre in the Great Lakes region and the biggest general and university teaching hospital funded by the Chinese government.' It can provide medical services to more than 300,000 local residents. Chinese Ambassador Gao Wenqi attended the August 28, 2026 handover ceremony alongside Rwandan Health Minister Nsanzimana. China dispatched its first medical team to Rwanda in 1982 and has had 22 medical teams and more than 270 Chinese doctors serve in Rwanda since. Rwanda signed its BRI MoU with China in 2018.

Name: UAE Abu Dhabi–Dubai High-Speed Rail (CSCEC / CHEC)
Description: The Abu Dhabi–Dubai High-Speed Rail is the UAE's most ambitious infrastructure project and the largest single BRI-linked construction contract awarded globally in the first half of 2026, with a total Phase 1 cost of $8 billion. The project is developed by Etihad Rail Mobility — a joint venture of UAE state-owned Etihad Rail and France's Keolis — and will deliver a 150 km dedicated high-speed line connecting Abu Dhabi's city centre (Al-Zahiyah) to Dubai (Al-Jaddaf), reducing journey time from the current 90 minutes by road to just 30 minutes by rail. Trains will operate at up to 320–350 km/h. Two major design-and-build EPC contracts for civil works and stations were awarded in February 2026. The Abu Dhabi section was awarded to a consortium led by UAE's National Projects Construction (NPC), with consortium partners Trojan Tunnelling (UAE), Kalyon (Turkey), and China State Construction Engineering Corporation (CSCEC); design by Jacobs Solutions (USA). The Dubai section was awarded to a consortium led by India's Larsen & Toubro, with China Harbour Engineering Company (CHEC — a CCCC subsidiary) as a key partner, alongside Wade Adams, Egis (France), and Surbana Jurong (Singapore). Physical construction commenced in August 2026 when Kalyon confirmed it had broken ground on its portion of the Abu Dhabi section, including an 11.2 km dual-bore tunnel and four stations. Rolling stock procurement is in late-stage negotiation with Siemens Mobility (Germany), Alstom (France), Hitachi (Japan), CRRC (China), and Talgo (Spain) for EMU sets capable of 350 km/h design speed. The line is scheduled for completion and opening in 2030–2031. The initial phase is the first of a planned network expansion to eventually include an inner-city Abu Dhabi loop, an Abu Dhabi–Al Ain link, a Sharjah connection, and further extensions. The UAE government projects the passenger rail network will contribute $39 billion to GDP over 50 years. CSCEC has extensive prior UAE rail involvement, having implemented Phase 1 of Etihad Rail's freight network. The Green Finance & Development Center identified this project as one of 32 BRI-linked projects globally with a value over $1 billion in H1 2026. The UAE signed its BRI MoU with China in 2018.

Name: Vietnam Ho Chi Minh City Metro Line 2 Ben Thanh–Tham Luong (China Railway Group)
Description: Ho Chi Minh City Metro Line 2 (Ben Thanh–Tham Luong) is the second urban metro line under construction in Vietnam's largest city, and a flagship BRI-aligned urban transit project featuring China Railway Group Limited as the primary EPC contractor. The line officially broke ground on January 15, 2026 in a ceremony attended by senior municipal and national government officials, marking one of four major infrastructure projects launched simultaneously in HCMC on that day. Phase 1 spans 11.3 km (9.3 km underground, 2 km elevated) with 11 stations (10 underground, 1 elevated at the Tham Luong terminus/depot), connecting the Ben Thanh central transit hub in District 1 — where it will interchange with the operational Metro Line 1 — to Tham Luong in District 12. Total Phase 1 investment is approximately $2.093 billion (VND 47.89 trillion), funded from HCMC's own public investment budget under special mechanisms approved via National Assembly Resolution 188. In March 2026, HCMC's Management Authority for Urban Railways (MAUR) confirmed the EPC contractor selection: a joint venture between Truong Hai Group Corporation (Thaco, Vietnam) and China Railway Group Limited (CREC, China), awarded an EPC contract worth $1.73 billion (VND 44.74 trillion) covering design, construction, equipment supply, and installation. The design consortium approved in 2025 includes Guangzhou Metro Design & Research Institute (China), Southern Transport Design Consultancy JSC, Port & Seafield Engineering Design Consulting JSC, and ARTELIA SAS (France). Construction is significantly more complex than Line 1: the underground section is triple the length, passing through soft waterlogged soil, old utilities, and densely built urban neighbourhoods. Rolling stock has not been finalised; as of April 2026, South Korean manufacturer Hyundai Rotem is in advanced talks. The line is expected to be operational by 2030, serving as a vital east–west axis connecting the city centre with northwestern districts. Phase 2 extensions will add sections from Ben Thanh to Thu Thiem and from Tan Binh to An Suong Bus Station. HCMC plans to build 255 km of metro lines by 2030 across eight priority lines. Vietnam signed its BRI MoU with China in 2017.

Name: Zambia Sinazongwe Coal Power Plant (Wonderful Group / Ziquan Group)
Description: The Sinazongwe Coal Power Plant is a proposed 300 MW (Phase 1) to 600 MW (Phase 2) coal-fired thermal power station in Sinazongwe District, Southern Province, Zambia, representing one of the most controversial Chinese-linked energy investments in Sub-Saharan Africa in 2026 — announced at a time when the BRI is otherwise pivoting toward green energy. The project was announced on June 1, 2026 via a deal signed between Chinese-owned Wonderful Group Services (a Singapore-registered entity with Chinese management) and ZCCM Investments Holdings Plc (ZCCM-IH), the Zambian government's state-owned mining investment arm. Under the agreement, ZCCM-IH committed $54.2 million for a 30% equity stake in the special purpose vehicle Ever Great Energy Company Limited (EGE), a subsidiary of Wonderful Group Services which holds the majority 70% stake. Engineering, Procurement and Construction will be executed on a turnkey basis by Ziquan Group (Singapore) Pte Limited, which has delivered thermal power projects in Zimbabwe, the Democratic Republic of Congo, and China. Phase 1 involves construction of a 300 MW coal-fired plant comprising two 150 MW units using circulating fluidised bed combustion (CFBC) boiler technology, a water treatment facility, and transmission infrastructure, at a total estimated cost of $451.7 million. Phase 2 will double capacity to 600 MW within five years of Phase 1 completion. A coal mine covering an 8,150-hectare site in Southern Province will also be developed to supply fuel for the plant. Wonderful Group's longer-term plan is to develop up to 900 MW of thermal generation capacity in Zambia. The project directly targets Zambia's critical electricity deficit: ZCCM-IH estimates the country's peak baseload generation shortfall at approximately 1,400 MW. Severe drought conditions impacting the Kariba and Kafue hydropower stations have caused repeated grid collapse and extended load-shedding across the country. The project requires approval from the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC) before financial close. The Green Finance & Development Center flagged this as a new coal project announced in June 2026 that still requires multiple approval steps before construction can proceed. Zambia signed its BRI MoU with China in 2018.

Name: Serbia Vožd Karadŕordе Expressway (Shandong Hi-Speed Group)
Description: The Vožd Karadŕordе Expressway is Serbia's largest Chinese infrastructure contract signed in 2026 and the most significant new Chinese-built road project in the Balkans, awarded to Shandong Hi-Speed Group on May 7, 2026 in a ceremony attended by Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić at Villa Mir in Belgrade. The total contract value is €1.3 billion ($1.5 billion), covering the design and construction of Sections 2 and 3 of the 125 km expressway (Phase 1), spanning 82.71 km from the Belosavci interchange near Belgrade's southern suburbs through Rača to Markovac in central Serbia, eventually linking Sumadija and Pomoravlje regions to Pan-European Corridor X. The road is named after Djordje Petrović Karadŕordе, leader of the First Serbian Uprising, who originated from the Sumadija region through which the road passes. Shandong Hi-Speed Group is a Chinese state-owned company with an established Balkans presence, having previously won a €138 million contract to build the New Belgrade Railway Station. Construction was scheduled to commence in July 2026, three years after the groundbreaking, with completion expected by 2029. The Chinese side has provided pre-financing, easing immediate budgetary pressure on Belgrade. When complete, the full 125 km Vožd Karadŕordе corridor will connect Belgrade's southeastern suburbs to the Pan-European Corridor X by 2035. The project is part of Serbia's 'Serbia 2035' development plan and reflects the deepening of China-Serbia infrastructure ties: as of 2022 the European Parliament notes China had invested €10.3 billion in Serbia's economy, including €8 billion in infrastructure loans. Other active Chinese infrastructure projects in Serbia include: the Budapest-Belgrade railway (CRCC), Bor copper mine upgrades (Zijin Mining), Pupin Bridge (China Road and Bridge Corp), Belgrade Ring Road sections, the Belgrade Metro, and the Kostolac B thermal power plant. Serbia joined the BRI in 2016. Ambassador Li Ming described the expressway as a vital component of the China-Serbia 'iron-clad friendship.'

Name: Ethiopia Ming Yang 8.4 GW Wind & Solar + Green Ammonia Complex
Description: The Ming Yang Smart Energy 8.4 GW Renewable Energy and Green Ammonia Complex is the world's largest single Chinese energy investment in Africa, and one of the largest private Chinese overseas investments ever made — a transformative project that positions Ethiopia as a global green energy hub while fundamentally reshaping the country's electricity mix. China's Ming Yang Smart Energy Group (SHA: 601615) — one of China's largest wind turbine manufacturers with 36+ GW of installed capacity globally — secured an investment licence from the Ethiopian Investment Commission (EIC) on May 11, 2026, following a preliminary agreement announced at the 'Invest in Ethiopia 2026' Forum. The project's initial announced value of $10 billion was revised upward to a total of $14.17 billion by the EIC by June 2026, comprising two phases. Phase 1 ($7.47 billion): development of 5.4 GW of wind power capacity across the South Omo, Afar, and Somali regions, plus 2.8 GW of solar PV capacity in the same regions, for a combined 8.4 GW of new renewable generation — which would roughly double Ethiopia's current total installed electricity capacity of approximately 5,200 MW (of which 97% is hydropower). Phase 2 ($7.3 billion): construction of green ammonia production facilities (using renewable electricity to produce green hydrogen, then combining with atmospheric nitrogen to produce green ammonia for fertiliser and industrial export markets); plus manufacturing facilities for electric power transmission equipment and wind turbine components, establishing a domestic clean energy manufacturing ecosystem in Ethiopia. Addis Ababa China Daily described Ming Yang's Ethiopia project as 'one of the largest private foreign direct investments in Ethiopia's history.' The Green Finance and Development Center flagged Ethiopia as the #1 BRI country for Chinese energy engagement in H1 2026 with $18.9 billion total BRI inflows, driven primarily by this deal. Africa as a whole received $33.5 billion in Chinese BRI investment in H1 2026 — making it the world's top BRI regional recipient for the first time in history. Ethiopia signed its BRI MoU in November 2018. As of 2024, 97% of Ethiopian electricity was hydropower; expanding to wind and solar directly reduces the country's extreme vulnerability to droughts impacting GERD and other Nile-fed facilities.

Name: Indonesia BYD Electric Vehicle Manufacturing Plant, Subang (West Java)
Description: The BYD Subang Electric Vehicle Manufacturing Plant is China's BYD Company Limited's first overseas electric vehicle assembly factory in Southeast Asia and a flagship BRI-linked private sector manufacturing investment, located in the Subang Smartpolitan industrial complex in Subang, West Java, Indonesia. BYD — the world's largest EV manufacturer by sales volume (surpassing Tesla in 2023) — committed $1.0–1.3 billion to develop the facility, which has a designed annual production capacity of 150,000 electric vehicles. Construction was substantially complete by mid-2026, with mass production expected to commence in Q3 2026. Trial production runs were underway by May 2026. Key milestones: On May 26, 2026, BYD shipped 130 vehicle production line stamping dies (approximately 2,489 tonnes) from Xiaomo International Logistics Port in Shenzhen to Jakarta aboard the Haoyang 1. BYD has obtained Indonesia's IKD (Incompletely Knocked Down), LCEV (Low Carbon Emission Vehicle), and manufacturing eligibility certificates. The plant produces right-hand-drive vehicles for the Indonesian domestic market and for export across ASEAN, the Middle East, and Africa, leveraging Indonesia's nickel resources (23% of global total) for battery cell integration within the Subang complex under a fully closed-loop industrial chain strategy. BYD has targeted a localisation rate of 50–60%, reducing production costs by over 30% versus imported vehicles. The plant is integral to Indonesia's strategy to become the dominant Southeast Asian EV and EV battery hub, capitalising on its position as the world's largest nickel producer. BYD's Indonesia manufacturing is complemented by CATL's $5.9 billion battery production facility in Karawang (see separate CMS entry). Indonesia signed its BRI MoU with China in October 2018.

Name: Indonesia CATL Integrated EV Battery Hub, Karawang (West Java)
Description: The Indonesia-CATL Integrated EV Battery Hub in Karawang, West Java is Southeast Asia's largest battery industry project, a $5.9 billion integrated electric vehicle battery complex combining nickel mining and processing, battery cell manufacturing, and battery recycling — and the flagship BRI industrial partnership between China and Indonesia. The project was officially groundbroken by Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto on June 29, 2025. The joint venture is structured between Indonesia Battery Corporation (IBC) — a consortium of four Indonesian state-owned companies including PT Aneka Tambang (Antam) and PT PLN — and a Chinese consortium led by CATL (Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. Ltd, the world's largest lithium battery manufacturer), Brunp Recycling, and Lygend Resources. The 3,000-hectare Karawang complex includes 18 associated infrastructure facilities, a dedicated seaport, and spans the full battery value chain from raw materials to finished EV battery modules. Initial lithium-ion battery production capacity is 6.9 GWh per year, scaling to 15 GWh as full operations are achieved. Commercial operations at the battery plant were expected to commence by end of 2026. The project creates up to 8,000 direct jobs. It is integral to Indonesia's strategy to capture value from its nickel dominance (the country holds the world's largest nickel reserves, essential for NMC lithium-ion batteries) rather than simply exporting raw ore. Indonesia had previously banned raw nickel ore exports in 2020 to force downstream processing investment. CATL's partnership with IBC is the largest Chinese battery sector investment in Southeast Asia and a centrepiece of BRI's new manufacturing and technology investment model. Indonesia signed its BRI MoU with China in 2018.

Name: Kazakhstan Sinopec Geo-Jade Gas Field Exploration ($3.9B)
Description: The Sinopec Geo-Jade Kazakhstan Gas Field Exploration Investment is a $3.9 billion upstream oil and gas exploration commitment by Sinopec's subsidiary Geo-Jade Petroleum to explore a new gas field in Kazakhstan, announced in H1 2026 and identified by the Green Finance and Development Center as one of the largest single BRI investment deals of the period. Sinopec Group's Geo-Jade Petroleum Corporation is one of China's major overseas oil and gas exploration subsidiaries, active across Central Asia, Africa, the Middle East, and the Americas. Kazakhstan holds approximately 1.5% of proven global oil reserves and significant natural gas reserves, with Chinese companies already deeply embedded in the Kazakh energy sector through previous investments including CNPC's stakes in the Kashagan and Aktobe fields. The new gas field exploration deal deepens China's strategic position in Kazakhstan's energy sector at a time when Kazakhstan is diversifying its oil export routes away from Russia (the existing Caspian Pipeline Consortium route to Novorossiysk has faced disruptions) toward alternatives including the Trans-Caspian pipeline to Azerbaijan and China via the Central Asia-China Gas Pipeline system. Kazakhstan was the #1 BRI investment destination in H1 2026 ($25.8 billion total), driven by the East Hope Group aluminium complex ($12 billion), Sinopec Geo-Jade gas exploration ($3.9 billion), and multiple copper mining investments totalling $7.5 billion. The Geo-Jade deal is part of China's broader strategy to secure energy supply chain resilience amid global trade disruptions. Kazakhstan signed its BRI MoU in 2015 and is China's most strategically important Central Asian energy partner.

Name: Egypt ZC Rubber Tyre Manufacturing Complex (Zhongce Rubber Group)
Description:
On September 2, 2026, China's Zhongce Rubber Group (ZC Rubber) — one of the world's largest tyre manufacturers, headquartered in Hangzhou since 1958 — signed a letter of intent with the Suez Canal Economic Zone (SCZONE) authority to build an integrated tyre manufacturing complex in the Sokhna Industrial Zone, on the Gulf of Suez southeast of Cairo. The signing was witnessed by Egypt's Minister of Investment and Foreign Trade, Mohamed Farid, and SCZONE Chairperson Mostafa Sheikhoun.

The project carries an estimated investment of $500 million and will occupy roughly 600,000 square metres, producing passenger-car and truck tyres in three planned phases.
